routine:
Learners coming from Level 3 will recognize every step. Level 4 changes four things: the audio is longer and closer to natural speech (some reductions), Talk Time gets 3 more minutes (15), the Read & Write block runs 7:15–7:30 every week, and the exit ticket is a 3-sentence answer with a reason, written in the last 5 minutes of that block.

A. Listen. What have Lucía and Ahmed both done? Circle.

a. ridden a horse and gone camping b. seen snow and run a race c. worked in a restaurant and eaten sushi

B. Listen again. Check ✓ True or False.

TrueFalse
1. Lucía has taken a class at this center before.☐☐
2. Lucía worked in a pizza restaurant in 2019.☐☐
3. Ahmed saw snow for the first time last winter.☐☐
4. Ahmed has ridden a horse.☐☐

C. Listen again. Write have, has, or did.

  1. ____________ you ever taken a class at this center?
  2. No, I haven't. But my sister ____________.
  3. ____________ you ever worked in a restaurant?
  4. Really? When ____________ you do that?

Hear it, say it

gonna = going to: "Tonight we're going to find things we have in common." • wanna = want to: "I want to go camping." You can say going to and want to. Say it: Have you ever seen snow? • I've never ridden a horse.

sections.title: Grammar
sections.html:
Read across. A reads from the left side. B answers from the right side. Choose one part from each column.

Grammar Box 1: Have you ever…? (sometime in your life)

QUESTION
Have you everworked in a restaurant?
Has she everseen snow?
Has he everlived in a big city?
→
ANSWER
Yes, I have.I've worked in two restaurants.
No, I haven't. / No, never.I've never worked in a restaurant.
Yes, she has.She's seen snow two times.
No, he hasn't.He's never lived in a big city.

Grammar Box 2: the details (simple past)

QUESTION
Have you everbeen to Chicago?
When did yougo there?
How wasit?
Did youlike it?
→
ANSWER
Yes, I have.I went there in 2022.
I wentlast summer. / in 2022.
It wasexciting. / a little boring.
Yes, I did. / No, I didn't.It was too cold!

Rule of thumb: sometime in your life, no time → have / has + past participle (I've seen snow). Add a time (in 2022, last year, when I was ten) → simple past (I saw snow last year).

Grammar Box 3: 20 verbs to know (verb → past → past participle)
be → was / were → beengo → went → gone / beenride → rode → riddentravel → traveled → traveled
do → did → donehave → had → hadrun → ran → runtry → tried → tried
drive → drove → drivenlive → lived → livedsee → saw → seenwin → won → won
eat → ate → eatenmake → made → madeswim → swam → swumwork → worked → worked
fly → flew → flownmeet → met → mettake → took → takenwrite → wrote → written

Regular verbs (live, work, travel): past participle = past form (-ed). • I've = I have. • She's lived = she has lived (not she is).

Grammar Box 4: Which one?

WHEN?EXAMPLE
have / has + past participlesometime in your life; no timeI've ridden a horse. She's never flown.
simple pasta finished time (in 2015, last year, when I was ten)I rode a horse in 2015. She flew to Texas last year.

Questions and answers

Q: Can I say I have seen snow in 2022?

A: No. With a finished time, use the simple past: I saw snow in 2022.

Q: Why eaten, not eat?

A: After have / has, use the past participle: Have you ever eaten sushi? Look at Box 3.

Q: How do I answer Have you ever…? short?

A: Yes, I have. or No, I haven't. or No, never. Then add a detail in the past: Yes, I have. I went there in 2022.

Practice A: Write the past participle.

  1. Have you ever ____________ sushi? (eat)
  2. I've never ____________ a horse. (ride)
  3. She has ____________ in three cities. (live)
  4. Have you ever ____________ in a plane? (fly)
  5. We've ____________ the ocean two times. (see)
  6. He's never ____________ a prize. (win)

Practice B: Circle the correct words.

  1. (Have / Did) you ever tried Thai food?
  2. I (went / have gone) to Texas last year.
  3. Have you ever seen the ocean? Yes, I (have / have seen).
  4. When (did you go / have you gone) there?
  5. She (has never / never have) eaten sushi.
  6. I (saw / 've seen) a famous person in 2023.

Common mistakes

✗ Don't say✓ Say
I have seen snow last year.I saw snow last year.
Have you ever eat sushi?Have you ever eaten sushi?
Yes, I have seen.Yes, I have. (+ a detail: I saw it in 2022.)
She have lived in two cities.She has lived in two cities.
I never have flown.I've never flown. / I have never flown.

Contrast tip (optional): Spanish has a similar form (¿Alguna vez has trabajado…?), but English never uses a finished time with it: I worked there in 2020 (not I've worked there in 2020). What does your language do?

lessons.teacher:
How to Use This Plan

You don't need to speak Spanish or any other language. Teach in English. Show, point, and gesture. Some Grammar pages have one short contrast tip, only where a common mix-up exists. Learners read it on their own. You never need to read, translate, or explain it.

Instructions: use the same short task words every week: Listen. Circle. Check. Write. Work with a partner. Work in a group. Ask a follow-up question. Give a reason. An optional Task Words page is at the back of the workbook for learners who want it.

Instruction rule: Model it (do it with one learner while everyone watches), check it (ask: "Do you ask or answer first? How many sentences do you say?"), then go. Say less, show more.

Grouping toolkit: Pairs: turn to a neighbor; with an odd number, make one group of 3. Groups: 3–4 learners. Inside–outside circles: the inner circle faces out, the outer circle faces in; the outer circle moves one person to the right each round. Mingle: everyone stands and talks to many classmates. The teacher joins a pair only if one learner is left over.

When a learner is stuck or speaks another language to you: (1) show it: the picture, a gesture, or the board; (2) give one more short English example; (3) point to the grammar box on their page; (4) a classmate can help for a few seconds, then back to English. You don't need to understand what classmates say to each other.

Three sentences, not one: in Level 4, every Talk Time answer and every exit ticket has about three connected sentences: the answer, a reason, and a detail or example.

Lesson 1 (Week 1): Have You Ever…?

At a glance

Objectives: learners can…

  • ask Have you ever…? and answer Yes, I have. / No, I haven't. / No, never.
  • say I've never… / She's lived… with have / has + a past participle
  • ask a follow-up in the simple past (When did you…? How was it?)
  • tell a classmate about one experience in 3 sentences (the experience, when, how it was)
  • write a short introduction email to the teacher (5–8 sentences)

Materials

  • Student Pages for Lesson 1 (print for the number expected + 3 spares)
  • Board and markers; tape for a timeline across the board
  • Name tags or folded paper and markers
  • Can-Do Self-Check page (in the workbook) and the baseline snapshot notes (see Teacher notes)
  • Listening: no recording yet. Read the listening script aloud (with a volunteer if you can), at a natural speed, two times.
  • Prep time: 15 minutes (read the plan; draw the "my life → now" timeline on the board; practice reading the listening script).

Key vocabulary (with pictures on the New Words page)

★ try (a new food) • ★ travel • ★ fly • ★ snow • ★ ocean • ★ mountain • ★ desert • ★ win a prize • ★ ride a horse • ★ run a race • go camping • see a famous person

Also: ever, never, in common, both, a goal, a tent, sushi, a 5K (a 5-kilometer race), exciting, boring.

Clock-time plan

Times are loose. If the listening or Talk Time runs long, take the time from Read & Write.

TimeStepMinGrouping (15 / 7–8)If running behind
6:00–6:08Opening Talk + Homework Check (+ welcome and orientation, 2 min)8Pairs (7 pairs + 1 trio / 3–4 pairs)One card only
6:08–6:15New Words (picture page) + pair game (+ My Words and the Task Words page)7Whole class, then pairsTeach the ★ words only
6:15–6:30Listening: play 1 (Task A), play 2 (Tasks B and C) + "Hear it, say it"15Individuals, then pairs checkDo Task C together on the board
6:30–6:45Grammar Q&A: Have you ever…? and the simple past for details + pair check15Whole class, then pairsSkip the pair check; Talk Time practices it
6:45–7:00BREAK15
7:00–7:15Talk Time: Find Someone Who Has… + Two True, One Invented (+ baseline snapshot, 5 learners)**15Mingle, then groups of 3 / one circle, then 2 groupsRound 1 only
7:15–7:25Read & Write: Meet Our Class + an email to the teacher (+ Can-Do Self-Check, 3 min)10Pairs read, then individual writingReading questions only; the writing becomes homework
7:25–7:30Exit Ticket + Homework5IndividualsNever skip

Skip order if you're running behind: (1) the Read & Write writing task (it becomes homework); (2) the pair check at the end of Grammar; (3) the second round of Talk Time. Never skip: the listening tasks, the grammar boxes and the mistakes table, and the exit ticket.

Attendance (15 → 7–8 → 5 or fewer): every step lists the sizes. With 5 or fewer, sit at one table and do Talk Time as one group (each person asks every other person 2 prompts). Late arrivals join any pair or group right away, and you show them the workbook after class.

Step by step

Step 1 · 6:00–6:08 · Welcome, orientation, and Opening Talk · 8 min

  • Grouping: pairs, the same partner for both parts. 15 learners: 7 pairs + 1 group of 3. 7–8 learners: 3–4 pairs. 5 or fewer: pairs, or one group with you.
  • Before class: write on the board: Welcome! Level 4 · 6:00–7:30 · Break 6:45 · Homework every week (15–20 minutes) and the question What did you do last weekend?
  • Opening Talk (5 min): learners open the Opening Talk page. A asks a card question; B answers in 3 sentences (the answer, a reason, a detail); A asks one follow-up. Switch after each card.
  • Model with one learner: you ask, "What did you do last weekend?" The learner answers. Help them add a reason and a detail: "I went to the park. I went because it was sunny. My kids played soccer." Then you ask a follow-up: "How was it?"
  • Then (3 min): Pairs fill in the box at the bottom of the Opening Talk page: the partner's name and one thing the partner did last weekend. Two or three pairs introduce their partner to the class: "This is Rosa. She went to a birthday party."
  • Welcome and orientation (2 min, first): say your name and write it on the board. Show the workbook: "This is your book for tonight. Every week has the same parts." Point to the times on the board. Say: "We speak English in class. It's OK to make mistakes. Mistakes help us learn." Give out name tags.
  • Late arrivals: join any pair as a group of 3.
  • If behind: one card only.

Step 2 · 6:08–6:15 · New Words · 7 min

  • Grouping: whole class, then pairs. Show the New Words page.
  • Do: point to each picture and say the word. Learners repeat once.
  • Show the hard words: ocean (a wave, very big water) vs. a lake; desert (hot, dry, sand); win a prize (first place, a trophy); ride a horse (sit on it). Mime fly, run a race, and ride.
  • Check meaning (1 min): ask "Is the ocean salty or sweet?" (salty) • "Is a desert hot and dry or cold and wet?" (hot and dry) • "Do you sleep in a tent when you go camping?" (yes).
  • Pairs (2 min): A says a word; B points to the picture and makes a sentence (I've seen the ocean. / I've never ridden a horse.). Switch. 15 learners: finish with a quick team round (3 teams; you say a clue, the first team with the word gets a point). 7–8: 2 teams. 5 or fewer: one team against the clock.
  • My Words: "Write any word you want in your language on the My Words page. It's your personal list. It's optional." Learners do it at home.
  • Show the two new pages (1 min): the My Words page (a personal word list, optional) and the Task Words page at the back (optional). Say: "These pages are for you. Use them if you want."
  • If behind: teach the ★ words only.

Step 3 · 6:15–6:30 · Listening + "Hear it, say it" · 15 min

  • Grouping: individuals, then pairs check. With 5 or fewer, check together as a group.
  • Before you listen (2 min): say: "This is the first night of an English class. Lucía and Ahmed meet. Then the teacher, Ms. Grant, gives them a job. Listen: what have they both done?"
  • Play 1 → Task A (the main idea). Pairs compare. Check together.
  • Read Tasks B and C together (1 min) so learners know what to listen for.
  • Play 2 → Tasks B and C. Pairs compare. Then show the answers (answer key).
  • "Hear it, say it" (3 min): Point to the script lines. gonna = going to: "Tonight we're going to find things we have in common." wanna = want to: "I want to go camping." Say: "People often say gonna and wanna. This listening uses going to and want to." Then practice the weak, short have (it sounds like "h'v"): Have you ever seen snow? and the contraction: I've never ridden a horse. The class repeats the two lines twice.
  • No recording yet: read the script aloud with a volunteer (about 2:06), at a natural speed, two times. The script says going to and want to. People often say gonna and wanna; learners only need to recognize those words. When the audio is ready, it plays the conversation once; press play again for play 2. A third play is fine if the class needs it.
  • If behind: do Task C together on the board, reading the lines yourself.

Step 4 · 6:30–6:45 · Grammar Q&A · 15 min

  • Grouping: whole class, then pairs. Show the Grammar page. The left side is the question. The right side is the answer.
  • Show it (2 min): draw a long line on the board: "my life → now." Put three X's on the line with no dates: "I've seen snow. I've run a race. I've never ridden a horse." Then write a date under one X: "I ran a race in 2023." Say: "No time → have + past participle. A time → simple past."
  • The boxes (5 min): Box 1: read across: Have you ever worked in a restaurant? → Yes, I have. / No, I haven't. Point out Has with he / she. Box 2: the follow-up in the simple past: When did you go there? → I went in 2022. How was it? → It was exciting. Box 3: read the 20 verbs together once; learners circle 5 they want to learn first. Box 4: which one? No time or a time.
  • Rule of thumb and Questions and answers (2 min): read the rule of thumb aloud. Read each Q and A; the class reads the right sentence after you.
  • Check questions: "I have seen snow in 2022. Right or wrong?" (wrong: I saw snow in 2022.) • "Have you ever eat sushi? Right or wrong?" (wrong: eaten) • "She's lived in three cities. She's = she is or she has?" (she has).
  • Practice A and B (3 min): learners write, then pairs check. Go over the answers. Read the Common mistakes table together: "Don't say… Say…".
  • Pair check (last 3 min): A asks Have you ever…? with a word from the New Words page. B answers Yes, I have + a past detail (I… in…), or No, never. A asks How was it? Switch. 15 learners: swap partners once. 5 or fewer: you join one pair.
  • If behind: skip the pair check. Talk Time practices it.

Break · 6:45–7:00 · 15 min

  • Write on the board: Have you ever…? → Yes, I have. I… (last year). / No, I've never… and When did you…? How was it?

Step 5 · 7:00–7:15 · Talk Time: Find Someone Who Has… + Two True, One Invented · 15 min

  • Model it first (1 min): take the sheet and ask one learner, "Have you ever flown in a plane?" When they say yes, ask two follow-ups: "When did you fly? How was it?" Write their name on your sheet. Say: "Two follow-ups. Then write the name."
  • Round 1 (7 min): Find Someone Who Has… (mingle). Learners stand with the Talk Time sheet and ask classmates. When someone says Yes, they ask two follow-ups in the past (When? Where? How was it?) and write the name and a short note. One name per classmate, then move on.
  • Round 2 (6 min): Two True, One Invented (groups). Each learner writes three sentences on the second Talk Time page: two true and one invented (I've… / I've never…). The others in the group ask follow-up questions and then guess the invented one.
  • 15 learners: whole-room mingle for round 1; then 5 groups of 3 for round 2.
  • 7–8 learners: mingle in one circle for round 1; then 2 groups for round 2.
  • 5 or fewer: one group. In round 1, each person asks every other person 2 prompts. Round 2 in the same group.
  • Every answer needs a reason; every partner asks a follow-up. Walk around and listen. Note 2 good sentences to praise and 1 common error for next week.
  • Baseline snapshot (during Talk Time): listen to about 5 learners for 1 minute each (a different 5 each week until you have heard everyone). For each one, note: 3 connected sentences? a follow-up question? any present perfect? Use the snapshot notes in the Teacher notes. This is not a test; don't tell learners a score.
  • If behind: round 1 only.

Step 6 · 7:15–7:25 · Read & Write: Meet Our Class + an email to the teacher (+ Can-Do Self-Check) · 10 min

  • Grouping: pairs read and answer; individual writing. With 5 or fewer, read the text aloud together.
  • Read (4 min): Learners read the three profiles on the Read & Write page. Say: "Read fast first. Then find the answers." Pairs answer questions 1–5 together.
  • Check (1 min): go over the answers (answer key).
  • Write (5 min): Learners write an email to you (5–8 sentences): who they are, two things they've done, one thing they've never done, and one goal for this class with a reason. Show the example email. Invented details are fine. Learners start in class and finish at home (Homework item 2).
  • Can-Do Self-Check (3 min, 7:22–7:25): read each line on the Can-Do Self-Check page aloud. Learners check one face for each line and write one goal. Collect it with the exit ticket. This page comes back in Weeks 8 and 15.
  • If behind: questions 1–5 only; the writing becomes homework.

Step 7 · 7:25–7:30 · Exit Ticket + Homework · 5 min · NEVER SKIP

  • Exit ticket (3 min): learners open the Exit Ticket page and answer in 3 sentences with a reason: Tell me about something you have done (or never done). Example on the board: I've ridden a horse. I rode one in 2015 on my uncle's farm. It was exciting, but I was scared because the horse was big. With 5 or fewer, a learner can say it to you first and then write it.
  • Collect the pages. After class, sort them into ✓ / almost / not yet. Start next week with 2 corrections on the board (no names).
  • Homework (2 min): open the Homework page. Do item 1 together (item 1: I / never / see / the ocean → I've never seen the ocean.). Say: "About 15–20 minutes. Finish your Read & Write writing at home."

Listening script (not recorded yet; about 2:06 when recorded; the conversation plays once, so press play again for the second listen)

Audio: the recording is coming soon. Until then, read the script aloud two times, with a volunteer if you can, at a natural, friendly speed. The script says going to and want to. People often say gonna and wanna; learners only need to recognize those words.

Narrator: Lesson one. It's the first night of an English class at a community center. Lucía and Ahmed meet before class.

Ahmed: Hi, I'm Ahmed. Is this seat free?

Lucía: Sure. I'm Lucía. Nice to meet you. Is this your first class here?

Ahmed: Yes, it is. Have you ever taken a class at this center?

Lucía: No, I haven't. But my sister has. What kind of work do you do?

Ahmed: I work at a warehouse. Have you ever worked in a restaurant?

Lucía: Yes, I have. I worked in a pizza restaurant in 2019. It was hard, but I liked it.

Ms. Grant: Good evening! I'm Ms. Grant, your teacher. Tonight we're going to find things we have in common.

Ms. Grant: Lucía and Ahmed, find two things you've both done.

Lucía: OK. Ahmed, have you ever seen snow?

Ahmed: Yes! I saw snow for the first time last winter. It was cold, but beautiful.

Lucía: Me too. I've seen snow two times. Have you ever ridden a horse?

Ahmed: No, never. I've never ridden a horse. Have you?

Lucía: Yes, I have.

Ahmed: Really? When did you do that?

Lucía: When I was ten, on my uncle's farm. OK, snow is one thing. Have you ever run a race?

Ahmed: Yes, I ran a 5k last year. I didn't win, but I finished!

Lucía: I've run a race, too. My company has a race every summer.

Ahmed: Great. So we have both seen snow, and we have both run a race.

Ms. Grant: Good job! Now, what have you never done, but you want to try?

Ahmed: I want to go camping. I've never slept in a tent.

Lucía: And I want to try sushi. I've never eaten it.

Narrator: That's the end of the listening.

Answer key

  • Listening Task A: b (seen snow and run a race).
  • Listening Task B: 1 False (No, she hasn't; her sister has) • 2 True • 3 True • 4 False (he has never ridden a horse) • 5 False (he didn't win, but he finished) • 6 True.
  • Listening Task C: 1 Have, 2 has, 3 Have, 4 did, 5 have, 6 has.
  • Grammar Practice A: 1 eaten, 2 ridden, 3 lived, 4 flown, 5 seen, 6 won.
  • Grammar Practice B: 1 Have, 2 went, 3 have, 4 did you go, 5 has never, 6 saw.
  • Talk Time: answers will vary.
  • Homework 1: 1 I've never seen the ocean. 2 Has she ever ridden a horse? 3 We've flown to Miami two times. 4 He went camping last summer. Homework 2 and 3: answers will vary. Homework 4: 1 went, 2 ate, 3 didn't work, 4 Did / watch, 5 was.
  • Read & Write B: 1 For six years. • 2 In a hospital kitchen. • 3 Because he drives a truck. • 4 He's never flown in a plane. • 5 She ran her first race (a 5K). • Writing (C): answers will vary.
  • Exit ticket: answers will vary. A good answer: "I've ridden a horse. I rode one in 2015 on my uncle's farm. It was exciting, but I was scared because the horse was big."

Teacher notes

  • Learners choose what to share. Places, foods, and jobs are always safe topics. Never ask how or when learners came to the U.S. Invented answers are fine in every activity.
  • The timeline: keep the "my life → now" line on the board all night. X's with no dates = present perfect; a date under an X = simple past.
  • Participles: learners don't need all 20 tonight. Ask them to circle 5 in Box 3 and learn those first. The list comes back in Lessons 2 and 3.
  • Baseline snapshot: for each learner you hear (about 5 tonight), note three things: (1) 3 connected sentences? (2) a follow-up question? (3) any present perfect? Keep the notes private. Hear everyone by Week 3. The same notes help in Weeks 8 and 15.
  • Can-Do Self-Check: the faces are 😀 I can do it, 🙂 with a little help, 😐 not yet. Read each line aloud. Keep the pages; learners compare in Week 8.
  • Spanish and other languages: the contrast tip on the Grammar page is optional. Learners read it on their own. You never need to read, translate, or explain it.
  • Reductions: the listening says going to and want to. People often say gonna and wanna. Learners only need to recognize the short forms; they can always say the full forms.

sections.title: Listening
sections.html:
Marisol is at a leasing office. She wants to rent an apartment. Mr. Chen helps her with the application.

A. Listen. What is Marisol applying for? Circle.

a. a job at a clinic b. an apartment c. a class at a bakery

B. Listen again. Complete Marisol's application. Circle the answers.

  1. How long at the current address: (two years / three years / since 2022)
  2. Previous address: (Elm Street / Lake Road / Parkview)
  3. Employer: (a bakery / Green Valley Clinic / Parkview Apartments)
  4. Position: (medical assistant / supervisor / baker)
  5. Start date: (March 5, 2022 / March 15, 2022 / June 1, 2022)
  6. Roommate: (yes / no)

C. Listen again. Write for or since.

  1. I've lived there ____________ two years.
  2. I lived there ____________ three years.
  3. ____________ March 2022.
  4. Before that, I worked at a bakery ____________ two years.
  5. She's known me ____________ I started.
  6. The lease is ____________ one year.

Hear it, say it

wanna = want to: "I want to fill out an application." • gonna = going to: "My mother is going to live with me." You can say want to and going to. Say it with a short for ("fer"): I've lived there for two years. • How long have you lived here?

sections.title: Grammar
sections.html:
Read across. A reads from the left side. B answers from the right side. Choose one part from each column.

Grammar Box 1: How long…? with for and since

QUESTION
How long have youlived here?
How long has sheworked at the clinic?
How long has heknown his supervisor?
→
ANSWER
I've lived herefor two years.
since 2024.
She's worked theresince March.
He's known hersince he started.

Grammar Box 2: still true or finished?

QUESTION
How long have youworked at the hotel?
How long did youwork at the bakery?
When did youmove here?
Did youuse to live with family?
→
ANSWER
I've worked theresince 2022. (still true)
I worked therefor two years. (finished)
I moved herein 2021. / five years ago.
Yes. I used to live with my cousins.Now I live with my mother.

Rule of thumb: still true now → have / has + past participle (I've lived here since 2020). finished → simple past (I lived there for three years). for + a length of time; since + a starting point.

Grammar Box 3: for or since?

for + a length of timesince + a starting point
for two years • for six monthssince 2020 • since March
for ten days • for a weeksince Monday • since last summer
for a long time • for 20 minutessince I was 18 • since I started

Grammar Box 4: Which one?

WHEN?EXAMPLE
have / has + past participleit started in the past and it is still true nowI've worked at the clinic since 2022.
simple pastit is finishedI worked at a bakery for two years.
simple past + in / agowhen it startedI moved here in 2021. / five years ago.

Questions and answers

Q: Can I say I live here since 2020?

A: No. Use the present perfect: I've lived here since 2020.

Q: For or since with March?

A: March is a starting point: since March. Three months is a length: for three months.

Q: I've worked or I worked at the bakery?

A: Do you work there now? Yes → I've worked there for two years. No → I worked there for two years.

Practice A: Write for or since.

  1. I've lived in this city ____________ 2021.
  2. She's worked at the clinic ____________ six months.
  3. We've had our car ____________ January.
  4. He's been a cook ____________ ten years.
  5. They've known each other ____________ they were kids.
  6. I've studied English ____________ a long time.

Practice B: Circle the correct words.

  1. How long (have you lived / do you live) here?
  2. I (worked / 've worked) at a bakery for two years. Then I changed jobs.
  3. She ('s had / has) her car since 2022.
  4. When (did you move / have you moved) here?
  5. I (moved / 've moved) here three years ago.
  6. He's lived here (since / for) last summer.

Common mistakes

✗ Don't say✓ Say
I live here since 2020.I've lived here since 2020.
I've lived here since three years.I've lived here for three years.
I've moved here in 2021.I moved here in 2021.
How long you have worked there?How long have you worked there?
I am here for two years. (still true)I've been here for two years.

Contrast tip (optional): Spanish says Vivo aquí desde 2020 (present tense). English uses have / has + past participle: I've lived here since 2020 (not I live here since 2020). What does your language do?

lessons.teacher:
How to Use This Plan

You don't need to speak Spanish or any other language. Teach in English. Show, point, and gesture. Some Grammar pages have one short contrast tip, only where a common mix-up exists. Learners read it on their own. You never need to read, translate, or explain it.

Instructions: use the same short task words every week: Listen. Circle. Check. Write. Work with a partner. Work in a group. Ask a follow-up question. Give a reason. An optional Task Words page is at the back of the workbook for learners who want it.

Instruction rule: Model it (do it with one learner while everyone watches), check it (ask: "Is it still true now? Is it a length of time or a starting point?"), then go. Say less, show more.

Grouping toolkit: Pairs: turn to a neighbor; with an odd number, make one group of 3. Groups: 3–4 learners. Inside–outside circles: the inner circle faces out, the outer circle faces in; the outer circle moves one person to the right each round. Mingle: everyone stands and talks to many classmates. The teacher joins a pair only if one learner is left over.

When a learner is stuck or speaks another language to you: (1) show it: the picture, a gesture, or the board; (2) give one more short English example; (3) point to the grammar box on their page; (4) a classmate can help for a few seconds, then back to English. You don't need to understand what classmates say to each other.

Three sentences, not one: in Level 4, every Talk Time answer and every exit ticket has about three connected sentences: the answer, a reason, and a detail or example.

Lesson 2 (Week 2): How Long Have You Lived Here?

At a glance

Objectives: learners can…

  • ask How long have you lived / worked…?
  • answer with for + a length of time and since + a starting point
  • choose the present perfect (still true) or the simple past (finished)
  • give an address, an employer, a position, and a start date on an application
  • write 5–8 sentences about how long you have done three things, with one used to

Materials

  • Student Pages for Lesson 2 (print for the number expected + 3 spares)
  • Board and markers; a timeline across the board ("2020 → now")
  • One copy of a real-looking blank rental application (optional; the Talk Time page works)
  • Index cards with times: 2020, March, six months, Monday, ten years, a long time, I was 18, three weeks
  • Listening: no recording yet. Read the listening script aloud (with a volunteer if you can), at a natural speed, two times.
  • Prep time: 15 minutes (read the plan; draw the timeline; write the time cards; practice reading the listening script).

Key vocabulary (with pictures on the New Words page)

★ application • ★ current address • ★ previous address • ★ employer • ★ position (job title) • ★ start date • ★ end date • ★ reference (a person) • ★ for (two years) • ★ since (2020) • roommate • lease

Also: apply, fill out, a leasing office, an agent, move in, a supervisor, a photo ID, a fee, refundable, a medical assistant, a mechanic.

Clock-time plan

Times are loose. If the listening or Talk Time runs long, take the time from Read & Write.

TimeStepMinGrouping (15 / 7–8)If running behind
6:00–6:08Opening Talk + Homework Check8Pairs (7 pairs + 1 trio / 3–4 pairs)One card only
6:08–6:15New Words (picture page) + pair game (+ My Words)7Whole class, then pairsTeach the ★ words only
6:15–6:30Listening: play 1 (Task A), play 2 (Tasks B and C) + "Hear it, say it"15Individuals, then pairs checkDo Task C together on the board
6:30–6:45Grammar Q&A: How long have you…? with for and since + pair check15Whole class, then pairsSkip the pair check; Talk Time practices it
6:45–7:00BREAK15
7:00–7:15Talk Time: Timeline Interviews + At the Leasing Office15Pairs, then groups of 3 / pairs, then 2 groupsRound 1 only
7:15–7:25Read & Write: A rental application + sentences about you10Pairs read, then individual writingReading questions only; the writing becomes homework
7:25–7:30Exit Ticket + Homework5IndividualsNever skip

Skip order if you're running behind: (1) the Read & Write writing task (it becomes homework); (2) the pair check at the end of Grammar; (3) the second round of Talk Time. Never skip: the listening tasks, the grammar boxes and the mistakes table, and the exit ticket.

Attendance (15 → 7–8 → 5 or fewer): every step lists the sizes. With 5 or fewer, sit at one table. Do Timeline Interviews as one group (each person interviews the person on their left), then pairs for the leasing office. Late arrivals join any pair right away and take the applicant (B) role.

Step by step

Step 1 · 6:00–6:08 · Opening Talk · 8 min

  • Grouping: pairs, the same partner for both parts. 15 learners: 7 pairs + 1 group of 3. 7–8 learners: 3–4 pairs. 5 or fewer: pairs, or one group with you.
  • Before class: write on the board: How long have you…? and Have you ever…?
  • Opening Talk (5 min): learners open the Opening Talk page. A asks a card question; B answers in 3 sentences (the answer, a reason, a detail); A asks one follow-up. Switch after each card.
  • Model with one learner: you ask, "Have you ever tried a new food?" The learner answers. Then you ask, "When did you try it? How was it?" Help them say 3 sentences: the experience, when, and how it was.
  • Homework Check (3 min): Pairs compare Homework item 1 (sentences with have / has + a past participle) and read one answer from item 3 to each other. Then they fill in the box on the Opening Talk page. Walk around. Write 2 common errors on the board (often I have seen it last year (→ I saw it last year) and a missing participle (I've never eat → eaten)) and correct them together. Also put up 2 corrections from last week's exit tickets.
  • Late arrivals: join any pair as a group of 3.
  • If behind: one card only.

Step 2 · 6:08–6:15 · New Words · 7 min

  • Grouping: whole class, then pairs. Show the New Words page.
  • Do: point to each picture and say the word. Learners repeat once.
  • Show the hard words: current address (now) vs. previous address (before); employer (the company) vs. position (your job title); start date and end date (point to two dates on the board); reference (a person who knows you at work; not family). Show for as a length (from one date to another) and since as a starting point (one date).
  • Check meaning (1 min): ask "Is your employer a company or a person?" (a company, usually) • "Can your mother be your reference?" (no, usually not) • "Is 2020 a length or a starting point?" (a starting point → since).
  • Pairs (2 min): A says a word; B points to the picture and makes a sentence (What's your current address? → It's four eighteen Elm Street.). Switch. 15 learners: finish with a quick team round (3 teams; you say a clue, the first team with the word gets a point). 7–8: 2 teams. 5 or fewer: one team against the clock.
  • My Words: "Write any word you want in your language on the My Words page. It's your personal list. It's optional." Learners do it at home.
  • If behind: teach the ★ words only.

Step 3 · 6:15–6:30 · Listening + "Hear it, say it" · 15 min

  • Grouping: individuals, then pairs check. With 5 or fewer, check together as a group.
  • Before you listen (2 min): say: "Marisol is at a leasing office. She wants to rent an apartment. Mr. Chen helps her with the application. Listen: what is she applying for?"
  • Play 1 → Task A (the main idea). Pairs compare. Check together.
  • Read Tasks B and C together (1 min) so learners know what to listen for.
  • Play 2 → Tasks B and C. Pairs compare. Then show the answers (answer key).
  • "Hear it, say it" (3 min): Point to the script lines. wanna = want to: "I want to fill out an application." gonna = going to: "My mother is going to live with me." Then practice the weak, short for (it sounds like "fer"): for two years • for three years, and link the words: How long have you lived here? The class repeats the two lines twice.
  • No recording yet: read the script aloud with a volunteer (about 1:46), at a natural speed, two times. The script says going to and want to. People often say gonna and wanna; learners only need to recognize those words. When the audio is ready, it plays the conversation once; press play again for play 2. A third play is fine if the class needs it.
  • If behind: do Task C together on the board, reading the lines yourself.

Step 4 · 6:30–6:45 · Grammar Q&A · 15 min

  • Grouping: whole class, then pairs. Show the Grammar page. The left side is the question. The right side is the answer.
  • Show it (2 min): draw a timeline: "2020 ———————→ now." Say: "I moved here in 2020. I still live here. I've lived here since 2020. That's six years. I've lived here for six years." Point to 2020 (since) and the whole line (for).
  • The boxes (5 min): Box 1: read across: How long have you lived here? → I've lived here for two years / since 2024. Box 2: still true or finished? I've worked at the hotel since 2022 (still true) vs. I worked at a bakery for two years (finished). Box 3: sort the time words. Box 4: which one?
  • Rule of thumb and Questions and answers (2 min): read the rule of thumb aloud. Read each Q and A; the class reads the right sentence after you.
  • Check questions: "I live here since 2020. Right or wrong?" (wrong: I've lived here since 2020.) • "since three years or for three years?" (for) • "I worked at a bakery for two years. Do I work there now?" (no).
  • Practice A and B (3 min): learners write, then pairs check. Go over the answers. Read the Common mistakes table together: "Don't say… Say…".
  • Pair check (last 3 min): Use the time cards. A picks a card and says it (March). B makes a sentence with for or since: I've lived here since March. Switch. 15 learners: swap partners once. 5 or fewer: you join one pair.
  • If behind: skip the pair check. Talk Time practices it.

Break · 6:45–7:00 · 15 min

  • Write on the board: How long have you lived / worked…? → I've… for (two years). / I've… since (2020).

Step 5 · 7:00–7:15 · Talk Time: Timeline Interviews + At the Leasing Office · 15 min

  • Model it first (1 min): ask one learner, "How long have you lived in this city?" When they answer, ask, "Where did you live before? How long did you live there?" Write the answers on the board on a timeline. Say: "Still true → have lived. Finished → lived."
  • Round 1 (7 min): Timeline Interviews (pairs). Learners mark 4 points on their own timeline on the first Talk Time page (moved to this city, started a job or class, a hobby, a phone or car). Then they interview a partner: How long have you…? Since when? and write 3 sentences about the partner.
  • Round 2 (6 min): At the Leasing Office (pairs). A is the agent and asks the questions on the role card. B is the applicant and answers (invented answers are fine). A fills in the application form. Then switch.
  • 15 learners: pairs for both rounds; rotate once between rounds.
  • 7–8 learners: pairs for both rounds; one rotation between rounds.
  • 5 or fewer: one group for round 1 (each person interviews the person on their left); pairs or one group of 3 for round 2.
  • Every answer needs a reason; every partner asks a follow-up. Walk around and listen. Note 2 good sentences to praise and 1 common error for next week.
  • If behind: round 1 only.

Step 6 · 7:15–7:25 · Read & Write: A rental application + sentences about you · 10 min

  • Grouping: pairs read and answer; individual writing. With 5 or fewer, read the text aloud together.
  • Read (4 min): Learners read the rental application on the Read & Write page and answer the questions. Say: "Read fast first. Then find the answers." Pairs answer questions 1–5 together.
  • Check (1 min): go over the answers (answer key).
  • Write (5 min): Learners write 5–8 sentences about how long they (or an invented person) have done three things, with for and since and one used to. Show the example. Invented details are fine. Learners start in class and finish at home (Homework item 2).
  • If behind: questions 1–5 only; the writing becomes homework.

Step 7 · 7:25–7:30 · Exit Ticket + Homework · 5 min · NEVER SKIP

  • Exit ticket (3 min): learners open the Exit Ticket page and answer in 3 sentences with a reason: How long have you lived in this city (or worked at your job)? Example on the board: I've lived in this city for four years. I moved here in 2022. I moved here because my sister lives here. With 5 or fewer, a learner can say it to you first and then write it.
  • Collect the pages. After class, sort them into ✓ / almost / not yet. Start next week with 2 corrections on the board (no names).
  • Homework (2 min): open the Homework page. Do item 1 together (item 1: she / work / at the hotel / ___ / March → She's worked at the hotel since March.). Say: "About 15–20 minutes. Finish your Read & Write writing at home."

Listening script (not recorded yet; about 1:46 when recorded; the conversation plays once, so press play again for the second listen)

Audio: the recording is coming soon. Until then, read the script aloud two times, with a volunteer if you can, at a natural, friendly speed. The script says going to and want to. People often say gonna and wanna; learners only need to recognize those words.

Narrator: Lesson two. Marisol is at a leasing office. She wants to rent an apartment, and Mr. Chen helps her.

Mr. Chen: Good afternoon. Welcome to Parkview Apartments. How can I help you?

Marisol: Hi. I'm here about the two-bedroom apartment. I want to fill out an application.

Mr. Chen: Great. Let's do it together. What's your current address?

Marisol: It's four eighteen Elm Street, apartment 3.

Mr. Chen: And how long have you lived there?

Marisol: I've lived there for two years.

Mr. Chen: OK. And your previous address?

Marisol: Before that, I lived on Lake Road with my cousins. I lived there for three years.

Mr. Chen: Why are you moving?

Marisol: My apartment is too small. My mother is going to live with me.

Mr. Chen: I see. Now, your job. Who's your employer?

Marisol: Green Valley Clinic. I'm a medical assistant.

Mr. Chen: How long have you worked there?

Marisol: Since March 2022. Before that, I worked at a bakery for two years.

Mr. Chen: And what day in March did you start at the clinic?

Marisol: March fifteenth.

Mr. Chen: Thank you. We also need one reference. Not a family member, please.

Marisol: Can I give my supervisor's name? She's known me since I started.

Mr. Chen: Sure, that's fine. And will you have a roommate?

Marisol: No, just my mother. When can we move in?

Mr. Chen: The apartment is ready on June first. The lease is for one year.

Narrator: That's the end of the listening.

Answer key

  • Listening Task A: b (an apartment).
  • Listening Task B: 1 two years, 2 Lake Road, 3 Green Valley Clinic, 4 medical assistant, 5 March 15, 2022, 6 no.
  • Listening Task C: 1 for, 2 for, 3 Since, 4 for, 5 since, 6 for.
  • Grammar Practice A: 1 since, 2 for, 3 since, 4 for, 5 since, 6 for.
  • Grammar Practice B: 1 have you lived, 2 worked, 3 's had, 4 did you move, 5 moved, 6 since.
  • Talk Time: answers will vary.
  • Homework 1: 1 She's worked at the hotel since March. 2 We've known our neighbors for five years. 3 He's had his car since 2023. 4 I worked at a bakery for two years. Homework 2 and 3: answers will vary. Homework 4: 1 used to, 2 used to, 3 use to, 4 didn't use to, 5 used to.
  • Read & Write B: 1 Since August 2023. • 2 For four years (2019–2023). • 3 City Bus Company. • 4 Ana Ruiz, his supervisor. • 5 He needs a bigger apartment for his family. • Writing (C): answers will vary.
  • Exit ticket: answers will vary. A good answer: "I've lived in this city for four years. I moved here in 2022. I moved here because my sister lives here."

Teacher notes

  • Learners choose what to share. Always ask about this city or this job, never this country. Never ask about income, rent, or immigration papers. Invented addresses and answers are fine in every activity.
  • The timeline: keep "2020 → now" on the board all night. The starting point = since; the length = for. Still true now → have lived; finished → lived.
  • Real forms: a rental application often asks for 3–5 years of addresses and a reference who is not family. Learners can write N/A (not applicable) when a line doesn't fit them.
  • Spelling and numbers: in the leasing office role play, the agent asks Can you spell that? Encourage learners to say street numbers in pairs: 418 = "four eighteen."
  • Spanish and other languages: the contrast tip on the Grammar page is optional. Learners read it on their own. You never need to read, translate, or explain it.
  • Reductions: the listening says going to and want to. People often say gonna and wanna. Learners only need to recognize the short forms; they can always say the full forms.

sections.title: Listening
sections.html:
It's the end of the evening shift at a grocery store. Ms. Rivera, the night supervisor, checks the work with Jamal and Kim.

A. Listen. Is all the work finished? Circle.

a. Yes, everything is done. b. No, two things aren't done yet. c. No, nothing is done yet.

B. Listen again. Look at the checklist. Circle done or not yet.

  1. restock the shelves: (done / not yet)
  2. put away the milk and the eggs: (done / not yet)
  3. clean the cooler: (done / not yet)
  4. check the bakery inventory: (done / not yet)
  5. clean the break room: (done / not yet)
  6. Kim's safety training: (done / not yet)

C. Listen again. Write already, yet, or just.

  1. Yes, I've ____________ restocked them.
  2. Has the truck arrived ____________?
  3. Yes, it's ____________ arrived.
  4. I haven't cleaned it ____________.
  5. I've ____________ finished it.
  6. We have ____________ put away the milk and the eggs.

Hear it, say it

gonna = going to: "I'm going to clean it before I clock out." • wanna = want to: "I want to finish it this week." You can say going to and want to. Listen for 's = has: It's just arrived. Say it with stress: I've JUST finished it. • I've alREADY restocked them.

sections.title: Grammar
sections.html:
Read across. A reads from the left side. B answers from the right side. Choose one part from each column.

Grammar Box 1: already / yet / just

QUESTION
Have youcleaned the break room yet?
Has the truckarrived yet?
Have theyrestocked the shelves yet?
Has shefinished the training yet?
→
ANSWER
Yes, I have.I've already cleaned it.
No, not yet.I haven't cleaned it yet.
Yes, it has.It's just arrived.
Yes, they have.They've already restocked them.
No, she hasn't.She's going to finish it on Friday.

Grammar Box 2: done → when? (simple past)

QUESTION
Have youfinished the orders?
When did youfinish them?
What have youdone this week?
→
ANSWER
Yes, I have.I've finished them.
I finished themat 3:00. / an hour ago.
I've checked the inventory,and I've cleaned the cooler.

Rule of thumb: already = done (maybe sooner than expected). yet = in questions and not sentences, at the end. just = a very short time ago. Add a time (at 3:00, yesterday) → simple past.

Grammar Box 3: word place

WORDWHERE?EXAMPLE
alreadybefore the past participleI've already cleaned it.
justbefore the past participleThe truck has just arrived.
yetat the end (questions and not)Have you finished yet? I haven't finished yet.
it / themafter the verbthe cooler → I've cleaned it. the shelves → I've restocked them.

Grammar Box 4: Which one?

WHEN?EXAMPLE
have / has + past participleit is done (or not done); no timeI've finished the orders. I haven't called her yet.
simple pasta finished time (at 3:00, yesterday, an hour ago)I finished the orders at 3:00.

Questions and answers

Q: Can I say I've finished it yesterday?

A: No. With a finished time, use the simple past: I finished it yesterday.

Q: Where does yet go?

A: At the end: Have you clocked out yet? I haven't clocked out yet.

Q: What does It's just arrived mean?

A: It's = it has. just = a very short time ago. The truck arrived a minute ago.

Practice A: Write already, yet, or just.

  1. Have you clocked out ____________?
  2. The truck arrived one minute ago. It has ____________ arrived.
  3. She hasn't restocked the shelves ____________.
  4. Has the supervisor given you feedback ____________?
  5. The deadline is Friday, but I've ____________ finished the training. It's only Monday!
  6. I can't talk now. I've ____________ clocked in, and I need to start work.

Practice B: Circle the correct words.

  1. I (haven't / didn't) cleaned the cooler yet.
  2. I (finished / 've finished) the inventory at 8:00.
  3. The shelves? Yes, I've restocked (them / it).
  4. (Has / Have) the truck arrived yet?
  5. The delivery (has just / just has) arrived.
  6. When (did you clock in / have you clocked in)?

Common mistakes

✗ Don't say✓ Say
I've finished it yesterday.I finished it yesterday.
I didn't finish yet.I haven't finished yet.
Have you yet finished?Have you finished yet?
I have already clean it.I've already cleaned it.
Has arrived the truck?Has the truck arrived?

Contrast tip (optional): Spanish ya can mean already (Ya terminé = I've already finished) and yet in questions (¿Ya terminaste? = Have you finished yet?). Todavía no = not yet. In English, yet goes at the end. What does your language do?

lessons.teacher:
How to Use This Plan

You don't need to speak Spanish or any other language. Teach in English. Show, point, and gesture. Some Grammar pages have one short contrast tip, only where a common mix-up exists. Learners read it on their own. You never need to read, translate, or explain it.

Instructions: use the same short task words every week: Listen. Circle. Check. Write. Work with a partner. Work in a group. Ask a follow-up question. Give a reason. An optional Task Words page is at the back of the workbook for learners who want it.

Instruction rule: Model it (do it with one learner while everyone watches), check it (ask: "Is it done? Did it happen a minute ago? Is it a question or a not sentence?"), then go. Say less, show more.

Grouping toolkit: Pairs: turn to a neighbor; with an odd number, make one group of 3. Groups: 3–4 learners. Inside–outside circles: the inner circle faces out, the outer circle faces in; the outer circle moves one person to the right each round. Mingle: everyone stands and talks to many classmates. The teacher joins a pair only if one learner is left over.

When a learner is stuck or speaks another language to you: (1) show it: the picture, a gesture, or the board; (2) give one more short English example; (3) point to the grammar box on their page; (4) a classmate can help for a few seconds, then back to English. You don't need to understand what classmates say to each other.

Three sentences, not one: in Level 4, every Talk Time answer and every exit ticket has about three connected sentences: the answer, a reason, and a detail or example.

Lesson 3 (Week 3): Have You Finished Yet?

At a glance

Objectives: learners can…

  • say what they've already done and what they've just done
  • ask Have you… yet? and answer Yes, I've already… / No, not yet.
  • put already, just, and yet in the right place
  • answer a supervisor's check-in questions in 3 sentences
  • write a reply email (5–8 sentences) about what is done and not done yet

Materials

  • Student Pages for Lesson 3 (print for the number expected + 3 spares)
  • Board and markers; a 5-line checklist drawn on the board
  • Talk Time Cards A and B (in the workbook); 3 check-in question cards per group (copy them from the Talk Time page onto index cards, optional)
  • A folder for each learner for the writing checks (Writing Check 1 is tonight)
  • Listening: no recording yet. Read the listening script aloud (with a volunteer if you can), at a natural speed, two times.
  • Prep time: 15 minutes (read the plan; draw the checklist; practice reading the listening script).

Key vocabulary (with pictures on the New Words page)

★ to-do list • ★ task • ★ checklist • ★ supervisor • ★ deadline • ★ restock • ★ inventory • ★ clock in • ★ clock out • ★ break room • ★ feedback • check-in (a short meeting)

Also: a shift, a delivery, put away, a cooler, an aisle, a time clock, a training, a reminder, a handoff, a coworker.

Clock-time plan

Times are loose. If the listening or Talk Time runs long, take the time from Read & Write.

TimeStepMinGrouping (15 / 7–8)If running behind
6:00–6:08Opening Talk + Homework Check8Pairs (7 pairs + 1 trio / 3–4 pairs)One card only
6:08–6:15New Words (picture page) + pair game (+ My Words)7Whole class, then pairsTeach the ★ words only
6:15–6:30Listening: play 1 (Task A), play 2 (Tasks B and C) + "Hear it, say it"15Individuals, then pairs checkDo Task C together on the board
6:30–6:45Grammar Q&A: already / yet / just with the present perfect + pair check15Whole class, then pairsSkip the pair check; Talk Time practices it
6:45–7:00BREAK15
7:00–7:15Talk Time: Shift Handoff + Check-in15Pairs, then groups of 3Round 1 only
7:15–7:25Read & Write: An email from a supervisor + a reply (Writing Check 1)10Pairs read, then individual writingReading questions only; the writing becomes homework
7:25–7:30Exit Ticket + Homework5IndividualsNever skip

Skip order if you're running behind: (1) the Read & Write writing task (it becomes homework); (2) the pair check at the end of Grammar; (3) the second round of Talk Time. Never skip: the listening tasks, the grammar boxes and the mistakes table, and the exit ticket.

Attendance (15 → 7–8 → 5 or fewer): every step lists the sizes. With 5 or fewer, do Shift Handoff in pairs (or one group of 3, taking turns), and in the Check-in you play the supervisor first. Late arrivals join any pair and take Card B.

Step by step

Step 1 · 6:00–6:08 · Opening Talk · 8 min

  • Grouping: pairs, the same partner for both parts. 15 learners: 7 pairs + 1 group of 3. 7–8 learners: 3–4 pairs. 5 or fewer: pairs, or one group with you.
  • Before class: write on the board: How long have you…? and for / since
  • Opening Talk (5 min): learners open the Opening Talk page. A asks a card question; B answers in 3 sentences (the answer, a reason, a detail); A asks one follow-up. Switch after each card.
  • Model with one learner: you ask, "How long have you lived in this city?" The learner answers with for or since. Then you ask, "Where did you live before? How long did you live there?" Help them say 3 sentences.
  • Homework Check (3 min): Pairs compare Homework item 1 (for / since sentences) and read one answer from item 3 to each other. Then they fill in the box on the Opening Talk page. Walk around. Write 2 common errors on the board (often I live here since 2020 (→ I've lived here since 2020) and since three years (→ for three years)) and correct them together. Also put up 2 corrections from last week's exit tickets.
  • Late arrivals: join any pair as a group of 3.
  • If behind: one card only.

Step 2 · 6:08–6:15 · New Words · 7 min

  • Grouping: whole class, then pairs. Show the New Words page.
  • Do: point to each picture and say the word. Learners repeat once.
  • Show the hard words: to-do list (things to do) vs. checklist (a list with boxes to tick ✓); restock (put more on the shelves); inventory (count what you have); clock in / clock out (start and end work; mime a time clock); deadline (the last day); feedback (what a supervisor says about your work); check-in (a short meeting).
  • Check meaning (1 min): ask "Is a deadline the first day or the last day?" (the last day) • "Do you clock in at the start or the end of your shift?" (the start) • "Is Great job! feedback?" (yes, positive feedback).
  • Pairs (2 min): A says a word; B points to the picture and makes a sentence (Have you clocked in yet? → Yes, I've already clocked in.). Switch. 15 learners: finish with a quick team round (3 teams; you say a clue, the first team with the word gets a point). 7–8: 2 teams. 5 or fewer: one team against the clock.
  • My Words: "Write any word you want in your language on the My Words page. It's your personal list. It's optional." Learners do it at home.
  • If behind: teach the ★ words only.

Step 3 · 6:15–6:30 · Listening + "Hear it, say it" · 15 min

  • Grouping: individuals, then pairs check. With 5 or fewer, check together as a group.
  • Before you listen (2 min): say: "It's the end of the evening shift at a grocery store. Ms. Rivera, the supervisor, talks to two workers, Jamal and Kim. Listen: is all the work finished?"
  • Play 1 → Task A (the main idea). Pairs compare. Check together.
  • Read Tasks B and C together (1 min) so learners know what to listen for.
  • Play 2 → Tasks B and C. Pairs compare. Then show the answers (answer key).
  • "Hear it, say it" (3 min): Point to the script lines. gonna = going to: "I'm going to clean it before I clock out." wanna = want to: "I want to finish it this week." Then practice hearing 's = has: It's just arrived (= it has just arrived), the weak have in Have you… yet?, and the stress: I've JUST finished it. • I've alREADY restocked them. The class repeats the two lines twice.
  • No recording yet: read the script aloud with a volunteer (about 1:53), at a natural speed, two times. The script says going to and want to. People often say gonna and wanna; learners only need to recognize those words. When the audio is ready, it plays the conversation once; press play again for play 2. A third play is fine if the class needs it.
  • If behind: do Task C together on the board, reading the lines yourself.

Step 4 · 6:30–6:45 · Grammar Q&A · 15 min

  • Grouping: whole class, then pairs. Show the Grammar page. The left side is the question. The right side is the answer.
  • Show it (2 min): draw a checklist on the board with 5 tasks. Tick two and say, "I've already restocked the shelves. I've already clocked in." Tick one now, in front of the class: "I've just cleaned the board." Point to an empty box: "I haven't checked the inventory yet."
  • The boxes (5 min): Box 1: read across: Have you cleaned the break room yet? → Yes, I've already cleaned it. / No, not yet. Box 2: add a time → simple past: I finished them at 3:00. Box 3: word place (already and just before the past participle; yet at the end). Box 4: which one?
  • Rule of thumb and Questions and answers (2 min): read the rule of thumb aloud. Read each Q and A; the class reads the right sentence after you.
  • Check questions: "I've finished it yesterday. Right or wrong?" (wrong: I finished it yesterday.) • "Where does yet go?" (at the end) • "It's just arrived. It's = it is or it has?" (it has).
  • Practice A and B (3 min): learners write, then pairs check. Go over the answers. Read the Common mistakes table together: "Don't say… Say…".
  • Pair check (last 3 min): A reads a task from the board checklist and asks Have you… yet? B answers Yes, I've already… / I've just… / No, not yet. Switch. 15 learners: swap partners once. 5 or fewer: you join one pair.
  • If behind: skip the pair check. Talk Time practices it.

Break · 6:45–7:00 · 15 min

  • Write on the board: Have you… yet? → Yes, I've already… / I've just… / No, not yet. I haven't… yet.

Step 5 · 7:00–7:15 · Talk Time: Shift Handoff + Check-in · 15 min

  • Model it first (1 min): hold up Card A and ask a learner to ask you, "Have you restocked aisle 3 yet?" Answer, "Yes, I've already restocked it." Then point to a task with no tick: "No, not yet. I'm going to do it before I clock out." Say: "Answer, then add one more sentence."
  • Round 1 (7 min): Shift Handoff (pairs, information gap). A looks at Card A; B covers it. B asks Have you… yet? about each task and ticks done or not yet in the notes. Then switch: A asks about Card B.
  • Round 2 (6 min): Check-in (groups of 3). The supervisor reads the 3 question cards. The worker answers with already and yet (invented answers are fine). The observer ticks each already / yet / just they hear. Rotate roles so everyone is the worker once.
  • 15 learners: pairs for round 1; then 5 groups of 3 for round 2.
  • 7–8 learners: pairs for round 1; then 2 groups for round 2 (the group of 4 has two workers).
  • 5 or fewer: pairs (or one group of 3) for round 1. In round 2, you play the supervisor first; then learners take turns.
  • Every answer needs a reason; every partner asks a follow-up. Walk around and listen. Note 2 good sentences to praise and 1 common error for next week.
  • If behind: round 1 only.

Step 6 · 7:15–7:25 · Read & Write: An email from a supervisor + a reply · 10 min

  • Grouping: pairs read and answer; individual writing. With 5 or fewer, read the text aloud together.
  • Read (4 min): Learners read the email from Sandra on the Read & Write page and answer the questions. Say: "Read fast first. Then find the answers." Pairs answer questions 1–5 together.
  • Check (1 min): go over the answers (answer key).
  • Write (5 min): Learners write a reply email (5–8 sentences): what they've already done, what they haven't done yet, when they'll finish it, and one question. Show the example. Invented details are fine. This is Writing Check 1: collect it. Learners start in class and finish at home (Homework item 2).
  • If behind: questions 1–5 only; the writing becomes homework.

Step 7 · 7:25–7:30 · Exit Ticket + Homework · 5 min · NEVER SKIP

  • Exit ticket (3 min): learners open the Exit Ticket page and answer in 3 sentences with a reason: What have you done this week, and what haven't you done yet? Example on the board: I've already paid my phone bill. I haven't done my laundry yet. I haven't done it because I worked late every night. With 5 or fewer, a learner can say it to you first and then write it.
  • Collect the pages. After class, sort them into ✓ / almost / not yet. Start next week with 2 corrections on the board (no names).
  • Homework (2 min): open the Homework page. Do item 1 together (item 1: you / finish / the checklist / yet? → Have you finished the checklist yet?). Say: "About 15–20 minutes. Finish your Read & Write writing at home."

Listening script (not recorded yet; about 1:53 when recorded; the conversation plays once, so press play again for the second listen)

Audio: the recording is coming soon. Until then, read the script aloud two times, with a volunteer if you can, at a natural, friendly speed. The script says going to and want to. People often say gonna and wanna; learners only need to recognize those words.

Narrator: Lesson three. It's the end of the evening shift at a grocery store. Ms. Rivera, the supervisor, talks to Jamal and Kim.

Ms. Rivera: OK, team, it's almost nine. Let's look at the checklist. Jamal, have you restocked the shelves yet?

Jamal: Yes, I've already restocked them. Those shelves are done.

Ms. Rivera: Great. And the delivery? Has the truck arrived yet?

Jamal: Yes, it's just arrived. Kim and I are putting it away.

Kim: We have already put away the milk and the eggs.

Ms. Rivera: Good. Kim, have you cleaned the cooler yet?

Kim: No, not yet. I haven't cleaned it yet. The delivery came late.

Ms. Rivera: That's OK. Are you going to have time tonight?

Kim: I think so. I'm going to start it after the delivery. It takes about twenty minutes.

Ms. Rivera: Perfect. Jamal, have you checked the bakery inventory?

Jamal: I've just finished it. I gave you the list at eight.

Ms. Rivera: Oh, right, I have it here. Thanks. And the break room?

Jamal: Not yet. I'm going to clean it before I clock out.

Ms. Rivera: OK. So the cooler and the break room aren't done yet. Everything else is done.

Kim: Ms. Rivera, have you seen the new training schedule yet?

Ms. Rivera: Yes, I've just seen it. The deadline for the safety training is Friday.

Kim: Thanks. I want to finish it this week.

Ms. Rivera: Good idea. And some quick feedback: you both did great work tonight. The shelves look really good.

Jamal: Thank you!

Kim: Thanks, Ms. Rivera. See you tomorrow.

Narrator: That's the end of the listening.

Answer key

  • Listening Task A: b (No, two things aren't done yet.).
  • Listening Task B: 1 done, 2 done, 3 not yet, 4 done, 5 not yet, 6 not yet.
  • Listening Task C: 1 already, 2 yet, 3 just, 4 yet, 5 just, 6 already.
  • Grammar Practice A: 1 yet, 2 just, 3 yet, 4 yet, 5 already, 6 just.
  • Grammar Practice B: 1 haven't, 2 finished, 3 them, 4 Has, 5 has just, 6 did you clock in.
  • Talk Time: answers will vary.
  • Homework 1: 1 Have you finished the checklist yet? 2 She hasn't clocked out yet. 3 The truck has just arrived. 4 We've already restocked the shelves. Homework 2 and 3: answers will vary. Homework 4: 1 them, 2 it, 3 them, 4 it, 5 them.
  • Read & Write B: 1 The evening team. • 2 By Thursday. • 3 Friday, May 16. • 4 On the computer in the break room. • 5 The new schedule. • Writing (C): answers will vary.
  • Exit ticket: answers will vary. A good answer: "I've already paid my phone bill. I haven't done my laundry yet. I haven't done it because I worked late every night."

Teacher notes

  • Keep work talk positive and invented. Learners never discuss real problems with real bosses or coworkers. Any job works in the role plays; invented answers are fine.
  • The board checklist: keep it up all night. A tick = already (or just, if you tick it now); an empty box = not yet.
  • Word place: teach already before the past participle. In speaking, I've cleaned it already is also common; accept it. yet always goes at the end.
  • 's = has: It's just arrived. She's already left. Ask: "is or has?" If a past participle comes next, it is has.
  • Writing Check 1: collect the reply emails. Write one strength and one fix on each (for example, the place of yet). Return them next week; learners keep them in a folder to see progress. No scores.
  • Spanish and other languages: the contrast tip on the Grammar page is optional. Learners read it on their own. You never need to read, translate, or explain it.
  • Reductions: the listening says going to and want to. People often say gonna and wanna. Learners only need to recognize the short forms; they can always say the full forms.

Amina is at a clinic for back pain. First, Daniel, the medical assistant, asks her health history questions. Then, at checkout, she talks to Ms. Park, the receptionist.

A. Listen. Why is Amina at the clinic? Circle.

a. for a flu shot b. for back pain c. for a teeth cleaning

B. Listen again. Complete Amina's form. Circle the answer.

  1. Symptom: (a rash / back pain / a cough)
  2. How long? (two days / about two weeks / since January)
  3. Back problems before? (yes / no)
  4. Allergy: (peanuts / penicillin / none)
  5. Dizzy? (yes / no)
  6. Copay today: ($10 / $20 / $40)

C. Listen again. Write for, since, or ever.

  1. I've had it ____________ about two weeks.
  2. Have you ____________ had back problems before?
  3. Have you ____________ had surgery?
  4. I've had it ____________ January.
  5. Also, you haven't had a teeth cleaning ____________ a year
  6. and you haven't had a checkup ____________ last spring.

Hear it, say it

gonna = going to: "The doctor's going to see you in a few minutes." • wanna = want to: "I want to make an appointment." You can say going to and want to. Say Why don't you…? as one smooth group, with your voice going down at the end: it's a suggestion, not a real question. Stress: I've had a RASH since MONday.

sections.title: Grammar
sections.html:
Read across. A reads from the left side. B answers from the right side. Choose one part from each column.

Grammar Box 1: How long…? / Have you ever…?

QUESTION
How long have youhad this rash?
How long has your backhurt?
Have you everhad surgery?
Have youtried anything for it?
→
ANSWER
I've had itfor three days.
since Monday.
It's hurtfor about two weeks.
No, never. / Yes, I have.I had knee surgery in 2018.
Yes, I have.I've used a heating pad.

Grammar Box 2: a problem → a suggestion

PROBLEM
My back hurts.What can I do?
I sit all day at work.Any ideas?
I haven't had a checkupfor two years.
My tooth has hurtsince Friday.
→
SUGGESTION
Why don't youcall the clinic?
You couldtake a short walk at lunch.
It's a good idea toget one every year.
You shouldsee a dentist soon.

Rule of thumb: Use have / has + past participle + for / since for a problem that started in the past and is still true. After Why don't you, You could, It's a good idea to, and should, use the base verb (call, try, get).

Grammar Box 3: how to say a symptom

SAYEXAMPLES
I have / I've had + a nouna rash, a cough, a backache, a sore throat → I've had a cough since Sunday.
My ___ hurts / has hurtMy back hurts. My tooth has hurt for a week.
I feel / I've felt + a worddizzy, tired → I've felt tired for three days.

Grammar Box 4: strong or soft?

HOW STRONG?EXAMPLE
You should…strong adviceYou should see a doctor.
It's a good idea to…a general idea (good for everyone)It's a good idea to get a flu shot every year.
Why don't you…? / You could…a soft idea; the person choosesWhy don't you try a heating pad? You could stretch.

Questions and answers

Q: Can I say I have a rash since Monday?

A: No. It started in the past and is still true: I've had a rash since Monday.

Q: Is Why don't you call the clinic? a real question?

A: No. It's a suggestion. Answer: Good idea. / Thanks, I will. Your voice goes down at the end.

Q: You could to try or You could try?

A: After could, use the base verb: You could try a heating pad.

Practice A: Write the correct form of the verb.

  1. How long have you ____________ the cough? (have)
  2. Why don't you ____________ the clinic? (call)
  3. I've ____________ dizzy since this morning. (feel)
  4. You could ____________ some easy stretches. (try)
  5. It's a good idea to ____________ a flu shot every year. (get)
  6. Have you ever ____________ surgery? (have)

Practice B: Circle the correct words.

  1. I ('ve had / have) a rash since Saturday.
  2. You could (try / to try) a heating pad.
  3. (Why don't you / Why you don't) call the dentist?
  4. My tooth has hurt (for / since) a week.
  5. I (had / 've had) knee surgery in 2018.
  6. It's a good idea (to get / get) a checkup.

Common mistakes

✗ Don't say✓ Say
I have a rash since Monday.I've had a rash since Monday.
You could to call the clinic.You could call the clinic.
Why you don't try a heating pad?Why don't you try a heating pad?
It's a good idea get a checkup.It's a good idea to get a checkup.
I've had surgery in 2018.I had surgery in 2018.

Contrast tip (optional): Spanish ¿Por qué no llamas a la clínica? = Why don't you call the clinic? It's a suggestion, not a real question, in Spanish and in English. But Spanish Tengo un sarpullido desde el lunes is I've had a rash since Monday in English, not I have. What does your language do?
