lessons.teacher:
How to Use This Plan

You don't need to speak Spanish or any other language. Teach in English. Show, point, and gesture. Some Grammar pages have one short contrast tip, only where a common mix-up exists. Learners read it on their own. You never need to read, translate, or explain it.

Instructions: use the same short task words every week: Listen. Circle. Check. Write. Work with a partner. Work in a group. Ask a follow-up question. Give a reason. An optional Task Words page is at the back of the workbook for learners who want it.

Instruction rule: Model it (do it with one learner while everyone watches), check it (ask: "Is it still true now? Is it a strong idea or a soft idea?"), then go. Say less, show more.

Grouping toolkit: Pairs: turn to a neighbor; with an odd number, make one group of 3. Groups: 3–4 learners. Inside–outside circles: the inner circle faces out, the outer circle faces in; the outer circle moves one person to the right each round. Mingle: everyone stands and talks to many classmates. The teacher joins a pair only if one learner is left over.

When a learner is stuck or speaks another language to you: (1) show it: the picture, a gesture, or the board; (2) give one more short English example; (3) point to the grammar box on their page; (4) a classmate can help for a few seconds, then back to English. You don't need to understand what classmates say to each other.

Three sentences, not one: in Level 4, every Talk Time answer and every exit ticket has about three connected sentences: the answer, a reason, and a detail or example.

Lesson 4 (Week 4): How Long Have You Had It?

At a glance

Objectives: learners can…

  • describe a symptom and say how long they've had it (for / since)
  • answer health history questions (Have you ever had…?)
  • make a suggestion with Why don't you…? / You could… / It's a good idea to…
  • find key information on an insurance card and a clinic letter (copay, deductible)
  • write an email to a friend (5–8 sentences) with suggestions and reasons

Materials

  • Student Pages for Lesson 4 (print for the number expected + 3 spares)
  • Board and markers
  • Symptom cards and problem cards (in the workbook Talk Time pages; copy them onto index cards, optional)
  • Optional: an old, blank clinic form or a sample insurance card (invented, no real names or numbers)
  • Listening: no recording yet. Read the listening script aloud (with a volunteer if you can), at a natural speed, two times.
  • Prep time: 15 minutes (read the plan; practice reading the listening script; draw a simple form on the board).

Key vocabulary (with pictures on the New Words page)

★ checkup • ★ health history • ★ symptom • ★ allergy • ★ blood pressure • ★ rash • ★ dizzy • ★ teeth cleaning • ★ cavity • ★ flu shot • ★ prescription • copay

Also: a medical assistant, a receptionist, a backache, a cough, a sore throat, a heating pad, a stretch, surgery, allergic to, an insurance card, a member ID, a deductible.

Clock-time plan

Times are loose. If the listening or Talk Time runs long, take the time from Read & Write.

TimeStepMinGrouping (15 / 7–8)If running behind
6:00–6:08Opening Talk + Homework Check8Pairs (7 pairs + 1 trio / 3–4 pairs)One card only
6:08–6:15New Words (picture page) + pair game (+ My Words)7Whole class, then pairsTeach the ★ words only
6:15–6:30Listening: play 1 (Task A), play 2 (Tasks B and C) + "Hear it, say it"15Individuals, then pairs checkDo Task C together on the board
6:30–6:45Grammar Q&A: Present perfect for health + suggestions + pair check15Whole class, then pairsSkip the pair check; Talk Time practices it
6:45–7:00BREAK15
7:00–7:15Talk Time: Clinic Intake + Good Idea Circle15Pairs back to back, then circles of 5Round 1 only
7:15–7:25Read & Write: A clinic letter + an insurance card; an email to a friend10Pairs read, then individual writingReading questions only; the writing becomes homework
7:25–7:30Exit Ticket + Homework5IndividualsNever skip

Skip order if you're running behind: (1) the Read & Write writing task (it becomes homework); (2) the pair check at the end of Grammar; (3) the second round of Talk Time. Never skip: the listening tasks, the grammar boxes and the mistakes table, and the exit ticket.

Attendance (15 → 7–8 → 5 or fewer): every step lists the sizes. With 5 or fewer, do Clinic Intake in pairs (you are a patient if there is an odd number), then one Good Idea Circle; you add problem cards. Late arrivals join a circle and suggest first.

Step by step

Step 1 · 6:00–6:08 · Opening Talk · 8 min

  • Grouping: pairs, the same partner for both parts. 15 learners: 7 pairs + 1 group of 3. 7–8 learners: 3–4 pairs. 5 or fewer: pairs, or one group with you.
  • Before class: write on the board: Have you… yet? and already / just
  • Opening Talk (5 min): learners open the Opening Talk page. A asks a card question; B answers in 3 sentences (the answer, a reason, a detail); A asks one follow-up. Switch after each card.
  • Model with one learner: you ask, "Have you done your laundry yet this week?" The learner answers with already or not yet. Then you ask, "When did you do it?" Help them say 3 sentences.
  • Homework Check (3 min): Pairs compare Homework item 1 (already / yet / just sentences) and read their to-do list (item 3) to each other. Then they fill in the box on the Opening Talk page. Walk around. Write 2 common errors on the board (often I've finished it yesterday (→ I finished it yesterday) and Have you yet…? (→ yet at the end)) and correct them together. Also put up 2 corrections from last week's exit tickets.
  • Late arrivals: join any pair as a group of 3.
  • If behind: one card only.

Step 2 · 6:08–6:15 · New Words · 7 min

  • Grouping: whole class, then pairs. Show the New Words page.
  • Do: point to each picture and say the word. Learners repeat once.
  • Show the hard words: checkup (a visit when you are well); health history (a form: your past illnesses, surgery, allergies); symptom (what you feel: a cough, a rash); allergy (I'm allergic to peanuts); blood pressure (mime the arm cuff: 120 over 80); dizzy (mime the room turning); teeth cleaning and cavity (a hole in a tooth); flu shot; prescription (paper from the doctor for medicine); copay (the money you pay at each visit).
  • Check meaning (1 min): ask "Do you get a checkup when you are sick or when you are well?" (when you are well; it's every year) • "Is a cough a symptom?" (yes) • "Do you pay a copay at the clinic or at home?" (at the clinic).
  • Pairs (2 min): A says a word; B points to the picture and makes a sentence (How long have you had the cough? → I've had it since Sunday.). Switch. 15 learners: finish with a quick team round (3 teams; you say a clue, the first team with the word gets a point). 7–8: 2 teams. 5 or fewer: one team against the clock.
  • My Words: "Write any word you want in your language on the My Words page. It's your personal list. It's optional." Learners do it at home.
  • If behind: teach the ★ words only.

Step 3 · 6:15–6:30 · Listening + "Hear it, say it" · 15 min

  • Grouping: individuals, then pairs check. With 5 or fewer, check together as a group.
  • Before you listen (2 min): say: "Amina is at a clinic. First, Daniel, the medical assistant, asks her some questions. Then she talks to Ms. Park, the receptionist. Listen: why is Amina at the clinic?"
  • Play 1 → Task A (the main idea). Pairs compare. Check together.
  • Read Tasks B and C together (1 min) so learners know what to listen for.
  • Play 2 → Tasks B and C. Pairs compare. Then show the answers (answer key).
  • "Hear it, say it" (3 min): Point to the script lines. gonna = going to: "The doctor's going to see you in a few minutes." wanna = want to: "I want to make an appointment." Then practice Why don't you…? as one smooth group with falling intonation (a suggestion, not a real question), and the stress: I've had a RASH since MONday. The class repeats the two lines twice.
  • No recording yet: read the script aloud with a volunteer (about 2:07), at a natural speed, two times. The script says going to and want to. People often say gonna and wanna; learners only need to recognize those words. When the audio is ready, it plays the conversation once; press play again for play 2. A third play is fine if the class needs it.
  • If behind: do Task C together on the board, reading the lines yourself.

Step 4 · 6:30–6:45 · Grammar Q&A · 15 min

  • Grouping: whole class, then pairs. Show the Grammar page. The left side is the question. The right side is the answer.
  • Show it (2 min): say, "I have a cough. It started on Sunday. Today is Thursday." Write: I've had a cough since Sunday. I've had it for four days. Then hold your back: "My back hurts." Point to a learner and help them say, "Why don't you call the clinic?" Write three suggestions on the board.
  • The boxes (5 min): Box 1: read across: How long have you had this rash? → I've had it for three days. and Have you ever had surgery? → Yes, I had knee surgery in 2018. Box 2: a problem → a suggestion. Box 3: how to say a symptom. Box 4: strong or soft?
  • Rule of thumb and Questions and answers (2 min): read the rule of thumb aloud. Read each Q and A; the class reads the right sentence after you.
  • Check questions: "I have a rash since Monday. Right or wrong?" (wrong: I've had a rash since Monday.) • "You could to try or You could try?" (You could try) • "Is Why don't you call? a real question?" (no, it's a suggestion).
  • Practice A and B (3 min): learners write, then pairs check. Go over the answers. Read the Common mistakes table together: "Don't say… Say…".
  • Pair check (last 3 min): A says a problem from Box 2. B gives a suggestion with Why don't you… / You could… A says, "Good idea." Switch. 15 learners: swap partners once. 5 or fewer: you join one pair.
  • If behind: skip the pair check. Talk Time practices it.

Break · 6:45–7:00 · 15 min

  • Write on the board: How long have you had it? → I've had it for… / since… • Why don't you…? / You could… / It's a good idea to…

Step 5 · 7:00–7:15 · Talk Time: Clinic Intake + Good Idea Circle · 15 min

  • Model it first (1 min): sit back to back with a learner. You are the medical assistant: "What brings you in today?" The learner reads a symptom card: "I have a rash on my arm." You ask, "How long have you had it?" Then switch: the learner asks you. Say: "Answer, then add one more detail."
  • Round 1 (7 min): Clinic Intake (pairs, back to back). A is the medical assistant and asks the 8 form questions; B chooses a symptom card and answers (invented answers). A writes short notes. Then switch, with a new card.
  • Round 2 (6 min): Good Idea Circle (circles of 5). One learner reads a problem card. The next two learners each give a suggestion. The first learner chooses one and says why: "Good idea. I'm going to… because…" Then the next learner reads a card.
  • 15 learners: pairs for round 1; then 3 circles of 5 for round 2.
  • 7–8 learners: pairs for round 1; then one circle for round 2.
  • 5 or fewer: pairs (you join if there is an odd number) for round 1. In round 2, make one circle; you add problem cards and suggest first.
  • Every answer needs a reason; every partner asks a follow-up. Walk around and listen. Note 2 good sentences to praise and 1 common error for next week.
  • If behind: round 1 only.

Step 6 · 7:15–7:25 · Read & Write: A clinic letter + an insurance card · 10 min

  • Grouping: pairs read and answer; individual writing. With 5 or fewer, read the text aloud together.
  • Read (4 min): Learners read the letter from the clinic and the insurance card on the Read & Write page and answer the questions. Point to copay and deductible on the card. Say: "Read fast first. Then find the answers." Pairs answer questions 1–5 together.
  • Check (1 min): go over the answers (answer key).
  • Write (5 min): Learners write an email to a friend (5–8 sentences). The friend has had a backache for a week. Ask how long, give two suggestions with reasons, and say what to bring to the clinic. Show the example. Invented details are fine. Learners start in class and finish at home (Homework item 2).
  • If behind: questions 1–5 only; the writing becomes homework.

Step 7 · 7:25–7:30 · Exit Ticket + Homework · 5 min · NEVER SKIP

  • Exit ticket (3 min): learners open the Exit Ticket page and answer in 3 sentences with a reason: A friend has had a backache for a week. What do you say? Example on the board: How long have you had it? Why don't you call the clinic? It's a good idea because a week is a long time. With 5 or fewer, a learner can say it to you first and then write it.
  • Collect the pages. After class, sort them into ✓ / almost / not yet. Start next week with 2 corrections on the board (no names).
  • Homework (2 min): open the Homework page. Do item 1 together (item 1: she / have / a rash / ___ / three days → She's had a rash for three days.). Say: "About 15–20 minutes. Finish your Read & Write writing at home."

Listening script (not recorded yet; about 2:07 when recorded; the conversation plays once, so press play again for the second listen)

Audio: the recording is coming soon. Until then, read the script aloud two times, with a volunteer if you can, at a natural, friendly speed. The script says going to and want to. People often say gonna and wanna; learners only need to recognize those words.

Narrator: Lesson four. Amina is at a clinic. First, she talks to Daniel, the medical assistant.

Daniel: Hi, Amina. I'm Daniel. I'm going to ask you a few questions for your health history. What brings you in today?

Amina: My lower back hurts. It isn't very bad, but it hasn't stopped.

Daniel: I'm sorry to hear that. How long have you had the back pain?

Amina: I've had it for about two weeks. It started when I moved some heavy boxes.

Daniel: OK. Have you ever had back problems before?

Amina: No, never. This is the first time.

Daniel: Have you ever had surgery?

Amina: Yes, I had knee surgery in 2018.

Daniel: Thank you. Do you have any allergies?

Amina: Yes, I'm allergic to penicillin. I get a rash.

Daniel: I'll write that down. Have you tried anything for the pain?

Amina: I've used a heating pad a few times. It helps a little.

Daniel: Have you felt dizzy?

Amina: No, I haven't.

Daniel: Good. Now let me check your blood pressure. It looks normal. The doctor's going to see you in a few minutes.

Narrator: Later, at checkout, Amina talks to Ms. Park, the receptionist.

Ms. Park: Hi, Amina. Your copay today is twenty dollars.

Amina: OK. Here's my new insurance card. I've had it since January.

Ms. Park: Thank you. Also, you haven't had a teeth cleaning for a year, and you haven't had a checkup since last spring. It's a good idea to get one every six months.

Amina: You're right. I want to make an appointment with the dentist.

Ms. Park: Why don't you call the dental office tomorrow? Here's the number. And you could get a flu shot here next week.

Amina: Good idea. Thank you!

Narrator: That's the end of the listening.

Answer key

  • Listening Task A: b (for back pain).
  • Listening Task B: 1 back pain, 2 about two weeks, 3 no, 4 penicillin, 5 no, 6 $20.
  • Listening Task C: 1 for, 2 ever, 3 ever, 4 since, 5 for, 6 since.
  • Grammar Practice A: 1 had, 2 call, 3 felt, 4 try, 5 get, 6 had.
  • Grammar Practice B: 1 've had, 2 try, 3 Why don't you, 4 for, 5 had, 6 to get.
  • Talk Time: answers will vary.
  • Homework 1: 1 She's had a rash for three days. 2 Why don't you call the dentist? 3 You could try a heating pad. 4 Has he ever had surgery? Homework 2 and 3: answers will vary. Homework 4: 1 already, 2 yet, 3 just, 4 yet, 5 already.
  • Read & Write B: 1 In March 2025. • 2 Every six months. • 3 Her insurance card, a photo ID, and a list of her medicines. • 4 $20. • 5 $1,000. • Writing (C): answers will vary.
  • Exit ticket: answers will vary. A good answer: "How long have you had it? Why don't you call the clinic? It's a good idea because a week is a long time."

Teacher notes

  • Keep health invented and mild. All patients and symptoms are invented. Never ask learners about their own health, medicines, or insurance. If a learner shares something, thank them and move on.
  • Real health questions: say, "For a real health question, ask your doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency, call 911." It is printed on the Good Idea Circle page.
  • Insurance: stay at "read the card; know copay and deductible." A copay is what you pay at each visit; a deductible is what you pay first in a year before the plan pays more. Don't explain plans or prices.
  • for / since: for + a length of time (three days); since + a start (Monday, January). With a finished time (in 2018), use the simple past.
  • Why don't you…? is a suggestion, not a real question. Model falling intonation. Learners answer Good idea or Thanks, I will, not Because….
  • Spanish and other languages: the contrast tip on the Grammar page is optional. Learners read it on their own. You never need to read, translate, or explain it.
  • Reductions: the listening says going to and want to. People often say gonna and wanna. Learners only need to recognize the short forms; they can always say the full forms.

sections.title: Listening
sections.html:
Patricia is going away for a week. First, she asks her older neighbor, Mr. Wilson, for some favors. The next day at work, her coworker Omar asks her for a favor.

A. Listen. What favors do they ask for? Circle.

a. get the mail, water the plants, feed the cat, and cover a shift b. borrow a ladder and switch shifts c. pick up a package and lend a car

B. Listen again. Yes or no, and why? Circle the answer.

  1. The mail: Mr. Wilson says (yes / no).
  2. The plants: water them on (Tuesday and Friday / Monday and Thursday).
  3. The key: Patricia will give him (her spare key / her car key) tonight.
  4. The packages: Mr. Wilson can put them (inside / at the office).
  5. The Saturday shift: Patricia says (yes / no).
  6. Why? She (will be away / has a soccer game).

C. Listen again. Write the missing word: an -ing word or if.

  1. Would you mind ____________ my mail?
  2. And would you mind ____________ my plants?
  3. Oh, and would you mind ____________ my cat, too?
  4. Do you mind ____________ I put your packages inside, too?
  5. Would you mind ____________ my Saturday shift?
  6. Do you mind ____________ I tell her you suggested it?

Hear it, say it

gonna = going to: "I'm going to be away next week." • wanna = want to: "I want to help, but I can't." You can say going to and want to. Say Would you mind…? and Do you mind if I…? smoothly, with a friendly rise at the end. Answer with a thumbs-up: No, not at all!

sections.title: Grammar
sections.html:
Read across. A reads from the left side. B answers from the right side. Choose one part from each column.

Grammar Box 1: Would you mind + -ing?

QUESTION
Would you mindgetting my mail?
Would you mindcovering my shift?
Would you mindlending me a ladder?
→
ANSWER
No, not at all.I'll do it.
Sorry, I can't.I'll be away too.
No, not at all.I'm free on Saturday.
No problem.You can borrow mine.

Grammar Box 2: permission: Do you mind if I…?

QUESTION
Do you mind if Iopen the window?
Do you mind if Ileave early today?
Do you mind if Iswitch my Friday shift?
→
ANSWER
No, go ahead.It's hot in here.
Sorry,we need you until 5:00.
No, not at all.Ask the supervisor first.

Rule of thumb: After Would you mind, use -ing (getting, covering). After Do you mind if I, use the base verb (open, leave). The answer No means "No problem. I'll help." / "Yes, you can."

Grammar Box 3: saying yes, saying no

YOU CAN HELP (say no!)YOU CAN'T HELP (be polite)
No, not at all. • No problem. • Sure, I'll do it.Sorry, I can't, because… + another idea: Why don't you ask Lina?

Grammar Box 4: how polite?

WHEN?EXAMPLE
Can you…?a small favor, a friendCan you pass the salt?
Could you…?more politeCould you help me with this box?
Would you mind …ing?the most polite; a bigger favorWould you mind feeding my cat for a week?

Questions and answers

Q: Someone asks Would you mind helping me? I want to help. Do I say yes?

A: No! Say No, not at all. Mind asks "Is it a problem?" No = no problem.

Q: Would you mind to get or Would you mind getting?

A: After mind, use -ing: Would you mind getting my mail?

Q: How do I say no politely?

A: Say sorry, give a reason, and offer an idea: Sorry, I can't. I'll be away. Why don't you ask Lina?

Practice A: Write the correct form of the verb.

  1. Would you mind ____________ my plants? (water)
  2. Do you mind if I ____________ the window? (open)
  3. Would you mind ____________ the cat on Sunday? (feed)
  4. Would you mind ____________ shifts with me? (switch)
  5. Do you mind if I ____________ your ladder? (borrow)
  6. Would you mind ____________ my packages? (get)

Practice B: Circle the correct words.

  1. Would you mind (covering / to cover) my shift?
  2. A: Would you mind helping me? B: (No, not at all. / Yes, I do.) I'll help.
  3. Do you mind if I (leave / leaving) early?
  4. Could I borrow your pen? I forgot (mine / my).
  5. Sorry, I can't. I ('ll be / be) away.
  6. I'd like (to switch / switching) my Friday shift.

Common mistakes

✗ Don't say✓ Say
Would you mind to get my mail?Would you mind getting my mail?
Yes, I mind. I'll help you.No, not at all. I'll help you.
Do you mind if I using your phone?Do you mind if I use your phone?
Can I borrow your?Can I borrow yours?
I like to switch my shift.I'd like to switch my shift.

Contrast tip (optional): In many languages, a yes answer means "I'll help." But Would you mind…? asks "Is it a problem for you?", so in English No means "No problem." Spanish ¿Te importaría…? No, para nada works the same way. What does your language do?

lessons.teacher:
How to Use This Plan

You don't need to speak Spanish or any other language. Teach in English. Show, point, and gesture. Some Grammar pages have one short contrast tip, only where a common mix-up exists. Learners read it on their own. You never need to read, translate, or explain it.

Instructions: use the same short task words every week: Listen. Circle. Check. Write. Work with a partner. Work in a group. Ask a follow-up question. Give a reason. An optional Task Words page is at the back of the workbook for learners who want it.

Instruction rule: Model it (do it with one learner while everyone watches), check it (ask: "Is it a problem for you? If not, what do you say?"), then go. Say less, show more.

Grouping toolkit: Pairs: turn to a neighbor; with an odd number, make one group of 3. Groups: 3–4 learners. Inside–outside circles: the inner circle faces out, the outer circle faces in; the outer circle moves one person to the right each round. Mingle: everyone stands and talks to many classmates. The teacher joins a pair only if one learner is left over.

When a learner is stuck or speaks another language to you: (1) show it: the picture, a gesture, or the board; (2) give one more short English example; (3) point to the grammar box on their page; (4) a classmate can help for a few seconds, then back to English. You don't need to understand what classmates say to each other.

Three sentences, not one: in Level 4, every Talk Time answer and every exit ticket has about three connected sentences: the answer, a reason, and a detail or example.

Lesson 5 (Week 5): Would You Mind…?

At a glance

Objectives: learners can…

  • ask for a favor with Would you mind…?
  • answer No, not at all (= "Yes, I'll help") or say no politely, with a reason and another idea
  • ask permission with Do you mind if I…?
  • ask a coworker to switch a shift and confirm it in a short text
  • write a note to a neighbor (5–8 sentences) asking for a favor while they're away

Materials

  • Student Pages for Lesson 5 (print for the number expected + 3 spares)
  • Board and markers
  • Favor cards and "my week" cards (in the workbook Talk Time page; copy them onto index cards, optional)
  • A key and an envelope (optional, for the warm-up)
  • Listening: no recording yet. Read the listening script aloud (with a volunteer if you can), at a natural speed, two times.
  • Prep time: 15 minutes (read the plan; practice reading the listening script; practice the thumbs-up "No, not at all!").

Key vocabulary (with pictures on the New Words page)

★ favor • ★ borrow • ★ water the plants • ★ feed the cat • ★ get the mail • ★ spare key • ★ package • ★ switch shifts • ★ cover a shift • ★ be away • owe (someone) • thank-you note

Also: a neighbor, a coworker, lend, a ladder, a trip, a package room, a code, a text, ask the supervisor, I owe you one, go ahead.

7:15–7:25Read & Write: A building notice + a neighbor's note; a note to a neighbor10Pairs read, then individual writingReading questions only; the writing becomes homework
7:25–7:30Exit Ticket + Homework5IndividualsNever skip

Skip order if you're running behind: (1) the Read & Write writing task (it becomes homework); (2) the pair check at the end of Grammar; (3) the second round of Talk Time. Never skip: the listening tasks, the grammar boxes and the mistakes table, and the exit ticket.

Attendance (15 → 7–8 → 5 or fewer): every step lists the sizes. With 5 or fewer, make a circle for Favor Exchange: each person asks the person on the left. Do the Shift Switch Text in pairs; you join if there is an odd number. Late arrivals join the mingle with a new favor card.

Step by step

Step 1 · 6:00–6:08 · Opening Talk · 8 min

  • Grouping: pairs, the same partner for both parts. 15 learners: 7 pairs + 1 group of 3. 7–8 learners: 3–4 pairs. 5 or fewer: pairs, or one group with you.
  • Before class: write on the board: suggestions: Why don't you…? / You could… / It's a good idea to…
  • Opening Talk (5 min): learners open the Opening Talk page. A asks a card question; B answers in 3 sentences (the answer, a reason, a detail); A asks one follow-up. Switch after each card.
  • Model with one learner: you say, "I sit all day at work. Any ideas?" The learner gives a suggestion. Then you ask, "Why is that a good idea?" Help them say 3 sentences.
  • Homework Check (3 min): Pairs compare Homework item 1 (for / since and suggestions) and read their 3 good ideas (item 3) to each other. Then they fill in the box on the Opening Talk page. Walk around. Write 2 common errors on the board (often You could to try (→ You could try) and I have a cough since Sunday (→ I've had a cough since Sunday)) and correct them together. Also put up 2 corrections from last week's exit tickets.
  • Late arrivals: join any pair as a group of 3.
  • If behind: one card only.

Step 2 · 6:08–6:15 · New Words · 7 min

  • Grouping: whole class, then pairs. Show the New Words page.
  • Do: point to each picture and say the word. Learners repeat once.
  • Show the hard words: favor (help you ask for); borrow (take and give back) vs. lend (give and get back); water the plants, feed the cat, get the mail (mime each); spare key (an extra key: show two keys); package; switch shifts (you take my Friday, I take your Sunday) vs. cover a shift (you work my shift); be away (not at home); owe (I owe you one = I'll help you next time); thank-you note.
  • Check meaning (1 min): ask "If I borrow your pen, do I give it back?" (yes) • "If you cover my shift, who works?" (you do) • "Is a spare key the first key or an extra key?" (an extra key).
  • Pairs (2 min): A says a word; B points to the picture and makes a sentence (Would you mind getting my mail? → No, not at all.). Switch. 15 learners: finish with a quick team round (3 teams; you say a clue, the first team with the word gets a point). 7–8: 2 teams. 5 or fewer: one team against the clock.
  • My Words: "Write any word you want in your language on the My Words page. It's your personal list. It's optional." Learners do it at home.
  • If behind: teach the ★ words only.

Step 3 · 6:15–6:30 · Listening + "Hear it, say it" · 15 min

  • Grouping: individuals, then pairs check. With 5 or fewer, check together as a group.
  • Before you listen (2 min): say: "Patricia is going away for a week. First, she talks to her neighbor, Mr. Wilson. Then, at work, her coworker Omar asks her for a favor. Listen: what favors do they ask for?"
  • Play 1 → Task A (the main idea). Pairs compare. Check together.
  • Read Tasks B and C together (1 min) so learners know what to listen for.
  • Play 2 → Tasks B and C. Pairs compare. Then show the answers (answer key).
  • "Hear it, say it" (3 min): Point to the script lines. gonna = going to: "I'm going to be away next week." wanna = want to: "I want to help, but I can't." Then practice Would you mind…? and Do you mind if I…? said smoothly, with a friendly rise. The class repeats the two lines twice.
  • No recording yet: read the script aloud with a volunteer (about 1:48), at a natural speed, two times. The script says going to and want to. People often say gonna and wanna; learners only need to recognize those words. When the audio is ready, it plays the conversation once; press play again for play 2. A third play is fine if the class needs it.
  • If behind: do Task C together on the board, reading the lines yourself.

Step 4 · 6:30–6:45 · Grammar Q&A · 15 min

  • Grouping: whole class, then pairs. Show the Grammar page. The left side is the question. The right side is the answer.
  • Show it (2 min): give a learner your key. Say, "I'm going to be away. Would you mind getting my mail?" Show a thumbs-up and help the learner say, "No, not at all." Write: Would you mind + -ing? → No = "No problem. I'll do it." Then ask, "Do you mind if I open the window?" Help them say, "No, go ahead."
  • The boxes (5 min): Box 1: read across: Would you mind getting my mail? → No, not at all. I'll do it. / Sorry, I can't. Box 2: permission: Do you mind if I…? → No, go ahead. Box 3: saying yes and saying no politely. Box 4: how polite?
  • Rule of thumb and Questions and answers (2 min): read the rule of thumb aloud. Read each Q and A; the class reads the right sentence after you.
  • Check questions: "Would you mind helping me? You want to help. Do you say yes or no?" (No, not at all.) • "Would you mind to get or getting?" (getting) • "Do you mind if I leaving or if I leave?" (if I leave).
  • Practice A and B (3 min): learners write, then pairs check. Go over the answers. Read the Common mistakes table together: "Don't say… Say…".
  • Pair check (last 3 min): A asks a favor from the pictures with Would you mind…? B answers with a thumbs-up and No, not at all, or Sorry, I can't, because… Switch. 15 learners: swap partners once. 5 or fewer: you join one pair.
  • If behind: skip the pair check. Talk Time practices it.

Break · 6:45–7:00 · 15 min

  • Write on the board: Would you mind + -ing? → No, not at all. (= I'll help) / Sorry, I can't, because… • Do you mind if I…? → No, go ahead.

Step 5 · 7:00–7:15 · Talk Time: Favor Exchange + Shift Switch Text · 15 min

  • Model it first (1 min): hold up a favor card and ask a learner, "Would you mind getting my mail next week?" Help them check their "my week" card and answer, "No, not at all," or "Sorry, I can't, because I'll be away. Why don't you ask Ana?" Say: "Answer, give a reason, and offer an idea."
  • Round 1 (7 min): Favor Exchange (mingle). Each learner has a favor card and a "my week" card. Ask three people. Each person answers No, not at all or Sorry, I can't, because… and offers another idea. Write who said yes.
  • Round 2 (6 min): Shift Switch Text (pairs). Pairs write a 3-sentence text that confirms a shift switch (the day, the time, thanks). Then they read it to another pair. Remind them: "Ask your supervisor first."
  • 15 learners: a whole-room mingle for round 1; then pairs for round 2.
  • 7–8 learners: two lines face each other; move one place each round. Then pairs.
  • 5 or fewer: a circle for round 1: each person asks the person on the left. Then pairs (you join if there is an odd number).
  • Every answer needs a reason; every partner asks a follow-up. Walk around and listen. Note 2 good sentences to praise and 1 common error for next week.
  • If behind: round 1 only.

Step 6 · 7:15–7:25 · Read & Write: A building notice + a neighbor's note · 10 min

  • Grouping: pairs read and answer; individual writing. With 5 or fewer, read the text aloud together.
  • Read (4 min): Learners read the notice about packages and the note on the Read & Write page and answer the questions. Say: "Read fast first. Then find the answers." Pairs answer questions 1–5 together.
  • Check (1 min): go over the answers (answer key).
  • Write (5 min): Learners write a note to a neighbor (5–8 sentences) asking for a favor while they're away: the dates, what to do, where the key is, thanks, and an offer to help back. Show the example. Invented details are fine. Learners start in class and finish at home (Homework item 2).
  • If behind: questions 1–5 only; the writing becomes homework.

Step 7 · 7:25–7:30 · Exit Ticket + Homework · 5 min · NEVER SKIP

  • Exit ticket (3 min): learners open the Exit Ticket page and answer in 3 sentences with a reason: Ask a classmate for a favor with Would you mind…? Example on the board: Would you mind helping me with my homework? No, not at all. I'm asking because the last question is hard. With 5 or fewer, a learner can say it to you first and then write it.
  • Collect the pages. After class, sort them into ✓ / almost / not yet. Start next week with 2 corrections on the board (no names).
  • Homework (2 min): open the Homework page. Do item 1 together (item 1: you / mind / feed / my cat? → Would you mind feeding my cat?). Say: "About 15–20 minutes. Finish your Read & Write writing at home."

Listening script (not recorded yet; about 1:48 when recorded; the conversation plays once, so press play again for the second listen)

Audio: the recording is coming soon. Until then, read the script aloud two times, with a volunteer if you can, at a natural, friendly speed. The script says going to and want to. People often say gonna and wanna; learners only need to recognize those words.

Narrator: Lesson five. Patricia is going away for a week. First, she talks to her neighbor, Mr. Wilson.

Patricia: Hi, Mr. Wilson. Could I ask you a favor?

Mr. Wilson: Of course, Patricia. What is it?

Patricia: I'm going to be away next week. I'm visiting my sister. Would you mind getting my mail?

Mr. Wilson: No, not at all. I'm home all week.

Patricia: Thank you! And would you mind watering my plants? Just two times, on Tuesday and Friday.

Mr. Wilson: No problem. Where will the key be?

Patricia: I'm going to give you my spare key tonight. Oh, and would you mind feeding my cat, too?

Mr. Wilson: Sure, I'll do it. I love cats. Do you mind if I put your packages inside, too?

Patricia: No, go ahead. That's very kind.

Mr. Wilson: Have a good trip. Don't worry about anything.

Narrator: The next day, at work, Patricia talks to her coworker, Omar.

Omar: Hey, Patricia. Would you mind covering my Saturday shift? My son has a soccer game.

Patricia: Oh, I'm sorry, I can't. I'll be away on Saturday. I want to help, but I can't.

Omar: Oh, right. You told me.

Patricia: Why don't you ask Lina? She wants more hours this month.

Omar: Good idea. Do you mind if I tell her you suggested it?

Patricia: No, not at all. But ask the supervisor first, OK?

Omar: Sure. Thanks, Patricia. I owe you one.

Patricia: You're welcome. Good luck with the game!

Narrator: That's the end of the listening.

Answer key

  • Listening Task A: a (get the mail, water the plants, feed the cat, and cover a shift).
  • Listening Task B: 1 yes, 2 Tuesday and Friday, 3 her spare key, 4 inside, 5 no, 6 will be away.
  • Listening Task C: 1 getting, 2 watering, 3 feeding, 4 if, 5 covering, 6 if.
  • Grammar Practice A: 1 watering, 2 open, 3 feeding, 4 switching, 5 borrow, 6 getting.
  • Grammar Practice B: 1 covering, 2 No, not at all., 3 leave, 4 mine, 5 'll be, 6 to switch.
  • Talk Time: answers will vary.
  • Homework 1: 1 Would you mind feeding my cat? 2 Do you mind if I leave early? 3 Would you mind covering my shift on Sunday? 4 No, not at all. Homework 2 and 3: answers will vary. Homework 4: 1 Why, 2 try, 3 to, 4 since, 5 for.
  • Read & Write B: 1 To the new package room next to the mailroom. • 2 Within 5 days. • 3 Your text with the code. • 4 From June 10 to June 17. • 5 In an envelope under Ms. Lee's door (on Sunday). • Writing (C): answers will vary.
  • Exit ticket: answers will vary. A good answer: "Would you mind helping me with my homework? No, not at all. I'm asking because the last question is hard."

Teacher notes

  • No = yes: practice the answer first, with a thumbs-up: No, not at all! Learners often say Yes and mean "I'll help." Smile and model it again.
  • Invented details: all favor cards, keys, names, and addresses are invented. Learners never share real addresses or where they keep a key.
  • Shift switches: every employer has its own rules. Add "Ask your supervisor first." It is printed on the Shift Switch Text page.
  • mind + -ing: Would you mind getting…? But Do you mind if I + the base verb: Do you mind if I leave…?
  • Saying no: model sorry + a reason + another idea. A polite no is a good answer.
  • Spanish and other languages: the contrast tip on the Grammar page is optional. Learners read it on their own. You never need to read, translate, or explain it.
  • Reductions: the listening says going to and want to. People often say gonna and wanna. Learners only need to recognize the short forms; they can always say the full forms.

sections.title: Listening
sections.html:
A radio show called What Would You Do? The host, Mike, tells a situation. Two callers, Grace and Teresa, give their answers.

A. Listen. What is the situation? Circle.

a. A cashier gives you too much change. b. You find money on the floor at work. c. A friend asks you to tell a small lie.

B. Listen again. Who says it, and what? Circle the answer.

  1. Grace would (give the money back / keep the money).
  2. Grace's reason: the cashier (made a mistake / was her friend).
  3. Teresa once got ($10 / $20) too much.
  4. Teresa gave it back (the same day / the next day).
  5. If it were one dollar, Teresa would (probably keep it / give it back).
  6. Next week's situation: (an envelope with money at work / a lost phone on the bus).

C. Listen again. Write the missing word: would, were, I'd, or a past verb.

  1. Really? Why ____________ you go back?
  2. If I ____________ the money, she would have a problem at the end of her shift.
  3. And what would you do if it ____________ only one dollar?
  4. If it were one dollar, ____________ probably keep it.
  5. But ____________ feel a little bad.
  6. what would you do if you ____________ an envelope with money at work?

Hear it, say it

wanna = want to: "I want to hear your ideas." • gonna = going to: "If you're going to call, call early!" You can say want to and going to. Listen for I'd (= I would): the d is short but it is there. In What would you do?, the stress is on do.

sections.title: Grammar
sections.html:
Read across. A reads from the left side. B answers from the right side. Choose one part from each column.

Grammar Box 1: What would you do if…?

QUESTION
What would you doif you found $50 at work?
What would you doif you had a free week?
Would you keepthe extra money?
What would you doif you were me?
→
ANSWER
If I found $50,I'd give it to my supervisor.
If I had a free week,I'd visit my cousin.
No, I wouldn't.I'd give it back.
If I were you,I'd call the owner.

Grammar Box 2: possible or imaginary?

POSSIBLE (maybe it will happen)
If it rains tomorrow,I'll take the bus.
If I get the job,I'll buy a new phone.
If you find my keys,will you call me?
→
IMAGINARY (not real now)
If I had a car,I'd drive to work.
If I won $1,000,I'd pay my bills.
If I found a wallet,I'd look for the owner.

Rule of thumb: Imaginary: use the past form after if (found, had, were). Use would / 'd + base verb in the other half (I'd give, I'd visit). Never put would right after if.

Grammar Box 3: would short forms

LONGSHORTEXAMPLE
I wouldI'dI'd give it back.
she wouldshe'dShe'd keep it.
would notwouldn'tI wouldn't keep it.

Grammar Box 4: advice with If I were you…

USEEXAMPLE
If I were you, I'd…adviceIf I were you, I'd talk to the supervisor.
were for every personimaginaryIf it were one dollar, I'd keep it.
If I was…you hear it in speaking; it's OKin writing, use If I were

Questions and answers

Q: Can I say If I would have time, I'd take a class?

A: No. Never put would right after if: If I had time, I'd take a class.

Q: If I was you or If I were you?

A: Write If I were you. In speaking, many people say If I was you. That's OK.

Q: If it rains or If it rained?

A: Possible (maybe tomorrow): If it rains, I'll stay home. Imaginary (not real now): If I had a car, I'd drive.

Practice A: Write the correct form of the verb.

  1. If I ____________ a wallet, I'd look for the owner. (find)
  2. If I had more time, I'd ____________ a computer class. (take)
  3. If I ____________ you, I'd tell the truth. (be)
  4. What would you ____________ if you won $500? (do)
  5. If she ____________ a car, she'd drive to work. (have)
  6. If it rains tomorrow, ____________ take the bus. (I'll / I'd)

Practice B: Circle the correct words.

  1. If I (had / have) a magic wand, I'd fix all the potholes.
  2. If I found $50, I (would / will) give it back.
  3. If I (were / would be) you, I'd call the owner.
  4. If it (rains / rained) tomorrow, I'll stay home.
  5. Would you keep it? No, I (wouldn't / don't).
  6. (What would you do / What you would do) if you had a free week?

Common mistakes

✗ Don't say✓ Say
If I would have time, I'd take a class.If I had time, I'd take a class.
If I found $50, I will give it back.If I found $50, I'd give it back.
What you would do?What would you do?
If I am you, I'd call.If I were you, I'd call.
I'd to give it back.I'd give it back.

Contrast tip (optional): Spanish says Si tuviera…, haría… with special verb forms. English is easier: use the past after if (If I had…) and would in the other half (I'd go). Never put would after if. What does your language do?

A. Read the notice. Read fast first. Then read again and answer the questions.

ADVICE COLUMN · Ask Gloria: Work and Life

Dear Gloria, I work at a busy restaurant. My coworker, Leo, is very friendly, and everyone likes him. But he takes long breaks every day. Sometimes his break is 30 minutes, not 15. When he's on break, I do his work and mine. I don't want to make him angry. What would you do? Tired in Texas

Dear Tired, You are a good coworker, but you shouldn't do two jobs every day. If I were you, I'd talk to Leo first. I'd be friendly, and I'd talk to him alone, not in front of other people. You could say, "When you take a long break, I have a lot of extra work. Could you come back after 15 minutes?" Maybe he doesn't know there is a problem. If he still took long breaks after that, I'd talk to the supervisor. I wouldn't be angry. I'd just explain the problem. Good luck! Gloria

lessons.teacher:
How to Use This Plan

You don't need to speak Spanish or any other language. Teach in English. Show, point, and gesture. Some Grammar pages have one short contrast tip, only where a common mix-up exists. Learners read it on their own. You never need to read, translate, or explain it.

Instructions: use the same short task words every week: Listen. Circle. Check. Write. Work with a partner. Work in a group. Ask a follow-up question. Give a reason. An optional Task Words page is at the back of the workbook for learners who want it.

Instruction rule: Model it (do it with one learner while everyone watches), check it (ask: "If it happened to you, what would you do?"), then go. Say less, show more.

Grouping toolkit: Pairs: turn to a neighbor; with an odd number, make one group of 3. Groups: 3–4 learners. Inside–outside circles: the inner circle faces out, the outer circle faces in; the outer circle moves one person to the right each round. Mingle: everyone stands and talks to many classmates. The teacher joins a pair only if one learner is left over.

When a learner is stuck or speaks another language to you: (1) show it: the picture, a gesture, or the board; (2) give one more short English example; (3) point to the grammar box on their page; (4) a classmate can help for a few seconds, then back to English. You don't need to understand what classmates say to each other.

Three sentences, not one: in Level 4, every Talk Time answer and every exit ticket has about three connected sentences: the answer, a reason, and a detail or example.

Lesson 6 (Week 6): What Would You Do?

At a glance

Objectives: learners can…

  • ask and answer What would you do if…?
  • talk about an imaginary situation with If I + past, I'd + verb
  • give advice with If I were you, I'd… and a reason
  • tell a possible situation (If it rains, I'll…) from an imaginary one (If I had…, I'd…)
  • write a reply to an advice letter (5–8 sentences)

Materials

  • Student Pages for Lesson 6 (print for the number expected + 3 spares)
  • Board and markers
  • Situation cards (in the workbook Talk Time page; copy them onto index cards, optional)
  • A pencil or a stick as a "magic wand" (optional, for Talk Time)
  • Listening: no recording yet. Read the listening script aloud (with a volunteer if you can), at a natural speed, two times.
  • Prep time: 15 minutes (read the plan; practice reading the listening script; practice I'd and wouldn't).

Key vocabulary (with pictures on the New Words page)

★ imagine • ★ choose • ★ honest • ★ tell the truth • ★ keep (it) • ★ give back • ★ owner • ★ envelope • ★ extra money • ★ mistake • magic wand • dream job

Also: a situation, a cashier, change (money back), a caller, a radio show, a wallet, a lie, probably, feel bad, advice.

Clock-time plan

Times are loose. If the listening or Talk Time runs long, take the time from Read & Write.

TimeStepMinGrouping (15 / 7–8)If running behind
6:00–6:08Opening Talk + Homework Check8Pairs (7 pairs + 1 trio / 3–4 pairs)One card only
6:08–6:15New Words (picture page) + pair game (+ My Words)7Whole class, then pairsTeach the ★ words only
6:15–6:30Listening: play 1 (Task A), play 2 (Tasks B and C) + "Hear it, say it"15Individuals, then pairs checkDo Task C together on the board
6:30–6:45Grammar Q&A: If I had…, I'd… / What would you do if…? + pair check15Whole class, then pairsSkip the pair check; Talk Time practices it
6:45–7:00BREAK15
7:00–7:15Talk Time: What Would You Do? + Magic Wand Chain15Groups of 3–4, then a circleRound 1 only
7:15–7:25Read & Write: An advice column; a reply to a letter10Pairs read, then individual writingReading questions only; the writing becomes homework
7:25–7:30Exit Ticket + Homework5IndividualsNever skip

Skip order if you're running behind: (1) the Read & Write writing task (it becomes homework); (2) the pair check at the end of Grammar; (3) the second round of Talk Time. Never skip: the listening tasks, the grammar boxes and the mistakes table, and the exit ticket.

Attendance (15 → 7–8 → 5 or fewer): every step lists the sizes. With 5 or fewer, do What Would You Do? as one group: you read the card and everyone answers. Do the Magic Wand Chain as one circle. Late arrivals join a group and answer the next card.

Step by step

Step 1 · 6:00–6:08 · Opening Talk · 8 min

  • Grouping: pairs, the same partner for both parts. 15 learners: 7 pairs + 1 group of 3. 7–8 learners: 3–4 pairs. 5 or fewer: pairs, or one group with you.
  • Before class: write on the board: favors: Would you mind…? / Do you mind if I…?
  • Opening Talk (5 min): learners open the Opening Talk page. A asks a card question; B answers in 3 sentences (the answer, a reason, a detail); A asks one follow-up. Switch after each card.
  • Model with one learner: you say, "Would you mind lending me a pen?" The learner answers, "No, not at all," or "Sorry, I can't, because…" Then they ask you a favor. Help them say 3 sentences.
  • Homework Check (3 min): Pairs compare Homework item 1 (Would you mind + -ing) and ask each other their 3 favors (item 3). Then they fill in the box on the Opening Talk page. Walk around. Write 2 common errors on the board (often Would you mind to get…? (→ Would you mind getting…?) and Yes, I'll help as the answer (→ No, not at all)) and correct them together. Also put up 2 corrections from last week's exit tickets.
  • Late arrivals: join any pair as a group of 3.
  • If behind: one card only.

Step 2 · 6:08–6:15 · New Words · 7 min

  • Grouping: whole class, then pairs. Show the New Words page.
  • Do: point to each picture and say the word. Learners repeat once.
  • Show the hard words: imagine (point to your head: a picture in your mind); choose (hold up two things: pick one); honest and tell the truth (you don't lie); keep it vs. give it back (mime with a coin); owner (the person it belongs to); envelope; extra money (more than you should get); mistake; magic wand (wave a pencil); dream job (the job you want most).
  • Check meaning (1 min): ask "If a cashier gives you extra money, is it a mistake?" (yes) • "Is the owner the person who found it or the person it belongs to?" (it belongs to) • "If you tell the truth, are you honest?" (yes).
  • Pairs (2 min): A says a word; B points to the picture and makes a sentence (If I found a wallet, I'd give it back to the owner.). Switch. 15 learners: finish with a quick team round (3 teams; you say a clue, the first team with the word gets a point). 7–8: 2 teams. 5 or fewer: one team against the clock.
  • My Words: "Write any word you want in your language on the My Words page. It's your personal list. It's optional." Learners do it at home.
  • If behind: teach the ★ words only.

Step 3 · 6:15–6:30 · Listening + "Hear it, say it" · 15 min

  • Grouping: individuals, then pairs check. With 5 or fewer, check together as a group.
  • Before you listen (2 min): say: "This is a radio show called What Would You Do? Mike is the host. He tells a situation, and two people call the show with their answers. Listen: what is the situation?"
  • Play 1 → Task A (the main idea). Pairs compare. Check together.
  • Read Tasks B and C together (1 min) so learners know what to listen for.
  • Play 2 → Tasks B and C. Pairs compare. Then show the answers (answer key).
  • "Hear it, say it" (3 min): Point to the script lines. wanna = want to: "I want to hear your ideas." gonna = going to: "If you're going to call, call early!" Then practice I'd (say the d): I'd give it back, and What would you DO? with the stress on do. The class repeats the two lines twice.
  • No recording yet: read the script aloud with a volunteer (about 1:52), at a natural speed, two times. The script says going to and want to. People often say gonna and wanna; learners only need to recognize those words. When the audio is ready, it plays the conversation once; press play again for play 2. A third play is fine if the class needs it.
  • If behind: do Task C together on the board, reading the lines yourself.

Step 4 · 6:30–6:45 · Grammar Q&A · 15 min

  • Grouping: whole class, then pairs. Show the Grammar page. The left side is the question. The right side is the answer.
  • Show it (2 min): hold up a pencil as a magic wand. Say, "I don't have a magic wand. But if I had a magic wand, I'd fix all the potholes in this city." Write it in two halves: If I had a magic wand, | I'd fix the potholes. Say: "It's not real. We use the past form after if and would in the other half."
  • The boxes (5 min): Box 1: read across: What would you do if you found $50 at work? → If I found $50, I'd give it to my supervisor. Box 2: possible (If it rains, I'll…) vs. imaginary (If I had a car, I'd…). Box 3: I'd and wouldn't. Box 4: If I were you, I'd… for advice.
  • Rule of thumb and Questions and answers (2 min): read the rule of thumb aloud. Read each Q and A; the class reads the right sentence after you.
  • Check questions: "Do I have a magic wand?" (no) "So do I say If I have or If I had?" (If I had) • "If I would have time or If I had time?" (If I had time) • "If I were you or If I am you?" (If I were you).
  • Practice A and B (3 min): learners write, then pairs check. Go over the answers. Read the Common mistakes table together: "Don't say… Say…".
  • Pair check (last 3 min): A reads a situation from the pictures: "What would you do if you found an envelope with money?" B answers with If I found…, I'd… and a reason. Switch. 15 learners: swap partners once. 5 or fewer: you join one pair.
  • If behind: skip the pair check. Talk Time practices it.

Break · 6:45–7:00 · 15 min

  • Write on the board: What would you do if you found $50? → If I found $50, I'd give it back. • If I were you, I'd… • If it rains, I'll… (possible)

Step 5 · 7:00–7:15 · Talk Time: What Would You Do? + Magic Wand Chain · 15 min

  • Model it first (1 min): read a card: "You find $50 on the floor at work. What would you do?" Help a learner say, "If I found $50, I'd give it to my supervisor because it isn't mine." Say: "Your answer, then because."
  • Round 1 (7 min): What Would You Do? (groups of 3–4). One person reads a situation card. Each person answers with If I…, I'd… and a reason. The group writes the most common answer. Then the next person reads a card.
  • Round 2 (6 min): Magic Wand Chain (circle). Pass the "magic wand." Each person says, "If I had a magic wand, I'd…" One more round: "If I had my dream job, I'd…" Classmates can ask one follow-up question.
  • 15 learners: groups of 3–4 for round 1; then two circles for round 2.
  • 7–8 learners: two groups for round 1; then one circle.
  • 5 or fewer: one group for round 1: you read the cards. Then one circle.
  • Every answer needs a reason; every partner asks a follow-up. Walk around and listen. Note 2 good sentences to praise and 1 common error for next week.
  • If behind: round 1 only.

Step 6 · 7:15–7:25 · Read & Write: An advice column · 10 min

  • Grouping: pairs read and answer; individual writing. With 5 or fewer, read the text aloud together.
  • Read (4 min): Learners read a letter to an advice column and the answer on the Read & Write page and answer the questions. Say: "Read fast first. Then find the answers." Pairs answer questions 1–5 together.
  • Check (1 min): go over the answers (answer key).
  • Write (5 min): Learners read a short letter about a noisy neighbor and write a reply (5–8 sentences) with If I were you, I'd… because…. Show the example. Invented details are fine. Learners start in class and finish at home (Homework item 2).
  • If behind: questions 1–5 only; the writing becomes homework.

Step 7 · 7:25–7:30 · Exit Ticket + Homework · 5 min · NEVER SKIP

  • Exit ticket (3 min): learners open the Exit Ticket page and answer in 3 sentences with a reason: What would you do if you had a free week? Example on the board: If I had a free week, I'd visit my sister in Chicago. I'd also cook a big dinner for my family. I'd do that because I don't see them very often. With 5 or fewer, a learner can say it to you first and then write it.
  • Collect the pages. After class, sort them into ✓ / almost / not yet. Start next week with 2 corrections on the board (no names).
  • Homework (2 min): open the Homework page. Do item 1 together (item 1: if I / have / a free week, I / visit / my cousin → If I had a free week, I'd visit my cousin.). Say: "About 15–20 minutes. Finish your Read & Write writing at home."

Listening script (not recorded yet; about 1:52 when recorded; the conversation plays once, so press play again for the second listen)

Audio: the recording is coming soon. Until then, read the script aloud two times, with a volunteer if you can, at a natural, friendly speed. The script says going to and want to. People often say gonna and wanna; learners only need to recognize those words.

Narrator: Lesson six. This is a radio show called What Would You Do? Mike is the host. Two people call the show.

Mike: Good afternoon, and welcome to What Would You Do? Here's today's situation. You buy groceries, and the cashier gives you ten dollars too much change. You see it in the parking lot. What would you do?

Mike: Our first caller is Grace. Hi, Grace!

Grace: Hi, Mike. If that happened to me, I'd go back inside and give the money back.

Mike: Really? Why would you go back?

Grace: Because the cashier made a mistake. If I kept the money, she would have a problem at the end of her shift.

Mike: That's very honest. Thanks, Grace. Our next caller is Teresa. Teresa, what would you do?

Teresa: Well, Mike, this really happened to me once. A cashier gave me twenty dollars too much.

Mike: Really? What did you do?

Teresa: I gave it back the next day. I was in a hurry, so I couldn't go back that day.

Mike: Was the cashier happy?

Teresa: Yes, she was very happy. She said thank you three times!

Mike: And what would you do if it were only one dollar?

Teresa: Hmm. If it were one dollar, I'd probably keep it. But I'd feel a little bad.

Mike: Ha! That's an honest answer, too. Thank you, Teresa.

Mike: Next week's question is this: what would you do if you found an envelope with money at work? I want to hear your ideas. And if you're going to call, call early!

Narrator: That's the end of the listening.

Answer key

  • Listening Task A: a (A cashier gives you too much change.).
  • Listening Task B: 1 give the money back, 2 made a mistake, 3 $20, 4 the next day, 5 probably keep it, 6 an envelope with money at work.
  • Listening Task C: 1 would, 2 kept, 3 were, 4 I'd, 5 I'd, 6 found.
  • Grammar Practice A: 1 found, 2 take, 3 were, 4 do, 5 had, 6 I'll.
  • Grammar Practice B: 1 had, 2 would, 3 were, 4 rains, 5 wouldn't, 6 What would you do.
  • Talk Time: answers will vary.
  • Homework 1: 1 If I had a free week, I'd visit my cousin. 2 If I were you, I'd tell the truth. 3 What would you do if you won $500? 4 If she had a car, she'd drive to work. Homework 2 and 3: answers will vary. Homework 4: 1 watering, 2 if, 3 at, 4 mine, 5 covering.
  • Read & Write B: 1 At a busy restaurant. • 2 30 minutes, not 15. • 3 She'd talk to Leo. • 4 Alone, not in front of other people. • 5 If Leo still took long breaks after that. • Writing (C): answers will vary.
  • Exit ticket: answers will vary. A good answer: "If I had a free week, I'd visit my sister in Chicago. I'd also cook a big dinner for my family. I'd do that because I don't see them very often."

Teacher notes

  • Past form, present meaning: If I had a car is about now, not the past. Say it: "I don't have a car. It's imaginary."
  • If I were / If I was: teach If I were. Accept If I was in speaking. In writing, gently show If I were.
  • Situation cards: all situations are invented and everyday. No answer is wrong. Learners choose and give a reason; never judge a learner's choice.
  • Personal topics: learners never need to talk about real money problems. If I won $1,000 is just a game.
  • I'd: learners often drop the d. Model I'd give slowly, then smoothly.
  • Spanish and other languages: the contrast tip on the Grammar page is optional. Learners read it on their own. You never need to read, translate, or explain it.
  • Reductions: the listening says going to and want to. People often say gonna and wanna. Learners only need to recognize the short forms; they can always say the full forms.

sections.title: Listening
sections.html:
It's Nadia's first week at a bakery. She asks her coworker, Carmen, about the rules. Then the supervisor, Mr. Brooks, joins them.

A. Listen. What are they talking about? Circle.

a. the rules at work b. a party invitation c. a job interview

B. Listen again. Check the rules. Circle the answer.

  1. On time means (five minutes early / exactly seven o'clock).
  2. In the kitchen, you (must / don't have to) wear the hat and the apron.
  3. In the break room, you (must / don't have to) wear them.
  4. You (must / mustn't) use your phone in the kitchen.
  5. You (must / don't have to) wear closed-toe shoes.
  6. If you're going to be late, you must (call Mr. Brooks / text Carmen).

C. Listen again. Write the missing word: too, enough, or much.

  1. Is six fifty-five early ____________?
  2. Seven ten is ____________ late.
  3. They aren't safe ____________ for the kitchen.
  4. The trays are ____________ hot, and the floor is sometimes wet.
  5. Maybe they're ____________ big, but they're safe.
  6. There's too ____________ to remember!

Hear it, say it

wanna = want to: "What do you want to know?" • gonna = going to: "I'm going to buy some today." You can say want to and going to. too, two, and to sound the same: listen to the meaning. Stress: TOO late • not eNOUGH. In mustn't, you don't hear the first t.

sections.title: Grammar
sections.html:
Read across. A reads from the left side. B answers from the right side. Choose one part from each column.

Grammar Box 1: too + adjective, adjective + enough

QUESTION
Are jeans OKfor the interview?
Is 6:55early enough?
Is 7:10 OKfor a 7:00 shift?
Are sandalssafe enough?
→
ANSWER
No, they're too casual.They aren't formal enough.
Yes, it's early enough.That's perfect.
No, it's too late.Come at 6:55.
No, they aren't safe enough.Wear closed-toe shoes.

Grammar Box 2: too much / too many / enough + a noun

QUESTION
Do you haveenough time?
Are thereenough chairs?
Do we haveenough food?
→
ANSWER
No, I have too much work.I don't have enough time.
No, there are too many people.We need more chairs.
Yes, we have enough food.Don't buy more.

Rule of thumb: too = more than OK (a problem). enough = OK. enough goes after an adjective (early enough) and before a noun (enough time). too many + things you can count; too much + things you can't count.

Grammar Box 3: must / mustn't / don't have to

MEANINGEXAMPLE
mustit's a rule; do itYou must wear closed-toe shoes.
mustn'tit's against the rules; don't do itYou mustn't use your phone in the kitchen.
don't have toit's not necessary; you chooseYou don't have to wear a tie.

Grammar Box 4: comparing customs

TO SAYEXAMPLE
In my hometown…, but here…In my hometown, guests usually bring food, but here people often ask the host first.
usually / often / sometimesPeople usually arrive on time for work.
describe; don't judgeIt's different. I like both.

Questions and answers

Q: enough early or early enough?

A: After an adjective: early enough. Before a noun: enough time.

Q: Are mustn't and don't have to the same?

A: No! mustn't = don't do it (it's a rule). don't have to = not necessary (you can if you want).

Q: too much or too many?

A: too many + things you can count (people, chairs). too much + things you can't count (work, time, noise).

Practice A: Write too, much, many, or enough.

  1. 7:10 is ____________ late for a 7:00 shift.
  2. The room isn't big ____________ for 30 people.
  3. There are too ____________ cars in the parking lot.
  4. I have too ____________ work today.
  5. We don't have ____________ chairs.
  6. Jeans are ____________ casual for an interview.

Practice B: Circle the correct words.

  1. You (mustn't / don't have to) smoke in the building. (It's a rule.)
  2. It's Friday. You (mustn't / don't have to) wear a tie. (It's not necessary.)
  3. Is 6:55 (early enough / enough early)?
  4. There are too (many / much) people here.
  5. I don't have (enough time / time enough).
  6. Sandals (aren't safe enough / are too safe) for the kitchen.

Common mistakes

✗ Don't say✓ Say
It's enough big.It's big enough.
There are too much people.There are too many people.
You don't have to use your phone on the floor. (It's a rule.)You mustn't use your phone on the floor.
You must to wear a badge.You must wear a badge.
I have too many work.I have too much work.

Contrast tip (optional): Spanish demasiado covers too and too much / too many: demasiado caro = too expensive; demasiada gente = too many people. Suficiente = enough. English puts enough after an adjective: big enough (not enough big). What does your language do?
