lessons.teacher:
How to Use This Plan

You don't need to speak Spanish or any other language. Teach in English. Show, point, and gesture. Some Grammar pages have one short contrast tip, only where a common mix-up exists. Learners read it on their own. You never need to read, translate, or explain it.

Instructions: use the same short task words every week: Listen. Circle. Check. Write. Work with a partner. Work in a group. Ask a follow-up question. Give a reason. An optional Task Words page is at the back of the workbook for learners who want it.

Instruction rule: Model it (do it with one learner while everyone watches), check it (ask: "Is it OK, too much, or not enough?"), then go. Say less, show more.

Grouping toolkit: Pairs: turn to a neighbor; with an odd number, make one group of 3. Groups: 3–4 learners. Inside–outside circles: the inner circle faces out, the outer circle faces in; the outer circle moves one person to the right each round. Mingle: everyone stands and talks to many classmates. The teacher joins a pair only if one learner is left over.

When a learner is stuck or speaks another language to you: (1) show it: the picture, a gesture, or the board; (2) give one more short English example; (3) point to the grammar box on their page; (4) a classmate can help for a few seconds, then back to English. You don't need to understand what classmates say to each other.

Three sentences, not one: in Level 4, every Talk Time answer and every exit ticket has about three connected sentences: the answer, a reason, and a detail or example.

Lesson 7 (Week 7): Too Early or On Time?

At a glance

Objectives: learners can…

  • say what is too early, too late, or on time
  • use too + adjective and adjective + enough (too casual, safe enough)
  • use too much / too many / enough + a noun
  • explain a workplace rule with must / mustn't / don't have to
  • compare customs politely and write first-week tips for a new coworker (5–8 sentences)

Materials

  • Student Pages for Lesson 7 (print for the number expected + 3 spares)
  • Board and markers
  • Customs question cards and the dress code rule card (in the workbook Talk Time pages; copy them onto index cards, optional)
  • A clock or a phone with the time (optional, for the warm-up)
  • Listening: no recording yet. Read the listening script aloud (with a volunteer if you can), at a natural speed, two times.
  • Prep time: 15 minutes (read the plan; practice reading the listening script; practice mustn't (no first t) and eNOUGH).

Key vocabulary (with pictures on the New Words page)

★ on time • ★ early • ★ late • ★ dress code • ★ uniform • ★ casual • ★ formal • ★ closed-toe shoes • ★ name badge • ★ invitation • ★ RSVP • host

Also: an apron, sandals, jewelry, a front counter, a handbook, attendance, a custom, a hometown, a guest, take off (shoes).

Clock-time plan

Times are loose. If the listening or Talk Time runs long, take the time from Read & Write.

TimeStepMinGrouping (15 / 7–8)If running behind
6:00–6:08Opening Talk + Homework Check8Pairs (7 pairs + 1 trio / 3–4 pairs)One card only
6:08–6:15New Words (picture page) + pair game (+ My Words)7Whole class, then pairsTeach the ★ words only
6:15–6:30Listening: play 1 (Task A), play 2 (Tasks B and C) + "Hear it, say it"15Individuals, then pairs checkDo Task C together on the board
6:30–6:45Grammar Q&A: too / enough; too much / too many; must / mustn't / don't have to + pair check15Whole class, then pairsSkip the pair check; Talk Time practices it
6:45–7:00BREAK15
7:00–7:15Talk Time: Customs Compare + Dress Code Check15Groups, then pairsRound 1 only
7:15–7:25Read & Write: An employee handbook page; first-week tips10Pairs read, then individual writingReading questions only; the writing becomes homework
7:25–7:30Exit Ticket + Homework5IndividualsNever skip

Skip order if you're running behind: (1) the Read & Write writing task (it becomes homework); (2) the pair check at the end of Grammar; (3) the second round of Talk Time. Never skip: the listening tasks, the grammar boxes and the mistakes table, and the exit ticket.

Attendance (15 → 7–8 → 5 or fewer): every step lists the sizes. With 5 or fewer, do Customs Compare as one group, then Dress Code Check in pairs (you join if there is an odd number). Late arrivals join a group and answer the next card.

Step by step

Step 1 · 6:00–6:08 · Opening Talk · 8 min

  • Grouping: pairs, the same partner for both parts. 15 learners: 7 pairs + 1 group of 3. 7–8 learners: 3–4 pairs. 5 or fewer: pairs, or one group with you.
  • Before class: write on the board: imaginary situations: What would you do if…? / If I had…, I'd…
  • Opening Talk (5 min): learners open the Opening Talk page. A asks a card question; B answers in 3 sentences (the answer, a reason, a detail); A asks one follow-up. Switch after each card.
  • Model with one learner: you say, "What would you do if you found $50 at work?" The learner answers with If I found…, I'd… Then you ask, "Why?" Help them say 3 sentences.
  • Homework Check (3 min): Pairs compare Homework item 1 (If I had…, I'd…) and read their 3 dreams (item 3) to each other. Then they fill in the box on the Opening Talk page. Walk around. Write 2 common errors on the board (often If I would have time… (→ If I had time…) and If I found $50, I will… (→ I'd…)) and correct them together. Also put up 2 corrections from last week's exit tickets.
  • Late arrivals: join any pair as a group of 3.
  • If behind: one card only.

Step 2 · 6:08–6:15 · New Words · 7 min

  • Grouping: whole class, then pairs. Show the New Words page.
  • Do: point to each picture and say the word. Learners repeat once.
  • Show the hard words: on time, early, late (draw a clock: 6:50, 7:00, 7:20); dress code (the rules about clothes); uniform; casual (T-shirt, jeans) vs. formal (a shirt and tie); closed-toe shoes (point to a sneaker, then mime a sandal: "no"); name badge; invitation (a party card); RSVP (tell the host "yes" or "no"); host (the person who has the party).
  • Check meaning (1 min): ask "Is a T-shirt casual or formal?" (casual) • "Are sandals closed-toe shoes?" (no) • "If an invitation says RSVP by Friday, what do you do?" (tell the host by Friday).
  • Pairs (2 min): A says a word; B points to the picture and makes a sentence (Jeans are too casual for an interview.). Switch. 15 learners: finish with a quick team round (3 teams; you say a clue, the first team with the word gets a point). 7–8: 2 teams. 5 or fewer: one team against the clock.
  • My Words: "Write any word you want in your language on the My Words page. It's your personal list. It's optional." Learners do it at home.
  • If behind: teach the ★ words only.

Step 3 · 6:15–6:30 · Listening + "Hear it, say it" · 15 min

  • Grouping: individuals, then pairs check. With 5 or fewer, check together as a group.
  • Before you listen (2 min): say: "It's Nadia's first week at a bakery. She asks her coworker, Carmen, about the rules. Then the supervisor, Mr. Brooks, comes in. Listen: what are they talking about?"
  • Play 1 → Task A (the main idea). Pairs compare. Check together.
  • Read Tasks B and C together (1 min) so learners know what to listen for.
  • Play 2 → Tasks B and C. Pairs compare. Then show the answers (answer key).
  • "Hear it, say it" (3 min): Point to the script lines. wanna = want to: "What do you want to know?" gonna = going to: "I'm going to buy some today." Then practice too / two / to (the same sound) and the stress in TOO late and not eNOUGH. The class repeats the two lines twice.
  • No recording yet: read the script aloud with a volunteer (about 1:50), at a natural speed, two times. The script says going to and want to. People often say gonna and wanna; learners only need to recognize those words. When the audio is ready, it plays the conversation once; press play again for play 2. A third play is fine if the class needs it.
  • If behind: do Task C together on the board, reading the lines yourself.

Step 4 · 6:30–6:45 · Grammar Q&A · 15 min

  • Grouping: whole class, then pairs. Show the Grammar page. The left side is the question. The right side is the answer.
  • Show it (2 min): draw a clock at 7:10. Say, "My shift starts at 7:00. 7:10 is too late." Draw 6:55: "6:55 is early enough." Write: too = more than OK (a problem); enough = OK. Then show a sandal or mime one: "In a kitchen, you must wear closed-toe shoes. You mustn't wear sandals. You don't have to wear a tie."
  • The boxes (5 min): Box 1: read across: Are jeans OK for the interview? → No, they're too casual. / They aren't formal enough. Box 2: too much / too many / enough + a noun. Box 3: must / mustn't / don't have to. Box 4: comparing customs.
  • Rule of thumb and Questions and answers (2 min): read the rule of thumb aloud. Read each Q and A; the class reads the right sentence after you.
  • Check questions: "enough early or early enough?" (early enough) • "too much people or too many people?" (too many people) • "Is a tie a rule here?" (no) "So: You mustn't wear a tie or You don't have to wear a tie?" (don't have to).
  • Practice A and B (3 min): learners write, then pairs check. Go over the answers. Read the Common mistakes table together: "Don't say… Say…".
  • Pair check (last 3 min): A points to a picture and asks, "Are sandals OK for the kitchen?" B answers with too or enough and a rule with must / mustn't. Switch. 15 learners: swap partners once. 5 or fewer: you join one pair.
  • If behind: skip the pair check. Talk Time practices it.

Break · 6:45–7:00 · 15 min

  • Write on the board: too late / early enough • too much work / too many people / enough time • must / mustn't (a rule) / don't have to (not necessary)

Step 5 · 7:00–7:15 · Talk Time: Customs Compare + Dress Code Check · 15 min

  • Model it first (1 min): read a card: "A party starts at 7:00. When do people arrive in your hometown?" Help a learner say, "In my hometown, people usually arrive at 8:00, but here many people arrive at 7:15." Say: "Describe; don't judge. No place is better."
  • Round 1 (7 min): Customs Compare (groups). One person reads a question card. Each person answers. The group writes 2 sentences with In my hometown…, but here… No place is "better."
  • Round 2 (6 min): Dress Code Check (pairs). Pairs read the rule card and the 6 workers. For each worker, they say too casual, not safe enough, or OK, and the rule with must / mustn't / don't have to.
  • 15 learners: 5 groups of 3 for round 1; then pairs.
  • 7–8 learners: 2 groups for round 1; then pairs.
  • 5 or fewer: one group for round 1; then pairs (you join if there is an odd number).
  • Every answer needs a reason; every partner asks a follow-up. Walk around and listen. Note 2 good sentences to praise and 1 common error for next week.
  • If behind: round 1 only.

Step 6 · 7:15–7:25 · Read & Write: An employee handbook page · 10 min

  • Grouping: pairs read and answer; individual writing. With 5 or fewer, read the text aloud together.
  • Read (4 min): Learners read the handbook page on the Read & Write page and answer the questions. Say: "Read fast first. Then find the answers." Pairs answer questions 1–5 together.
  • Check (1 min): go over the answers (answer key).
  • Write (5 min): Learners write "Tips for your first week" for a new coworker (5–8 sentences) with must, don't have to, too, and enough. Show the example. Writing check 2: collect this writing and write one strength and one fix. Learners start in class and finish at home (Homework item 2).
  • If behind: questions 1–5 only; the writing becomes homework.

Step 7 · 7:25–7:30 · Exit Ticket + Homework · 5 min · NEVER SKIP

  • Exit ticket (3 min): learners open the Exit Ticket page and answer in 3 sentences with a reason: What is one custom here that is different from your hometown (or another place you know)? Example on the board: Here, people usually arrive on time for a doctor's appointment. In my hometown, people often arrive a little late. I like the custom here because I don't wait a long time. With 5 or fewer, a learner can say it to you first and then write it.
  • Collect the pages. After class, sort them into ✓ / almost / not yet. Start next week with 2 corrections on the board (no names).
  • Homework (2 min): open the Homework page. Do item 1 together (item 1: 6:55 / early / for a 7:00 shift? (enough) → Is 6:55 early enough for a 7:00 shift?). Say: "About 15–20 minutes. Finish your Read & Write writing at home."

Listening script (not recorded yet; about 1:50 when recorded; the conversation plays once, so press play again for the second listen)

Audio: the recording is coming soon. Until then, read the script aloud two times, with a volunteer if you can, at a natural, friendly speed. The script says going to and want to. People often say gonna and wanna; learners only need to recognize those words.

Narrator: Lesson seven. It's Nadia's first week at a bakery. She asks her coworker, Carmen, some questions.

Nadia: Carmen, can I ask you a few questions? I'm still learning the rules.

Carmen: Sure, Nadia. What do you want to know?

Nadia: My shift starts at seven. Is six fifty-five early enough?

Carmen: Yes, that's perfect. Here, on time means five minutes early. Seven ten is too late.

Nadia: OK. And what about the uniform? Do I have to wear the hat?

Carmen: Yes, you must wear the hat and the apron in the kitchen. But you don't have to wear them in the break room.

Nadia: Got it. What about my phone?

Carmen: You mustn't use your phone in the kitchen. You can use it on your break.

Nadia: And are these shoes OK? They're new.

Carmen: Hmm, those are sandals. They aren't safe enough for the kitchen.

Mr. Brooks: Carmen's right. Good morning, Nadia. I'm Mr. Brooks, the supervisor. You must wear closed-toe shoes. The trays are too hot, and the floor is sometimes wet.

Nadia: I'm sorry. I didn't know. I'm going to buy some today.

Mr. Brooks: That's OK. For today, there are extra shoes in the office. Maybe they're too big, but they're safe.

Nadia: Thank you. Is there anything else?

Mr. Brooks: Just one more thing. If you're going to be late, you must call me before your shift.

Carmen: Don't worry, Nadia. Everyone makes mistakes in the first week. There's too much to remember!

Nadia: That's true. Thanks, both of you.

Narrator: That's the end of the listening.

Answer key

  • Listening Task A: a (the rules at work).
  • Listening Task B: 1 five minutes early, 2 must, 3 don't have to, 4 mustn't, 5 must, 6 call Mr. Brooks.
  • Listening Task C: 1 enough, 2 too, 3 enough, 4 too, 5 too, 6 much.
  • Grammar Practice A: 1 too, 2 enough, 3 many, 4 much, 5 enough, 6 too.
  • Grammar Practice B: 1 mustn't, 2 don't have to, 3 early enough, 4 many, 5 enough time, 6 aren't safe enough.
  • Talk Time: answers will vary.
  • Homework 1: 1 Is 6:55 early enough for a 7:00 shift? 2 There are too many people in the store. 3 I don't have enough time for lunch. 4 You mustn't use your phone in the kitchen. Homework 2 and 3: answers will vary. Homework 4: 1 had, 2 were, 3 would, 4 I'll, 5 give.
  • Read & Write B: 1 5 to 10 minutes before your shift. • 2 Call your supervisor at least one hour before your shift. • 3 No. A text is not enough. • 4 No, but they must wear a name badge. • 5 In the break room. • Writing (C): answers will vary.
  • Exit ticket: answers will vary. A good answer: "Here, people usually arrive on time for a doctor's appointment. In my hometown, people often arrive a little late. I like the custom here because I don't wait a long time."

Teacher notes

  • Describe, don't judge: customs vary inside every country, including the U.S., and inside every family. No place is "better." Model It's different and I like both.
  • Rules come from each employer: the bakery, the kitchen, and their rules are invented. Learners can say "At my job…" if they want; they never have to.
  • mustn't vs. don't have to: this is the biggest mix-up. Use a thumbs-down for mustn't (don't do it) and a shrug for don't have to (you choose).
  • Writing check 2 (Week 7): collect the first-week tips. Write one strength and one fix on each. Learners keep them in their writing folder.
  • Week 8 is the midterm. It covers Lessons 1–7. Remind learners to bring their workbook.
  • Spanish and other languages: the contrast tip on the Grammar page is optional. Learners read it on their own. You never need to read, translate, or explain it.
  • Reductions: the listening says going to and want to. People often say gonna and wanna. Learners only need to recognize the short forms; they can always say the full forms.

sections.title: Listening
sections.html:
A short local radio news report about a road closure and a bus detour. Then, at work, two coworkers, Marco and Joy, talk about how it might change their commute.

A. Listen. What is the news? Circle.

a. Oak Street will close for a water pipe repair. b. A new grocery store is opening. c. The bus will be free next week.

B. Listen again. Complete the notes. Circle the answer.

  1. Where: Oak Street, between First and (Fifth / Ninth) Avenue
  2. When: starting (Monday / Friday)
  3. Why: workers will replace an old (water pipe / bus stop)
  4. How long: maybe (two weeks / two days)
  5. The bus detour: on (Pine Street / Main Street)
  6. Delays: about (fifteen / fifty) minutes

C. Listen again. Write the missing word: might, will, or a question word.

  1. The city says the construction ____________ take two weeks.
  2. The city ____________ post updates on its website.
  3. Do you know ____________ the bus leaves Pine Street?
  4. Do you know ____________ long the closure is?
  5. But it ____________ take longer if it rains.
  6. Do you know ____________ the detour starts?

Hear it, say it

gonna = going to: "The bus is going to take a detour." • "I'm going to look at the map tonight." You can say going to. In might, the last t is very short. In Do you know…?, the voice goes up at the end. Listen to the reporter: she pauses after each fact.

sections.title: Grammar
sections.html:
Read across. A reads from the left side. B answers from the right side. Choose one part from each column.

Grammar Box 1: might / may / could (maybe)

QUESTION
Will the roadbe closed tomorrow?
Will the repairtake two weeks?
When will the roadopen?
Will the busbe on time?
→
ANSWER
It might be.I'm not sure.
It may take longer.It depends on the rain.
I'm not sure.It could open next week.
It might not be.It might be 15 minutes late.

Grammar Box 2: Do you know where…? (a first look)

QUESTION
Do you knowwhere the meeting is?
Do you knowwhen the new bus route starts?
Do you knowwhat time the store opens?
Do you knowwhy the street is closed?
→
ANSWER
Yes, it'sat the library.
I thinkit starts in May.
I'm not sure.It might open at 8:00.
Yes. Workersare fixing a water pipe.

Rule of thumb: might / may / could + base verb: never to, never -s (It might rain). After Do you know where / when / why, use statement order: where the meeting is (not where is the meeting).

Grammar Box 3: will (sure) or might (maybe)?

HOW SURE?EXAMPLE
willsureThe road will close at 8:00 on Monday.
will probablyalmost sureIt will probably take two weeks.
might / may / couldmaybeIt might open early.
might not / may notmaybe notThe bus might not be on time.

Grammar Box 4: from a question to Do you know…?

QUESTIONDO YOU KNOW…?
Where is the meeting?Do you know where the meeting is?
When does the bus leave?Do you know when the bus leaves? (no does; add -s)
Why is the street closed?Do you know why the street is closed?

Questions and answers

Q: It might rains or It might rain?

A: might + base verb: It might rain. Never -s, never to.

Q: Can I say Do you know where is the meeting?

A: Use statement order: Do you know where the meeting is?

Q: will or might?

A: will = I'm sure. might = maybe. The road will close on Monday. It might open early.

Practice A: Write the correct word or form.

  1. It's very cloudy. It ____________ rain later. (might / will)
  2. The sign says the road ____________ close at 8:00 on Monday. (might / will)
  3. The store might ____________ next month. (open)
  4. Do you know where the library ____________? (be)
  5. Do you know when the bus ____________? (leave)
  6. I'm not sure. The bus may ____________ late. (be)

Practice B: Circle the correct words.

  1. The repair might (take / to take) two weeks.
  2. Do you know (where the meeting is / where is the meeting)?
  3. It (might not / doesn't might) rain tomorrow.
  4. Do you know what time the store (opens / does open)?
  5. The schedule says the bus (will / might) leave at 7:05. (sure)
  6. I'm not sure. It (may / will) open in June. (maybe)

Common mistakes

✗ Don't say✓ Say
It might rains tomorrow.It might rain tomorrow.
The road might to close.The road might close.
Do you know where is the bank?Do you know where the bank is?
Do you know when does the bus leave?Do you know when the bus leaves?
I'm sure. The road might close at 8:00.I'm sure. The road will close at 8:00.

Contrast tip (optional): Spanish Puede que cierren la calle uses a special verb form; English uses might + base verb: They might close the street (not might to close, not might closes). Spanish ¿Sabes dónde está…? keeps the verb right after dónde; English moves it: Do you know where the meeting is? What does your language do?

MAPLE FALLS NEWS · New Bus Route Will Connect Hospital and College (invented city)

Starting May 6, Maple Falls will have a new bus route, Route 9. The route will go from Riverside Hospital to Maple Falls Community College, with stops at the library, the West Side Market, and the train station. Buses will run every 20 minutes from 6:00 a.m. to 10:00 p.m., Monday to Saturday. A ride will cost $1.50, the same as other city buses.

"Many people asked for this route," said Ana Ruiz from the city transit office. "Nurses and students wanted an easier way to get to work and class." Students are happy too. "Now I don't have to take two buses," said one student.

The city might add Sunday service in the fall. It may also add two more stops near the new apartments on Elm Road, but this isn't decided yet.

Riders can see the map and the schedule on the city website or at the library. For the first week, all rides on Route 9 will be free.

lessons.teacher:
How to Use This Plan

You don't need to speak Spanish or any other language. Teach in English. Show, point, and gesture. Some Grammar pages have one short contrast tip, only where a common mix-up exists. Learners read it on their own. You never need to read, translate, or explain it.

Instructions: use the same short task words every week: Listen. Circle. Check. Write. Work with a partner. Work in a group. Ask a follow-up question. Give a reason. An optional Task Words page is at the back of the workbook for learners who want it.

Instruction rule: Model it (do it with one learner while everyone watches), check it (ask: "Are you sure, or is it maybe?"), then go. Say less, show more.

Grouping toolkit: Pairs: turn to a neighbor; with an odd number, make one group of 3. Groups: 3–4 learners. Inside–outside circles: the inner circle faces out, the outer circle faces in; the outer circle moves one person to the right each round. Mingle: everyone stands and talks to many classmates. The teacher joins a pair only if one learner is left over.

When a learner is stuck or speaks another language to you: (1) show it: the picture, a gesture, or the board; (2) give one more short English example; (3) point to the grammar box on their page; (4) a classmate can help for a few seconds, then back to English. You don't need to understand what classmates say to each other.

Three sentences, not one: in Level 4, every Talk Time answer and every exit ticket has about three connected sentences: the answer, a reason, and a detail or example.

Lesson 8 (Week 9): In the News

At a glance

Objectives: learners can…

  • understand the main points of a short local news report
  • say what might or may happen, and what will happen
  • ask Do you know where / when / why…? with statement order
  • tell a classmate about a local news story
  • write a text or email (5–8 sentences) telling a friend the news

Materials

  • Student Pages for Lesson 8 (print for the number expected + 3 spares)
  • Board and markers
  • News cards A and B and a headline (in the workbook Talk Time pages; copy them onto index cards, optional)
  • A local map or a drawing of streets (optional, for the warm-up)
  • Listening: no recording yet. Read the listening script aloud (with a volunteer if you can), at a natural speed, two times.
  • Prep time: 15 minutes (read the plan; practice reading the listening script; practice the news reader's pauses).

Key vocabulary (with pictures on the New Words page)

★ news • ★ reporter • ★ headline • ★ road closure • ★ detour • ★ construction • ★ water pipe • ★ bus route • ★ delay • ★ announce • ★ update • local

Also: a rider, a stop, a schedule, a website, a transit office, service, replace, connect, expect, post (online).

Clock-time plan

Times are loose. If the listening or Talk Time runs long, take the time from Read & Write.

TimeStepMinGrouping (15 / 7–8)If running behind
6:00–6:08Opening Talk + Homework Check8Pairs (7 pairs + 1 trio / 3–4 pairs)One card only
6:08–6:15New Words (picture page) + pair game (+ My Words)7Whole class, then pairsTeach the ★ words only
6:15–6:30Listening: play 1 (Task A), play 2 (Tasks B and C) + "Hear it, say it"15Individuals, then pairs checkDo Task C together on the board
6:30–6:45Grammar Q&A: might / may / could; Do you know where…? + pair check15Whole class, then pairsSkip the pair check; Talk Time practices it
6:45–7:00BREAK15
7:00–7:15Talk Time: News Swap + What Might Happen?15Pairs, then groupsRound 1 only
7:15–7:25Read & Write: A local news article; a text to a friend10Pairs read, then individual writingReading questions only; the writing becomes homework
7:25–7:30Exit Ticket + Homework5IndividualsNever skip

Skip order if you're running behind: (1) the Read & Write writing task (it becomes homework); (2) the pair check at the end of Grammar; (3) the second round of Talk Time. Never skip: the listening tasks, the grammar boxes and the mistakes table, and the exit ticket.

Attendance (15 → 7–8 → 5 or fewer): every step lists the sizes. With 5 or fewer, do News Swap in pairs (you take a card if there is an odd number), then What Might Happen? as one group. Late arrivals get news card A or B and join a pair.

Step by step

Step 1 · 6:00–6:08 · Opening Talk · 8 min

  • Grouping: pairs, the same partner for both parts. 15 learners: 7 pairs + 1 group of 3. 7–8 learners: 3–4 pairs. 5 or fewer: pairs, or one group with you.
  • Before class: write on the board: too / enough; must / mustn't / don't have to
  • Opening Talk (5 min): learners open the Opening Talk page. A asks a card question; B answers in 3 sentences (the answer, a reason, a detail); A asks one follow-up. Switch after each card.
  • Model with one learner: you say, "Is 6:55 early enough for a 7:00 shift?" The learner answers with too or enough and a reason. Then you ask, "What must you wear at your job or school?" Help them say 3 sentences.
  • Homework Check (3 min): Pairs compare Homework item 1 (too / enough / mustn't) and read their 3 rules (item 3) to each other. Then they fill in the box on the Opening Talk page. Also return the midterm and go over 2 common mistakes. Walk around. Write 2 common errors on the board (often It's enough big (→ It's big enough) and You don't have to smoke here for a rule (→ You mustn't smoke here)) and correct them together. Also put up 2 corrections from last week's exit tickets.
  • Late arrivals: join any pair as a group of 3.
  • If behind: one card only.

Step 2 · 6:08–6:15 · New Words · 7 min

  • Grouping: whole class, then pairs. Show the New Words page.
  • Do: point to each picture and say the word. Learners repeat once.
  • Show the hard words: news, local (in our city); reporter (the person who tells the news); headline (the big words at the top); road closure and detour (draw a street with an X and an arrow around it); construction; water pipe; bus route; delay (the bus is late); announce (say it to everyone); update (new information).
  • Check meaning (1 min): ask "If the road is closed, does the bus take a detour?" (yes) • "Is a headline long or short?" (short) • "If there is a delay, is the bus early or late?" (late).
  • Pairs (2 min): A says a word; B points to the picture and makes a sentence (The road might be closed until Friday.). Switch. 15 learners: finish with a quick team round (3 teams; you say a clue, the first team with the word gets a point). 7–8: 2 teams. 5 or fewer: one team against the clock.
  • My Words: "Write any word you want in your language on the My Words page. It's your personal list. It's optional." Learners do it at home.
  • If behind: teach the ★ words only.

Step 3 · 6:15–6:30 · Listening + "Hear it, say it" · 15 min

  • Grouping: individuals, then pairs check. With 5 or fewer, check together as a group.
  • Before you listen (2 min): say: "First, you'll hear a short local news report on the radio. Then two coworkers, Marco and Joy, talk about the news. Listen: what is the news?"
  • Play 1 → Task A (the main idea). Pairs compare. Check together.
  • Read Tasks B and C together (1 min) so learners know what to listen for.
  • Play 2 → Tasks B and C. Pairs compare. Then show the answers (answer key).
  • "Hear it, say it" (3 min): Point to the script lines. gonna = going to: "The bus is going to take a detour." Then practice might (the last t is very short: It migh' be late) and Do you know…? with the voice going up at the end. Listen to the reporter's pauses. The class repeats the two lines twice.
  • No recording yet: read the script aloud with a volunteer (about 1:59), at a natural speed, two times. The script says going to and want to. People often say gonna and wanna; learners only need to recognize those words. When the audio is ready, it plays the conversation once; press play again for play 2. A third play is fine if the class needs it.
  • If behind: do Task C together on the board, reading the lines yourself.

Step 4 · 6:30–6:45 · Grammar Q&A · 15 min

  • Grouping: whole class, then pairs. Show the Grammar page. The left side is the question. The right side is the answer.
  • Show it (2 min): draw a cloud. Say, "Will it rain tomorrow? I'm not sure. It might rain. It may rain." Draw a sign ROAD CLOSED MONDAY: "The road will close on Monday. I'm sure." Then ask a learner, "Do you know where the library is?" Write it and underline the library is: "Statement order."
  • The boxes (5 min): Box 1: read across: Will the road be closed tomorrow? → It might be. / It may be closed until Friday. Box 2: Do you know where / when / what time / why…? Box 3: will (sure) vs. might (maybe). Box 4: from a question to Do you know…?
  • Rule of thumb and Questions and answers (2 min): read the rule of thumb aloud. Read each Q and A; the class reads the right sentence after you.
  • Check questions: "It might rains or It might rain?" (might rain) • "Do you know where is the bank or where the bank is?" (where the bank is) • "The sign says Closed Monday. will or might?" (will).
  • Practice A and B (3 min): learners write, then pairs check. Go over the answers. Read the Common mistakes table together: "Don't say… Say…".
  • Pair check (last 3 min): A points to a picture and asks, "Do you know when the construction ends?" B answers with a fact or I'm not sure. It might… Switch. 15 learners: swap partners once. 5 or fewer: you join one pair.
  • If behind: skip the pair check. Talk Time practices it.

Break · 6:45–7:00 · 15 min

  • Write on the board: It might / may / could + base verb (maybe) • It will… (sure) • Do you know where the meeting is? (statement order)

Step 5 · 7:00–7:15 · Talk Time: News Swap + What Might Happen? · 15 min

  • Model it first (1 min): hold news card A. Ask a learner, "Do you know when the library will open on Sundays?" Help them find it and answer, "Yes, starting March 3." Then ask, "Do you know why?" Say: "Ask with Do you know…? Answer with a fact, or say I'm not sure. It might…"
  • Round 1 (7 min): News Swap (pairs). A and B have different news cards. Partners ask Do you know when / where / why…? and write the facts. Then they change partners and retell their partner's story.
  • Round 2 (6 min): What Might Happen? (groups). Groups choose a headline and write 4 predictions with might, may, and will probably. Then they read them to the class.
  • 15 learners: pairs with one rotation for round 1; then groups of 4.
  • 7–8 learners: pairs for round 1; then 2 groups.
  • 5 or fewer: pairs for round 1 (you take a card if there is an odd number); then one group.
  • Every answer needs a reason; every partner asks a follow-up. Walk around and listen. Note 2 good sentences to praise and 1 common error for next week.
  • If behind: round 1 only.

Step 6 · 7:15–7:25 · Read & Write: A local news article · 10 min

  • Grouping: pairs read and answer; individual writing. With 5 or fewer, read the text aloud together.
  • Read (4 min): Learners read the news article on the Read & Write page, find the main idea, and answer the questions. Say: "Read fast first. Then find the answers." Pairs answer questions 1–5 together.
  • Check (1 min): go over the answers (answer key).
  • Write (5 min): Learners write a text or email to a friend about the news (5–8 sentences) with one might or may and one Do you know…?. Show the example. Learners start in class and finish at home (Homework item 2).
  • If behind: questions 1–5 only; the writing becomes homework.

Step 7 · 7:25–7:30 · Exit Ticket + Homework · 5 min · NEVER SKIP

  • Exit ticket (3 min): learners open the Exit Ticket page and answer in 3 sentences with a reason: What might change in your neighborhood or at your job next year? Example on the board: A new store might open near my house. My job may change my schedule. I think so because there's construction on my street and my company is very busy. With 5 or fewer, a learner can say it to you first and then write it.
  • Collect the pages. After class, sort them into ✓ / almost / not yet. Start next week with 2 corrections on the board (no names).
  • Homework (2 min): open the Homework page. Do item 1 together (item 1: the store / may / open / in June → The store may open in June.). Say: "About 15–20 minutes. Finish your Read & Write writing at home."

Listening script (not recorded yet; about 1:59 when recorded; the conversation plays once, so press play again for the second listen)

Audio: the recording is coming soon. Until then, read the script aloud two times, with a volunteer if you can, at a natural, friendly speed. The script says going to and want to. People often say gonna and wanna; learners only need to recognize those words.

Narrator: Lesson eight. First, listen to a short news report on the radio. Then two coworkers talk about the news.

Diane Lee: Good morning. This is Diane Lee with your local news. Starting Monday, Oak Street will be closed between First and Fifth Avenue. Workers are going to replace an old water pipe under the street.

Diane Lee: The city says the construction might take two weeks. It may take longer if it rains.

Diane Lee: During the road closure, the number twelve bus will take a detour on Pine Street. Riders should expect delays of about fifteen minutes. The city will post updates on its website. I'm Diane Lee, and that's the news.

Narrator: Later that morning, at work, Marco and Joy talk about the news.

Marco: Joy, did you hear the news? They're closing Oak Street on Monday.

Joy: Oh no. I take the number twelve bus on Oak Street every day.

Marco: The bus is going to take a detour on Pine Street. It might be fifteen minutes late.

Joy: Fifteen minutes? I might be late for work. Do you know when the bus leaves Pine Street?

Marco: I'm not sure. You could check the city website.

Joy: Good idea. Do you know how long the closure is?

Marco: They said two weeks. But it might take longer if it rains.

Joy: Hmm. Maybe I'll take the earlier bus. I don't want to be late.

Marco: Or I could give you a ride. I drive past your street.

Joy: Really? That would be great. Do you know where the detour starts?

Marco: I think it starts at First Avenue. I'm going to look at the map tonight.

Joy: Thanks, Marco!

Narrator: That's the end of the listening.

Answer key

  • Listening Task A: a (Oak Street will close for a water pipe repair.).
  • Listening Task B: 1 Fifth, 2 Monday, 3 water pipe, 4 two weeks, 5 Pine Street, 6 fifteen.
  • Listening Task C: 1 might, 2 will, 3 when, 4 how, 5 might, 6 where.
  • Grammar Practice A: 1 might, 2 will, 3 open, 4 is, 5 leaves, 6 be.
  • Grammar Practice B: 1 take, 2 where the meeting is, 3 might not, 4 opens, 5 will, 6 may.
  • Talk Time: answers will vary.
  • Homework 1: 1 The store may open in June. 2 It might not rain this weekend. 3 Do you know where the meeting is? 4 Do you know when the bus leaves? Homework 2 and 3: answers will vary. Homework 4: 1 enough, 2 many, 3 mustn't, 4 too, 5 much.
  • Read & Write B: 1 A new bus route, Route 9, will start on May 6. • 2 Every 20 minutes. • 3 $1.50 (and free for the first week). • 4 Sunday service. • 5 On the city website or at the library. • Writing (C): answers will vary.
  • Exit ticket: answers will vary. A good answer: "A new store might open near my house. My job may change my schedule. I think so because there's construction on my street and my company is very busy."

Teacher notes

  • Class stories only: all news is invented and neutral (roads, buses, a library, a store). No politics, crime, injuries, or real current events. If a learner brings up real news, say, "Let's keep to our class stories."
  • After the midterm: this is Week 9. Return the midterm in the Opening Talk and put 2 common mistakes on the board.
  • Do you know where…? is a first look: practice it with where / when / what time / why only. Don't teach if / whether (Level 5).
  • might + base verb: learners often add to or -s. Point to the rule: no to, no -s.
  • News Swap: learners keep their card hidden. If a partner can't find a fact, they say, "I'm not sure. It might…"
  • Spanish and other languages: the contrast tip on the Grammar page is optional. Learners read it on their own. You never need to read, translate, or explain it.
  • Reductions: the listening says going to. People often say gonna. Learners only need to recognize it; they can always say the full form.

sections.title: Listening
sections.html:
A short neighborhood meeting. The leader, Mrs. Okafor, asks for opinions about the empty lot on Cedar Street. Ray and Lin give their opinions.

A. Listen. What are they deciding? Circle.

a. what to do with the empty lot b. when to have a street party c. where to put a new bus stop

B. Listen again. Match the person, the opinion, and the reason. Circle the answer.

  1. Ray wants (a parking lot / a community garden).
  2. Ray's reason: there (aren't enough parking spaces / are too many trees) on the street.
  3. Lin wants (a parking lot / a community garden).
  4. Lin's first reason: a garden (isn't as expensive as / is more expensive than) a parking lot.
  5. Ray's question: who's going to (take care of it / pay for it)?
  6. The plan: they will (do a survey / build the garden).

C. Listen again. Write the missing word in the polite phrase.

  1. In my ____________, we need a parking lot.
  2. how do you ____________ about it?
  3. I see your ____________, Ray, but I'm not sure I agree.
  4. That's a good ____________, but a garden is a lot of work.
  5. Well, I ____________ that a garden is nice.
  6. I agree. That's ____________.

Hear it, say it

wanna = want to • gonna = going to. You can say want to and going to. In I see your POINT, but…, the voice goes down on point. Stress: It isn't as EXpensive.

sections.title: Grammar
sections.html:
Read across. A reads from the left side. B answers from the right side. Choose one part from each column.

Grammar Box 1: asking for and giving an opinion

QUESTION
What do you thinkabout the empty lot?
How do you feelabout a parking lot?
What's your opinionabout the bus stop?
→
ANSWER
I thinkwe need a playground.
In my opinion,it's a good idea.
I'm not sure, butmaybe it's too far.

Grammar Box 2: agreeing and disagreeing politely

QUESTION
Do you agreewith Ray?
Do you agreewith Lin?
Do you agreeabout the survey?
→
ANSWER
Yes, I agree with him.That's true. Parking is a problem.
I see your point, buta garden is a lot of work.
I'm not sure I agree,because it takes a long time.

Rule of thumb: To disagree politely, say something positive first: I see your point, but… / That's a good idea, but… Say I agree (not I am agree) and I don't agree (not I am not agree).

Grammar Box 3: as … as / not as … as

MEANINGEXAMPLE
as important asthe sameA playground is as important as parking.
not as expensive aslessA garden isn't as expensive as a parking lot.
more … than (review)moreA parking lot is more expensive than a garden.

Grammar Box 4: an opinion paragraph

PARTWORDSEXAMPLE
topic sentenceIn my opinion, / I thinkIn my opinion, the lot should be a playground.
reason 1 and reason 2First, … Also, …First, kids need a safe place to play. Also, it isn't as expensive as a parking lot.
exampleFor example,For example, the nearest park is two miles away.
closingThat's whyThat's why I think a playground is the best plan.

Questions and answers

Q: I am agree or I agree?

A: I agree. agree is a verb, so there is no am. The negative is I don't agree.

Q: How do I disagree politely?

A: Say something positive first: I see your point, but… or That's a good idea, but…

Q: not as expensive as or not as expensive than?

A: Use as … as: A garden isn't as expensive as a parking lot.

Practice A: Write one word.

  1. I ____________ with you. That's true.
  2. A garden isn't ____________ expensive as a parking lot.
  3. What do you ____________ about the new bus stop?
  4. I see your ____________, but I'm not sure.
  5. In my ____________, we need more trees.
  6. If we ____________ a playground, kids would play outside more. (have)

Practice B: Circle the correct words.

  1. (I agree / I am agree) with Lin.
  2. A playground is as important (as / than) parking.
  3. (That's a good idea, but / That's wrong, and) it's a lot of work. (polite)
  4. How do you (feel / think) about the plan?
  5. A garden isn't as (expensive / more expensive) as a parking lot.
  6. If we had a garden, families (would / will) grow vegetables.

Common mistakes

✗ Don't say✓ Say
I am agree.I agree.
I am not agree.I don't agree.
A garden isn't as expensive than parking.A garden isn't as expensive as parking.
What do you think the plan?What do you think about the plan?
No, that's wrong. (in a meeting)I see your point, but I'm not sure.

Contrast tip (optional): In some languages, a direct "No, that's wrong" is normal in a discussion. In English, people usually soften it: I see your point, but… (Spanish: Entiendo, pero…). What do people say in your language?

sections.title: Read & Write
sections.html:
A. Read the notice. Read fast first. Then read again and answer the questions.

CEDAR STREET NEIGHBORS · A flyer + two letters (invented)

COMMUNITY MEETING. What should we do with the empty lot at 400 Cedar Street? Come and share your opinion! Thursday, May 12, 7:00 p.m., Cedar Street Library, Room B. Free childcare. Please bring your survey.

A playground, please! In my opinion, the lot should be a playground. First, our kids don't have a safe place to play. The nearest park is two miles away. Also, a playground isn't as expensive as a parking lot. If we had a playground, families would spend more time outside together. That's why I think a playground is the best plan. Maria G.

What about parking? I see the point about a playground, but I'm not sure I agree. Every night, I drive around for 20 minutes to find a space. Many neighbors work late, and the street is very dark at night. A small parking lot with good lights would help everyone. Maybe we could also put two benches and a small garden next to it. Ray T.

B. Answer the questions.

  1. When is the meeting? ______________________________________________
  2. What does Maria want? ______________________________________________
  3. What is Maria's first reason? ______________________________________________
  4. Does Ray agree with Maria? ______________________________________________
  5. What could go next to the parking lot? ______________________________________________

C. Write an opinion paragraph (5–8 sentences): what should the empty lot be? Use a topic sentence, two reasons (First… Also…), an example, and a closing sentence (That's why…).

Example: In my opinion, the empty lot should be a community garden. First, a garden isn't as expensive as a parking lot. Also, neighbors could meet and work together. For example, my grandmother loves to grow tomatoes, but she doesn't have a yard. I see the point about parking, but a garden helps more people. That's why I think a garden is the best plan.

lessons.teacher:
How to Use This Plan

You don't need to speak Spanish or any other language. Teach in English. Show, point, and gesture. Some Grammar pages have one short contrast tip, only where a common mix-up exists. Learners read it on their own. You never need to read, translate, or explain it.

Instructions: use the same short task words every week: Listen. Circle. Check. Write. Work with a partner. Work in a group. Ask a follow-up question. Give a reason. An optional Task Words page is at the back of the workbook for learners who want it.

Instruction rule: Model it (do it with one learner while everyone watches), check it (ask: "Do you agree? How do you say it politely?"), then go. Say less, show more.

Grouping toolkit: Pairs: turn to a neighbor; with an odd number, make one group of 3. Groups: 3–4 learners. Inside–outside circles: the inner circle faces out, the outer circle faces in; the outer circle moves one person to the right each round. Mingle: everyone stands and talks to many classmates. The teacher joins a pair only if one learner is left over.

When a learner is stuck or speaks another language to you: (1) show it: the picture, a gesture, or the board; (2) give one more short English example; (3) point to the grammar box on their page; (4) a classmate can help for a few seconds, then back to English. You don't need to understand what classmates say to each other.

Three sentences, not one: in Level 4, every Talk Time answer and every exit ticket has about three connected sentences: the answer, a reason, and a detail or example.

Lesson 9 (Week 10): I See Your Point

At a glance

Objectives: learners can…

  • give an opinion with a reason
  • ask for someone's opinion (What do you think about…? / How do you feel about…?)
  • agree and disagree politely (I agree. / I see your point, but…)
  • compare two ideas with as … as / not as … as
  • write an opinion paragraph (5–8 sentences) with First… Also… That's why…

Materials

  • Student Pages for Lesson 9 (print for the number expected + 3 spares)
  • Board and markers
  • Role cards (in the workbook Talk Time page; copy them onto index cards, optional)
  • Three signs for the room: AGREE, NOT SURE, DISAGREE (for Opinion Lines)
  • Listening: no recording yet. Read the listening script aloud (with a volunteer if you can), at a natural speed, two times.
  • Prep time: 15 minutes (read the plan; practice reading the listening script; put the three signs on the walls).

Key vocabulary (with pictures on the New Words page)

★ opinion • ★ agree • ★ disagree • ★ point (I see your point) • ★ community meeting • ★ empty lot • ★ community garden • ★ parking lot • ★ playground • ★ survey • ★ vote (raise your hand) • advantage / disadvantage

Also: a neighbor, a plan, a flyer, a newsletter, a parking space, a bench, a bus shelter, fair, take care of, a topic sentence.

Clock-time plan

Times are loose. If the listening or Talk Time runs long, take the time from Read & Write.

TimeStepMinGrouping (15 / 7–8)If running behind
6:00–6:08Opening Talk + Homework Check8Pairs (7 pairs + 1 trio / 3–4 pairs)One card only
6:08–6:15New Words (picture page) + pair game (+ My Words)7Whole class, then pairsTeach the ★ words only
6:15–6:30Listening: play 1 (Task A), play 2 (Tasks B and C) + "Hear it, say it"15Individuals, then pairs checkDo Task C together on the board
6:30–6:45Grammar Q&A: opinions; agree / disagree politely; as … as + pair check15Whole class, then pairsSkip the pair check; Talk Time practices it
6:45–7:00BREAK15
7:00–7:15Talk Time: Community Meeting + Opinion Lines15Groups of 4, then the whole roomRound 1 only
7:15–7:25Read & Write: A meeting flyer + two letters; an opinion paragraph10Pairs read, then individual writingReading questions only; the writing becomes homework
7:25–7:30Exit Ticket + Homework5IndividualsNever skip

Skip order if you're running behind: (1) the Read & Write writing task (it becomes homework); (2) the pair check at the end of Grammar; (3) the second round of Talk Time. Never skip: the listening tasks, the grammar boxes and the mistakes table, and the exit ticket.

Attendance (15 → 7–8 → 5 or fewer): every step lists the sizes. With 5 or fewer, do Community Meeting as one group; you take a role card. Do Opinion Lines with everyone. Late arrivals take a role card and join a group.

Step by step

Step 1 · 6:00–6:08 · Opening Talk · 8 min

  • Grouping: pairs, the same partner for both parts. 15 learners: 7 pairs + 1 group of 3. 7–8 learners: 3–4 pairs. 5 or fewer: pairs, or one group with you.
  • Before class: write on the board: might / may / could; Do you know where…?
  • Opening Talk (5 min): learners open the Opening Talk page. A asks a card question; B answers in 3 sentences (the answer, a reason, a detail); A asks one follow-up. Switch after each card.
  • Model with one learner: you say, "Do you know when the library opens?" The learner answers with a fact or I'm not sure. It might… Then you ask, "What might change in this city next year?" Help them say 3 sentences.
  • Homework Check (3 min): Pairs compare Homework item 1 (might and Do you know…?) and read their 3 changes (item 3) to each other. Then they fill in the box on the Opening Talk page. Walk around. Write 2 common errors on the board (often It might rains (→ It might rain) and Do you know where is the bank? (→ where the bank is)) and correct them together. Also put up 2 corrections from last week's exit tickets.
  • Late arrivals: join any pair as a group of 3.
  • If behind: one card only.

Step 2 · 6:08–6:15 · New Words · 7 min

  • Grouping: whole class, then pairs. Show the New Words page.
  • Do: point to each picture and say the word. Learners repeat once.
  • Show the hard words: opinion (what you think); agree (thumbs-up) and disagree (thumbs-down, with a smile); I see your point (I understand you); community meeting; empty lot (land with nothing on it); community garden, parking lot, playground; survey (questions for many people); vote (raise your hand); advantage (a plus) and disadvantage (a minus).
  • Check meaning (1 min): ask "Is an empty lot full or empty?" (empty) • "If you agree, do you say That's true or That's wrong?" (That's true) • "Is a survey for one person or many people?" (many people).
  • Pairs (2 min): A says a word; B points to the picture and makes a sentence (In my opinion, we need a playground.). Switch. 15 learners: finish with a quick team round (3 teams; you say a clue, the first team with the word gets a point). 7–8: 2 teams. 5 or fewer: one team against the clock.
  • My Words: "Write any word you want in your language on the My Words page. It's your personal list. It's optional." Learners do it at home.
  • If behind: teach the ★ words only.

Step 3 · 6:15–6:30 · Listening + "Hear it, say it" · 15 min

  • Grouping: individuals, then pairs check. With 5 or fewer, check together as a group.
  • Before you listen (2 min): say: "Neighbors are at a community meeting. Mrs. Okafor is the leader. Ray and Lin give their opinions about the empty lot on Cedar Street. Listen: what are they deciding?"
  • Play 1 → Task A (the main idea). Pairs compare. Check together.
  • Read Tasks B and C together (1 min) so learners know what to listen for.
  • Play 2 → Tasks B and C. Pairs compare. Then show the answers (answer key).
  • "Hear it, say it" (3 min): Point to the script lines. wanna = want to: "Tonight we want to talk about the empty lot." gonna = going to: "Who's going to take care of it?" Then practice I see your POINT, but… (the voice goes down on point, then a short pause) and the stress in It isn't as EXpensive. The class repeats the two lines twice.
  • No recording yet: read the script aloud with a volunteer (about 1:49), at a natural speed, two times. The script says going to and want to. People often say gonna and wanna; learners only need to recognize those words. When the audio is ready, it plays the conversation once; press play again for play 2. A third play is fine if the class needs it.
  • If behind: do Task C together on the board, reading the lines yourself.

Step 4 · 6:30–6:45 · Grammar Q&A · 15 min

  • Grouping: whole class, then pairs. Show the Grammar page. The left side is the question. The right side is the answer.
  • Show it (2 min): say, "In my opinion, summer is the best season." Ask a learner, "Do you agree?" Model two answers: a thumbs-up, "I agree. That's true," and a smile, "I see your point, but I like fall." Write: something positive first, then but. Then draw two prices: "A garden is $2,000. A parking lot is $20,000. A garden isn't as expensive as a parking lot."
  • The boxes (5 min): Box 1: read across: What do you think about the empty lot? → I think we need a playground. Box 2: agreeing and disagreeing politely. Box 3: as … as / not as … as. Box 4: the words in an opinion paragraph.
  • Rule of thumb and Questions and answers (2 min): read the rule of thumb aloud. Read each Q and A; the class reads the right sentence after you.
  • Check questions: "I am agree or I agree?" (I agree) • "Which is more polite: That's wrong or I see your point, but…?" (I see your point, but…) • "not as expensive as or not as expensive than?" (as … as).
  • Practice A and B (3 min): learners write, then pairs check. Go over the answers. Read the Common mistakes table together: "Don't say… Say…".
  • Pair check (last 3 min): A points to a picture and asks, "What do you think about a playground for the lot?" B gives an opinion and a reason. A agrees or disagrees politely. Switch. 15 learners: swap partners once. 5 or fewer: you join one pair.
  • If behind: skip the pair check. Talk Time practices it.

Break · 6:45–7:00 · 15 min

  • Write on the board: What do you think about…? → In my opinion… • I agree. / I see your point, but… • A garden isn't as expensive as a parking lot.

Step 5 · 7:00–7:15 · Talk Time: Community Meeting + Opinion Lines · 15 min

  • Model it first (1 min): take the parent role card. Say, "In my opinion, the lot should be a playground. First, kids need a safe place to play." Ask a learner with the store owner card, "Do you agree?" Help them say, "I see your point, but customers can't find parking." Say: "Polite language is the goal, not winning."
  • Round 1 (7 min): Community Meeting (groups of 4). Each person has a role card with a plan and 2 reasons. Each person gives an opinion; the others agree or disagree politely. The group chooses one plan and writes 3 reasons.
  • Round 2 (6 min): Opinion Lines (whole room). Read a statement. Learners stand by the AGREE, NOT SURE, or DISAGREE sign and explain. Someone on another side answers with I see your point, but…
  • 15 learners: 4 groups (one of 3) for round 1; then whole-room lines.
  • 7–8 learners: 2 groups for round 1; then lines.
  • 5 or fewer: one group for round 1: you take a role card. Then lines.
  • Every answer needs a reason; every partner asks a follow-up. Walk around and listen. Note 2 good sentences to praise and 1 common error for next week.
  • If behind: round 1 only.

Step 6 · 7:15–7:25 · Read & Write: A meeting flyer + two letters · 10 min

  • Grouping: pairs read and answer; individual writing. With 5 or fewer, read the text aloud together.
  • Read (4 min): Learners read the flyer and the two letters on the Read & Write page and answer the questions. Say: "Read fast first. Then find the answers." Pairs answer questions 1–5 together.
  • Check (1 min): go over the answers (answer key).
  • Write (5 min): Learners write an opinion paragraph (5–8 sentences) about the empty lot: a topic sentence, two reasons (First… Also…), an example, and a closing (That's why…). Show the example. Writing check 3: collect this paragraph and write one strength and one fix. Learners start in class and finish at home (Homework item 2).
  • If behind: questions 1–5 only; the writing becomes homework.

Step 7 · 7:25–7:30 · Exit Ticket + Homework · 5 min · NEVER SKIP

  • Exit ticket (3 min): learners open the Exit Ticket page and answer in 3 sentences with a reason: Which is better for an empty lot: a playground or a parking lot? Example on the board: In my opinion, a playground is better. Kids need a safe place to play because the park is far. I see the other point, but parking isn't as important as kids. With 5 or fewer, a learner can say it to you first and then write it.
  • Collect the pages. After class, sort them into ✓ / almost / not yet. Start next week with 2 corrections on the board (no names).
  • Homework (2 min): open the Homework page. Do item 1 together (item 1: playground / important / parking (as … as) → A playground is as important as parking.). Say: "About 15–20 minutes. Finish your Read & Write writing at home."

Listening script (not recorded yet; about 1:49 when recorded; the conversation plays once, so press play again for the second listen)

Audio: the recording is coming soon. Until then, read the script aloud two times, with a volunteer if you can, at a natural, friendly speed. The script says going to and want to. People often say gonna and wanna; learners only need to recognize those words.

Narrator: Lesson nine. Neighbors are at a community meeting. They are talking about the empty lot on Cedar Street.

Mrs. Okafor: Good evening, everyone. Thank you for coming. Tonight we want to talk about the empty lot on Cedar Street. The city says we can choose a plan. Ray, what do you think about it?

Ray: Thanks, Mrs. Okafor. In my opinion, we need a parking lot. There aren't enough parking spaces on our street. I drive around for twenty minutes every night.

Mrs. Okafor: That's true. Parking is a big problem. Lin, how do you feel about it?

Lin: I see your point, Ray, but I'm not sure I agree. I think a community garden is a better idea.

Ray: A garden? Why?

Lin: First, a garden isn't as expensive as a parking lot. Also, if we had a garden, families would grow vegetables, and kids would spend more time outside.

Ray: That's a good idea, but a garden is a lot of work. Who's going to take care of it?

Lin: I'd help, and I think many neighbors would help too.

Mrs. Okafor: Ray, do you agree with that?

Ray: Well, I agree that a garden is nice. But for me, parking is as important as a garden.

Mrs. Okafor: OK. Those are two good ideas. Let's do a survey. We'll ask every neighbor on Cedar Street.

Lin: I agree. That's fair.

Ray: Yes, that's a good plan. I'll help with the survey.

Mrs. Okafor: Great. We'll vote at the next meeting, on May twelfth. Thank you, everyone.

Narrator: That's the end of the listening.

Answer key

  • Listening Task A: a (what to do with the empty lot).
  • Listening Task B: 1 a parking lot, 2 aren't enough parking spaces, 3 a community garden, 4 isn't as expensive as, 5 take care of it, 6 do a survey.
  • Listening Task C: 1 opinion, 2 feel, 3 point, 4 idea, 5 agree, 6 fair.
  • Grammar Practice A: 1 agree, 2 as, 3 think, 4 point, 5 opinion, 6 had.
  • Grammar Practice B: 1 I agree, 2 as, 3 That's a good idea, but, 4 feel, 5 expensive, 6 would.
  • Talk Time: answers will vary.
  • Homework 1: 1 A playground is as important as parking. 2 A bus isn't as fast as a car. 3 What do you think about the new store? 4 I don't agree with you. Homework 2 and 3: answers will vary. Homework 4: 1 rain, 2 is, 3 will, 4 take, 5 leaves.
  • Read & Write B: 1 Thursday, May 12, at 7:00 p.m. • 2 A playground. • 3 Kids don't have a safe place to play. • 4 No. He sees her point, but he isn't sure he agrees. • 5 Two benches and a small garden. • Writing (C): answers will vary.
  • Exit ticket: answers will vary. A good answer: "In my opinion, a playground is better. Kids need a safe place to play because the park is far. I see the other point, but parking isn't as important as kids."

Teacher notes

  • Local and practical: topics stay with parks, parking, store hours, bus stops, and homework. No elections or political parties.
  • Praise polite language, not who "wins." Model disagreeing with a smile. Write good phrases you hear on the board.
  • I agree, not I am agree: this is very common. Point to the Q&A box and keep it on the board all evening.
  • Opinion Lines: learners who can't stand or move can hold up a sign or raise a hand from their seat.
  • Writing check 3 (Week 10): collect the opinion paragraph. Write one strength and one fix on each. Learners keep them in their writing folder.
  • Spanish and other languages: the contrast tip on the Grammar page is optional. Learners read it on their own. You never need to read, translate, or explain it.
  • Reductions: the listening says going to and want to. People often say gonna and wanna. Learners only need to recognize the short forms; they can always say the full forms.

sections.title: Grammar
sections.html:
Read across. A reads from the left side. B answers from the right side. Choose one part from each column.

Grammar Box 1: phrasal verbs + it / them

QUESTION
Can you turn offthe lights?
Can you turnthe TV down?
Can you take outthe trash?
→
ANSWER
OK, I'll turn them off.(not turn off them)
Sure, I'll turn it down.It's loud.
Yes, I'll take it outnow.

Grammar Box 2: the past

QUESTION
Did you take outthe trash?
Did you put awaythe dishes?
Did you shut offthe water?
→
ANSWER
Yes, I took it outthis morning.
No, I didn't put them awayyet.
Yes, I shut it offbefore I left.

Rule of thumb: With a noun, two places are OK: turn off the TV / turn the TV off. With it / them, only the middle: turn it off (not turn off it).

Grammar Box 3: 8 phrasal verbs for home

VERBMEANINGEXAMPLE
turn off / turn up / turn downstop / more / lessTurn off the lights. Turn the heat down at night.
put on / put awaywear / put in its placePut on a sweater. Put the dishes away.
take out / throw awaytake outside / put in the trashTake out the trash. Throw away old food.
shut offstop (water, gas)Shut off the water.

Grammar Box 4: home tips

STARTEXAMPLE
Make sure you…Make sure you lock the deadbolt at night.
Don't forget to…Don't forget to unplug the charger.
We use too much…We use too much electricity.

Questions and answers

Q: turn off it or turn it off?

A: turn it off. With it / them, the small word goes after: turn it off, put them away.

Q: Is turn off the TV OK?

A: Yes. With a noun, both are OK: turn off the TV and turn the TV off.

Q: turn down or turn off?

A: turn down = less. turn off = stop. Turn down the heat. Turn off the lights.

Practice A: Write one word.

  5. Make ____________ you lock the deadbolt.
  6. Don't ____________ to unplug the charger.

Practice B: Circle the correct words.

  1. Turn (it off / off it), please.
  2. Can you (throw away / throw on) the old milk?
  3. It's late. Please turn (down / up) the music.
  4. I (put them away / put away them) yesterday.
  5. Don't forget (to lock / lock) the door.
  6. We use too (much / many) water.

Common mistakes

✗ Don't say✓ Say
Turn off it.Turn it off.
I put away them.I put them away.
Close the light.Turn off the light.
Open the TV.Turn on the TV.
Don't forget lock the door.Don't forget to lock the door.

Contrast tip (optional): Many languages use one verb where English uses two words: Spanish apagar = turn off, bajar = turn down, tirar = throw away. With it / them, the small word goes after the pronoun: turn it off. How do you say these in your language?
