lessons.teacher:
How to Use This Plan

You don't need to speak Spanish or any other language. Teach in English. Show, point, and gesture. Some Grammar pages have one short contrast tip, only where a common mix-up exists. Learners read it on their own. You never need to read, translate, or explain it.

Instructions: use the same short task words every week: Listen. Circle. Check. Write. Work with a partner. Work in a group. Ask a follow-up question. Give a reason. An optional Task Words page is at the back of the workbook for learners who want it.

Instruction rule: Model it (do it with one learner while everyone watches), check it (ask: "How can you save energy and stay safe at home?"), then go. Say less, show more.

Grouping toolkit: Pairs: turn to a neighbor; with an odd number, make one group of 3. Groups: 3–4 learners. Inside–outside circles: the inner circle faces out, the outer circle faces in; the outer circle moves one person to the right each round. Mingle: everyone stands and talks to many classmates. The teacher joins a pair only if one learner is left over.

When a learner is stuck or speaks another language to you: (1) show it: the picture, a gesture, or the board; (2) give one more short English example; (3) point to the grammar box on their page; (4) a classmate can help for a few seconds, then back to English. You don't need to understand what classmates say to each other.

Three sentences, not one: in Level 4, every Talk Time answer and every exit ticket has about three connected sentences: the answer, a reason, and a detail or example.

Lesson 10 (Week 11): Turn It Off

At a glance

Objectives: learners can…

  • use phrasal verbs: turn off, turn down, turn up, put on, put away, take out, throw away, shut off
  • put it / them in the right place (turn it off, not turn off it)
  • give tips to save energy and stay safe at home (Make sure you… / Don't forget to…)
  • read the main parts of a utility bill (amount due, due date, usage)
  • write an email (5–8 sentences) to a roommate or family member about changes at home

Materials

  • Student Pages for Lesson 10 (print for the number expected + 3 spares)
  • Board and markers
  • A light switch, a lamp, or a phone charger to point to (optional)
  • Poster paper or the back of the Talk Time page for Home Tips
  • Listening: no recording yet. Read the listening script aloud (with a volunteer if you can), at a natural speed, two times.
  • Prep time: 15 minutes (read the plan; practice reading the listening script; find the light switch and an outlet in the classroom).

Key vocabulary (with pictures on the New Words page)

★ utility bill • ★ electricity • ★ thermostat • ★ save energy • ★ unplug • ★ charger • ★ outlet • ★ fan • ★ deadbolt • ★ peephole • ★ fire extinguisher • usage

Also: an account number, the amount due, a due date, a late fee, the heat, the air conditioner, a light bulb, plugged in, running water, a roommate.

Clock-time plan

Times are loose. If the listening or Talk Time runs long, take the time from Read & Write.

TimeStepMinGrouping (15 / 7–8)If running behind
6:00–6:08Opening Talk + Homework Check8Pairs (7 pairs + 1 trio / 3–4 pairs)One card only
6:08–6:15New Words (picture page) + pair game (+ My Words)7Whole class, then pairsTeach the ★ words only
6:15–6:30Listening: play 1 (Task A), play 2 (Tasks B and C) + "Hear it, say it"15Individuals, then pairs checkDo Task C together on the board
6:30–6:45Grammar Q&A: phrasal verbs + it / them + pair check15Whole class, then pairsSkip the pair check; Talk Time practices it
6:45–7:00BREAK15
7:00–7:15Talk Time: Energy Detective + Home Tips15Pairs, then groups of 3Round 1 only
7:15–7:25Read & Write: A utility bill + a flyer; an email10Pairs read, then individual writingReading questions only; the writing becomes homework
7:25–7:30Exit Ticket + Homework5IndividualsNever skip

Skip order if you're running behind: (1) the Read & Write writing task (it becomes homework); (2) the pair check at the end of Grammar; (3) the second round of Talk Time. Never skip: the listening tasks, the grammar boxes and the mistakes table, and the exit ticket.

Attendance (15 → 7–8 → 5 or fewer): every step lists the sizes. With 5 or fewer, do Energy Detective in pairs (you are a partner if needed), then make one Home Tips poster together. Late arrivals join a pair as the "checker" and then take a turn.

Step by step

Step 1 · 6:00–6:08 · Opening Talk · 8 min

  • Grouping: pairs, the same partner for both parts. 15 learners: 7 pairs + 1 group of 3. 7–8 learners: 3–4 pairs. 5 or fewer: pairs, or one group with you.
  • Before class: write on the board: opinions; agree / disagree politely; as … as
  • Opening Talk (5 min): learners open the Opening Talk page. A asks a card question; B answers in 3 sentences (the answer, a reason, a detail); A asks one follow-up. Switch after each card.
  • Model with one learner: you say, "What do you think about homework for kids?" The learner gives an opinion and a reason. Then you disagree politely: "I see your point, but…" Help them answer with 3 sentences.
  • Homework Check (3 min): Pairs compare Homework item 1 (as … as) and read their opinion and reasons (item 3) to each other. The partner agrees or disagrees politely. Then they fill in the box on the Opening Talk page. Walk around. Write 2 common errors on the board (often I am agree (→ I agree) and not as fast than (→ not as fast as)) and correct them together. Also put up 2 corrections from last week's exit tickets.
  • Late arrivals: join any pair as a group of 3.
  • If behind: one card only.

Step 2 · 6:08–6:15 · New Words · 7 min

  • Grouping: whole class, then pairs. Show the New Words page.
  • Do: point to each picture and say the word. Learners repeat once.
  • Show the hard words: utility bill (the bill for electricity, gas, or water); electricity; thermostat (it controls the heat); save energy (use less); unplug (take the plug out); charger; outlet (point to one in the room); fan; deadbolt (a strong lock); peephole (a small hole in the door to look out); fire extinguisher; usage (how much you use).
  • Check meaning (1 min): ask "Do you plug a charger into an outlet or a peephole?" (an outlet) • "Is a deadbolt a lock or a light?" (a lock) • "Does a thermostat control the heat or the water?" (the heat).
  • Pairs (2 min): A says a word; B points to the picture and makes a sentence (Make sure you unplug the charger.). Switch. 15 learners: finish with a quick team round (3 teams; you say a clue, the first team with the word gets a point). 7–8: 2 teams. 5 or fewer: one team against the clock.
  • My Words: "Write any word you want in your language on the My Words page. It's your personal list. It's optional." Learners do it at home.
  • If behind: teach the ★ words only.

Step 3 · 6:15–6:30 · Listening + "Hear it, say it" · 15 min

  • Grouping: individuals, then pairs check. With 5 or fewer, check together as a group.
  • Before you listen (2 min): say: "Two roommates, Sofia and Hana, look at a high electric bill and make a plan. Then Sofia calls the electric company. Listen: what is the problem?"
  • Play 1 → Task A (the main idea). Pairs compare. Check together.
  • Read Tasks B and C together (1 min) so learners know what to listen for.
  • Play 2 → Tasks B and C. Pairs compare. Then show the answers (answer key).
  • "Hear it, say it" (3 min): Point to the script line. gonna = going to: "I'm going to unplug my phone charger." Then practice the stress on the small word: turn it OFF, put it aWAY, and the linking: turn_it_off, take_it_out. The class repeats the two lines twice.
  • No recording yet: read the script aloud with a volunteer (about 2:07), at a natural speed, two times. The script says going to and want to. People often say gonna and wanna; learners only need to recognize those words. When the audio is ready, it plays the conversation once; press play again for play 2. A third play is fine if the class needs it.
  • If behind: do Task C together on the board, reading the lines yourself.

Step 4 · 6:30–6:45 · Grammar Q&A · 15 min

  • Grouping: whole class, then pairs. Show the Grammar page. The left side is the question. The right side is the answer.
  • Show it (2 min): point to the lights and say, "Can you turn off the lights?" A learner turns them off (or mimes it). You say, "Thank you. You turned them off." Turn them on again. Write: turn off the lights / turn the lights off → turn them off. Cross out turn off them.
  • The boxes (5 min): Box 1: read across: Can you turn off the lights? → OK, I'll turn them off. Box 2: the past: Did you take out the trash? → Yes, I took it out. Box 3: the 8 phrasal verbs. Box 4: Make sure you… / Don't forget to…
  • Rule of thumb and Questions and answers (2 min): read the rule of thumb aloud. Read each Q and A; the class reads the right sentence after you.
  • Check questions: "turn off it or turn it off?" (turn it off) • "Is turn the TV off OK?" (yes) • "It's too loud. Turn it up or turn it down?" (turn it down).
  • Practice A and B (3 min): learners write, then pairs check. Go over the answers. Read the Common mistakes table together: "Don't say… Say…".
  • Pair check (last 3 min): A points to a picture and says, "Can you unplug the charger?" B mimes and answers, "OK, I'll unplug it." A says, "Don't forget to lock the deadbolt." Switch. 15 learners: swap partners once. 5 or fewer: you join one pair.
  • If behind: skip the pair check. Talk Time practices it.

Break · 6:45–7:00 · 15 min

  • Write on the board: Can you turn off the lights? → OK, I'll turn them off. • Did you take out the trash? → Yes, I took it out. • Make sure you lock the deadbolt.

Step 5 · 7:00–7:15 · Talk Time: Energy Detective + Home Tips · 15 min

  • Model it first (1 min): read the first problem on the Apartment A card: "The lights are on in an empty room." Say to a learner, "Turn them off, please." The learner mimes and says, "OK, I'll turn them off." Do one more: "The window is open, and the heat is on." (Close it. Turn the heat down.)
  • Round 1 (7 min): Energy Detective (pairs). A reads a problem from the Apartment A card and gives an instruction (Turn them off. Close it. Put it away.). B mimes and answers with it / them. Then switch to the Apartment B card.
  • Round 2 (6 min): Home Tips (groups of 3). Groups write 5 tips to save energy or stay safe (Turn down the heat at night. Unplug the charger.) and present them in 1 minute.
  • 15 learners: pairs for round 1; then 5 groups of 3.
  • 7–8 learners: pairs; then 2 groups.
  • 5 or fewer: pairs; then one poster together.
  • Every answer needs a reason; every partner asks a follow-up. Walk around and listen. Note 2 good sentences to praise and 1 common error for next week.
  • If behind: round 1 only.

Step 6 · 7:15–7:25 · Read & Write: A utility bill + a "Save energy, stay safe" flyer · 10 min

  • Grouping: pairs read and answer; individual writing. With 5 or fewer, read the text aloud together.
  • Read (4 min): Learners read the invented bill and the flyer on the Read & Write page and answer the questions. Say: "Read fast first. Then find the answers." Pairs answer questions 1–5 together.
  • Check (1 min): go over the answers (answer key).
  • Write (5 min): Learners write an email (5–8 sentences) to a roommate or family member: what to change at home and why. Show the example. Check for 2 phrasal verbs and one it or them. Learners start in class and finish at home (Homework item 2).
  • If behind: questions 1–5 only; the writing becomes homework.

Step 7 · 7:25–7:30 · Exit Ticket + Homework · 5 min · NEVER SKIP

  • Exit ticket (3 min): learners open the Exit Ticket page and answer in 3 sentences with a reason: What can people do at home to save energy or stay safe? Example on the board: Turn off the lights when you leave a room. Unplug your charger and put it away. Make sure you lock the deadbolt at night, because it keeps your home safe. With 5 or fewer, a learner can say it to you first and then write it.
  • Collect the pages. After class, sort them into ✓ / almost / not yet. Start next week with 2 corrections on the board (no names).
  • Homework (2 min): open the Homework page. Do item 1 together (item 1: turn down / the heat (it) → Turn it down.). Say: "About 15–20 minutes. Finish your Read & Write writing at home."

Listening script (not recorded yet; about 2:07 when recorded; the conversation plays once, so press play again for the second listen)

Audio: the recording is coming soon. Until then, read the script aloud two times, with a volunteer if you can, at a natural, friendly speed. The script says going to and want to. People often say gonna and wanna; learners only need to recognize those words.

Narrator: Lesson ten. Two roommates, Sofia and Hana, look at their electric bill. Then Sofia calls the electric company.

Sofia: Hana, look at this. Our electric bill is one hundred and forty-two dollars this month!

Hana: What? Last month it was ninety dollars. Why is it so high?

Sofia: Well, we use too much electricity. The heat is on all day, and the lights are on in empty rooms.

Hana: You're right. I always forget to turn them off. Oh, the TV is on now, and nobody is watching. I'll turn it off.

Sofia: OK, let's make a plan. First, we can turn down the heat at night. Sixty-eight degrees is fine.

Hana: Good idea. And I'm going to unplug my phone charger in the morning. It uses electricity all day.

Sofia: Also, let's put on sweaters and not turn up the heat. Can you call the electric company? I have class.

Hana: Sorry, I have work. Can you call them tonight?

Sofia: Sure. I'll call them now.

Paul: Thank you for calling City Power. This is Paul. How can I help you?

Sofia: Hi. I'm calling about my bill. When is it due?

Paul: Can I have your account number, please?

Sofia: Yes. It's four, seven, two, one, nine.

Paul: Thank you. Your bill is due on March fifteenth.

Sofia: OK. Also, do you have any programs to help us save energy?

Paul: Yes. We have a free home energy check. Someone visits your apartment and gives you tips. And you can get free light bulbs.

Sofia: That sounds great. Can I sign up?

Paul: Sure. Is next Tuesday morning OK?

Sofia: Yes, that's perfect. Thank you.

Paul: You're welcome. And don't forget to turn off the lights when you leave a room!

Narrator: That's the end of the listening.

Answer key

  • Listening Task A: a (The electric bill is too high.).
  • Listening Task B: 1 $142, 2 down, 3 phone charger, 4 sweaters, 5 March 15, 6 free.
  • Listening Task C: 1 them, 2 it, 3 down, 4 on, 5 up, 6 off.
  • Grammar Practice A: 1 them, 2 up, 3 it, 4 on, 5 sure, 6 forget.
  • Grammar Practice B: 1 it off, 2 throw away, 3 down, 4 put them away, 5 to lock, 6 much.
  • Talk Time: answers will vary.
  • Homework 1: 1 Turn it down. 2 I took it out. 3 Put them away. 4 Make sure you lock the door. Homework 2 and 3: answers will vary. Homework 4: 1 agree, 2 as, 3 think, 4 point, 5 opinion.
  • Read & Write B: 1 $142.00. • 2 March 15. • 3 There is a $10 late fee. • 4 68 degrees. • 5 Look through the peephole. • Writing (C): answers will vary.
  • Exit ticket: answers will vary. A good answer: "Turn off the lights when you leave a room. Unplug your charger and put it away. Make sure you lock the deadbolt at night, because it keeps your home safe."

Teacher notes

  • Safety stays simple and calm: practical tips only, no fire stories. Point to where the classroom fire extinguisher is.
  • Bills are invented: never ask about learners' own bills, rent, or money.
  • Bill-help programs vary: list local ones on the "Keep practicing" sheet. Don't promise that a program exists in your area.
  • it / them in the middle: this is the main rule. Keep turn it off (not turn off it) on the board all evening.
  • Energy Detective: the problem cards replace a picture. Learners can also point to the My Words pictures.
  • Spanish and other languages: the contrast tip on the Grammar page is optional. Learners read it on their own. You never need to read, translate, or explain it.
  • Reductions: the listening says going to. People often say gonna. Learners only need to recognize it; they can always say the full form.

sections.title: Grammar
sections.html:
Read across. A reads from the left side. B answers from the right side. Choose one part from each column.

Grammar Box 1: to + verb answers Why?

QUESTION
Why are you takingtime off?
Why are you goingto Houston?
Why are youcalling?
→
ANSWER
To visitmy sister in Houston.
I'm going there to seemy family.
I'm calling to askabout my vacation days.

Grammar Box 2: verbs + to and verbs + -ing

QUESTION
What do you wantto do?
What do you enjoydoing on a trip?
What did you decideto do?
Do you minddriving?
→
ANSWER
I want to visitthe lake.
I enjoy takingpictures.
We decided to takethe bus.
No, I don't mind driving.It's fine.

Rule of thumb: There is no rule for which verbs take to and which take -ing: learn the two short lists in Box 3. to + verb also answers Why? (To visit my sister.)

Grammar Box 3: the two lists

+ to + verb+ -ing
want, need, plan, decideenjoy, don't mind
hope, forget, would likefinish, avoid, keep
I'm planning to leave on Friday.I enjoy traveling by bus.

Grammar Box 4: review

WORDSEXAMPLE
already / yetI've already packed. Have you packed yet?
Would you mind + -ing?Would you mind covering my shift?
going toI'm going to leave on Friday.

Questions and answers

Q: for see or to see?

A: Use to: I'm going to Houston to see my sister. (not for see, not for to see)

Q: enjoy to travel or enjoy traveling?

A: enjoy traveling. After enjoy, use -ing.

Q: How do I know: to or -ing?

A: Look at the two lists in Box 3. Learn them like vocabulary.

Practice A: Write one word.

  1. I'm taking a day off ____________ see the doctor.
  2. I enjoy ____________ by train. (travel)
  3. We decided ____________ stay for 3 days.
  4. Don't forget ____________ pack your charger.
  5. She doesn't mind ____________ on Saturday. (work)
  6. I've ____________ filled out the request form.

Practice B: Circle the correct words.

  1. I'm calling (to ask / for ask) about my vacation days.
  2. I want (to visit / visiting) my aunt.
  3. Did you finish (packing / to pack)?
  4. I hope (to see / seeing) you soon.
  5. Try to avoid (taking / to take) too many bags.
  6. Would you mind (covering / to cover) my shift?

Common mistakes

✗ Don't say✓ Say
I went to Houston for see my sister.I went to Houston to see my sister.
I enjoy to travel.I enjoy traveling.
I want visit my family.I want to visit my family.
I'm planning leave on Friday.I'm planning to leave on Friday.
Don't forget pack your toiletries.Don't forget to pack your toiletries.

Contrast tip (optional): Spanish uses para for purpose: Voy a Houston para ver a mi hermana. English uses only to: I'm going to Houston to see my sister (not for see, not for to see). After enjoy, use -ing: I enjoy traveling (not enjoy to travel). How do you say why in your language?

lessons.teacher:
How to Use This Plan

You don't need to speak Spanish or any other language. Teach in English. Show, point, and gesture. Some Grammar pages have one short contrast tip, only where a common mix-up exists. Learners read it on their own. You never need to read, translate, or explain it.

Instructions: use the same short task words every week: Listen. Circle. Check. Write. Work with a partner. Work in a group. Ask a follow-up question. Give a reason. An optional Task Words page is at the back of the workbook for learners who want it.

Instruction rule: Model it (do it with one learner while everyone watches), check it (ask: "Why do you need time off? What do you enjoy doing on a trip?"), then go. Say less, show more.

Grouping toolkit: Pairs: turn to a neighbor; with an odd number, make one group of 3. Groups: 3–4 learners. Inside–outside circles: the inner circle faces out, the outer circle faces in; the outer circle moves one person to the right each round. Mingle: everyone stands and talks to many classmates. The teacher joins a pair only if one learner is left over.

When a learner is stuck or speaks another language to you: (1) show it: the picture, a gesture, or the board; (2) give one more short English example; (3) point to the grammar box on their page; (4) a classmate can help for a few seconds, then back to English. You don't need to understand what classmates say to each other.

Three sentences, not one: in Level 4, every Talk Time answer and every exit ticket has about three connected sentences: the answer, a reason, and a detail or example.

Lesson 11 (Week 12): Time Off

At a glance

Objectives: learners can…

  • ask for time off and give a reason
  • say why with to + verb (I'm going to Houston to see my sister.)
  • use verbs + to (want, need, plan, decide, hope, forget, would like) and verbs + -ing (enjoy, don't mind, finish, avoid, keep)
  • leave a detailed voicemail and take voicemail notes
  • write an email (5–8 sentences) to a supervisor asking for time off

Materials

  • Student Pages for Lesson 11 (print for the number expected + 3 spares)
  • Board and markers
  • A phone or a toy phone for Voicemail Relay (optional)
  • A timer (a phone is fine)
  • Listening: no recording yet. Read the listening script aloud (with a volunteer if you can), at a natural speed, two times.
  • Prep time: 15 minutes (read the plan; practice reading the listening script; write the two verb lists on the board).

Key vocabulary (with pictures on the New Words page)

★ time off • ★ vacation days • ★ request form • ★ approve • ★ pack • ★ suitcase • ★ carry-on bag • ★ round-trip ticket • ★ boarding pass • ★ toiletries • ★ voicemail • itinerary

Also: a supervisor, a shift, cover (a shift), a coworker, a policy, ahead, deny, a callback number, a bus station, a surprise.

Clock-time plan

Times are loose. If the listening or Talk Time runs long, take the time from Read & Write.

TimeStepMinGrouping (15 / 7–8)If running behind
6:00–6:08Opening Talk + Homework Check8Pairs (7 pairs + 1 trio / 3–4 pairs)One card only
6:08–6:15New Words (picture page) + pair game (+ My Words)7Whole class, then pairsTeach the ★ words only
6:15–6:30Listening: play 1 (Task A), play 2 (Tasks B and C) + "Hear it, say it"15Individuals, then pairs checkDo Task C together on the board
6:30–6:45Grammar Q&A: to + verb (why); verbs + to / + -ing + pair check15Whole class, then pairsSkip the pair check; Talk Time practices it
6:45–7:00BREAK15
7:00–7:15Talk Time: Trip Planner + Voicemail Relay15Pairs, then back-to-back pairsRound 1 only
7:15–7:25Read & Write: A time-off policy + a packing list; an email10Pairs read, then individual writingReading questions only; the writing becomes homework
7:25–7:30Exit Ticket + Homework5IndividualsNever skip

Skip order if you're running behind: (1) the Read & Write writing task (it becomes homework); (2) the pair check at the end of Grammar; (3) the second round of Talk Time. Never skip: the listening tasks, the grammar boxes and the mistakes table, and the exit ticket.

Attendance (15 → 7–8 → 5 or fewer): every step lists the sizes. With 5 or fewer, do both rounds in pairs (you are a partner if needed) and check the voicemail notes yourself. Late arrivals join a pair for Trip Planner and leave a voicemail in round 2.

Step by step

Step 1 · 6:00–6:08 · Opening Talk · 8 min

  • Grouping: pairs, the same partner for both parts. 15 learners: 7 pairs + 1 group of 3. 7–8 learners: 3–4 pairs. 5 or fewer: pairs, or one group with you.
  • Before class: write on the board: phrasal verbs + it / them
  • Opening Talk (5 min): learners open the Opening Talk page. A asks a card question; B answers in 3 sentences (the answer, a reason, a detail); A asks one follow-up. Switch after each card.
  • Model with one learner: you say, "What do you turn off before you go to bed?" The learner answers with it / them (I turn the TV off. I turn it off at 10:00.). Then you ask, "What do you put on when it's cold?" Help them say 3 sentences.
  • Homework Check (3 min): Pairs compare Homework item 1 (it / them) and read their 3 home tips (item 3) to each other. Then they fill in the box on the Opening Talk page. Walk around. Write 2 common errors on the board (often turn off it (→ turn it off) and close the light (→ turn off the light)) and correct them together. Also put up 2 corrections from last week's exit tickets.
  • Late arrivals: join any pair as a group of 3.
  • If behind: one card only.

Step 2 · 6:08–6:15 · New Words · 7 min

  • Grouping: whole class, then pairs. Show the New Words page.
  • Do: point to each picture and say the word. Learners repeat once.
  • Show the hard words: time off (days you don't work); vacation days (paid days off); request form; approve (say yes); pack (put things in a bag); suitcase; carry-on bag (a small bag on the plane or bus); round-trip ticket (there and back); boarding pass; toiletries (toothbrush, soap); voicemail (a phone message); itinerary (the plan for a trip, with times).
  • Check meaning (1 min): ask "Does a supervisor approve or pack a request?" (approve) • "Is a round-trip ticket for one way or there and back?" (there and back) • "Is a toothbrush a toiletry or a boarding pass?" (a toiletry).
  • Pairs (2 min): A says a word; B points to the picture and makes a sentence (I need to pack my toiletries.). Switch. 15 learners: finish with a quick team round (3 teams; you say a clue, the first team with the word gets a point). 7–8: 2 teams. 5 or fewer: one team against the clock.
  • My Words: "Write any word you want in your language on the My Words page. It's your personal list. It's optional." Learners do it at home.
  • If behind: teach the ★ words only.

Step 3 · 6:15–6:30 · Listening + "Hear it, say it" · 15 min

  • Grouping: individuals, then pairs check. With 5 or fewer, check together as a group.
  • Before you listen (2 min): say: "Luis asks his supervisor, Ms. Adams, for time off. Then he leaves a voicemail for his sister, Rosa, and she calls back. Listen: why does he need time off?"
  • Play 1 → Task A (the main idea). Pairs compare. Check together.
  • Read Tasks B and C together (1 min) so learners know what to listen for.
  • Play 2 → Tasks B and C. Pairs compare. Then show the answers (answer key).
  • "Hear it, say it" (3 min): Point to the script lines. wanna = want to: "When do you want to take it?" gonna = going to: "I'm going to take the bus." Then practice the phone number in groups with pauses: 555 · 214 · 8830. The class repeats the two lines twice.
  • No recording yet: read the script aloud with a volunteer (about 1:53), at a natural speed, two times. The script says going to and want to. People often say gonna and wanna; learners only need to recognize those words. When the audio is ready, it plays the conversation once; press play again for play 2. A third play is fine if the class needs it.
  • If behind: do Task C together on the board, reading the lines yourself.

Step 4 · 6:30–6:45 · Grammar Q&A · 15 min

  • Grouping: whole class, then pairs. Show the Grammar page. The left side is the question. The right side is the answer.
  • Show it (2 min): say, "I'm going to the store." Ask, "Why?" Answer, "To buy milk." Write: Why? → To + verb. Then say, "I enjoy cooking. I want to cook for my family." Write two lists on the board: + to: want, need, plan, decide, hope, forget, would like; + -ing: enjoy, don't mind, finish, avoid, keep.
  • The boxes (5 min): Box 1: read across: Why are you taking time off? → To visit my sister. Box 2: verbs + to and verbs + -ing. Box 3: the two lists. Box 4: review (already, Would you mind…?, going to).
  • Rule of thumb and Questions and answers (2 min): read the rule of thumb aloud. Read each Q and A; the class reads the right sentence after you.
  • Check questions: "for see or to see?" (to see) • "enjoy to travel or enjoy traveling?" (enjoy traveling) • "want to visit or want visiting?" (want to visit).
  • Practice A and B (3 min): learners write, then pairs check. Go over the answers. Read the Common mistakes table together: "Don't say… Say…".
  • Pair check (last 3 min): A points to a picture and asks, "Why do you need a suitcase?" B answers with to + verb: "To pack my clothes." Then B asks, "What do you enjoy doing on a trip?" Switch. 15 learners: swap partners once. 5 or fewer: you join one pair.
  • If behind: skip the pair check. Talk Time practices it.

Break · 6:45–7:00 · 15 min

  • Write on the board: Why are you taking time off? → To visit my sister. • I want to go. I enjoy traveling. • I'm calling to ask about my vacation days.

Step 5 · 7:00–7:15 · Talk Time: Trip Planner + Voicemail Relay · 15 min

  • Model it first (1 min): read trip card A: "Visit family in another state for 4 days." Say, "I'm going to Dallas to visit my cousins. I want to see the new baby. I enjoy cooking with my aunt." Then model a voicemail: "Hi, it's Ms. Lee. I'm calling to tell you about my trip. I'm leaving on Friday. Call me back at 555 · 301 · 7720."
  • Round 1 (7 min): Trip Planner (pairs). Pairs choose a trip card. They plan why (to…), what they want to do and enjoy doing, and what to pack. Then they fill in the time-off request.
  • Round 2 (6 min): Voicemail Relay (back to back). A leaves a voicemail of 30–45 seconds: name, reason for calling (to…), dates, and an invented callback number. B takes notes and reads them back. Switch.
  • 15 learners: pairs; then back-to-back rows.
  • 7–8 learners: pairs; then one rotation.
  • 5 or fewer: pairs; you check the notes.
  • Every answer needs a reason; every partner asks a follow-up. Walk around and listen. Note 2 good sentences to praise and 1 common error for next week.
  • If behind: round 1 only.

Step 6 · 7:15–7:25 · Read & Write: A time-off policy + a packing list · 10 min

  • Grouping: pairs read and answer; individual writing. With 5 or fewer, read the text aloud together.
  • Read (4 min): Learners read the invented company policy and Luis's packing list on the Read & Write page and answer the questions. Say: "Read fast first. Then find the answers." Pairs answer questions 1–5 together.
  • Check (1 min): go over the answers (answer key).
  • Write (5 min): Learners write an email (5–8 sentences) to a supervisor asking for time off: the dates, the reason (to…), who can cover, and thanks. Show the example. Writing check 4: collect this email and write one strength and one fix. Learners start in class and finish at home (Homework item 2).
  • If behind: questions 1–5 only; the writing becomes homework.

Step 7 · 7:25–7:30 · Exit Ticket + Homework · 5 min · NEVER SKIP

  • Exit ticket (3 min): learners open the Exit Ticket page and answer in 3 sentences with a reason: Where would you like to go on a trip, and why? Example on the board: I would like to go to the beach to relax. I enjoy swimming in the ocean. It's also a good place for my family, because my kids love the water. With 5 or fewer, a learner can say it to you first and then write it.
  • Collect the pages. After class, sort them into ✓ / almost / not yet. Start next week with 2 corrections on the board (no names).
  • Homework (2 min): open the Homework page. Do item 1 together (item 1: I / enjoy / travel / by bus → I enjoy traveling by bus.). Say: "About 15–20 minutes. Finish your Read & Write writing at home."

Listening script (not recorded yet; about 1:53 when recorded; the conversation plays once, so press play again for the second listen)

Audio: the recording is coming soon. Until then, read the script aloud two times, with a volunteer if you can, at a natural, friendly speed. The script says going to and want to. People often say gonna and wanna; learners only need to recognize those words.

Narrator: Lesson eleven. Luis asks his supervisor for time off. Then he leaves a voicemail for his sister.

Luis: Ms. Adams, do you have a minute? I'd like to ask for some time off.

Ms. Adams: Sure, Luis. When do you want to take it?

Luis: Next month, from Thursday, June fifth, to Saturday, June seventh. That's three days.

Ms. Adams: And why are you taking time off?

Luis: To visit my mother in San Antonio. It's her seventieth birthday.

Ms. Adams: How nice! Did you fill out the request form?

Luis: Yes, I've already filled it out. Here it is.

Ms. Adams: Thanks. Who can cover your shifts?

Luis: Ana has agreed to cover Thursday and Friday. I'm still looking for someone for Saturday.

Ms. Adams: Ask Ben. He doesn't mind working on weekends. Then I can approve it.

Luis: Great. Thank you, Ms. Adams.

Luis: Hi, Rosa, it's Luis. I'm calling to tell you about my trip. I'm going to take the bus on Thursday, June fifth. It's bus number forty-two, and it gets to San Antonio at six thirty p.m. Can you pick me up at the bus station? Also, don't forget to bring Mom's birthday card. I want everyone to sign it. Call me back at five five five, two one four, eight eight three zero. Bye!

Rosa: Hi, Luis! I got your message. Yes, I can pick you up at six thirty.

Luis: Thanks, Rosa. Mom doesn't know I'm coming, right?

Rosa: No, it's a surprise. She's going to be so happy. I enjoy planning surprises!

Luis: Me too. See you on Thursday!

Narrator: That's the end of the listening.

Answer key

  • Listening Task A: a (to visit his mother).
  • Listening Task B: 1 5 to 7, 2 birthday, 3 Thursday and Friday, 4 Ben, 5 42, 6 6:30 p.m..
  • Listening Task C: 1 to, 2 working, 3 to, 4 to, 5 to, 6 planning.
  • Grammar Practice A: 1 to, 2 traveling, 3 to, 4 to, 5 working, 6 already.
  • Grammar Practice B: 1 to ask, 2 to visit, 3 packing, 4 to see, 5 taking, 6 covering.
  • Talk Time: answers will vary.
  • Homework 1: 1 I enjoy traveling by bus. 2 We're planning to leave on Friday. 3 I'm calling to ask about my vacation days. 4 Don't forget to pack your charger. Homework 2 and 3: answers will vary. Homework 4: 1 them, 2 it, 3 up, 4 sure, 5 to.
  • Read & Write B: 1 At least two weeks ahead. • 2 From your supervisor or in the break room. • 3 Within three days. • 4 5. • 5 A birthday card. • Writing (C): answers will vary.
  • Exit ticket: answers will vary. A good answer: "I would like to go to the beach to relax. I enjoy swimming in the ocean. It's also a good place for my family, because my kids love the water."

Teacher notes

  • Trips can be invented: don't assume learners can travel or have paid vacation days. A day trip in the city is always fine.
  • No passport, visa, or immigration topics. Keep trips to visiting family, a lake, or a city.
  • Time-off rules vary by employer: the policy is invented. Learners can check their own workplace rules.
  • Writing check 4 (Week 12): collect the time-off email. Write one strength and one fix on each. Learners keep them in their writing folder.
  • Phone numbers are invented and use 555. Practice saying them in groups with pauses (3-3-4).
  • Spanish and other languages: the contrast tip on the Grammar page is optional. Learners read it on their own. You never need to read, translate, or explain it.
  • Reductions: the listening says going to and want to. People often say gonna and wanna. Learners only need to recognize the short forms, and they never write them.

lessons.title: Is It a Scam?
lessons.function: Recognize a scam and say what to do
lessons.topic: Consumer protection, calm and practical: recognizing common scams by phone, text, and email (a fake prize, a fake bank text, a fake "pay your bill today" call, payment with gift cards) and what to do: stop, don't pay, check with the real company, and tell someone. Learners describe people and messages with who / that. All messages, names, and numbers are invented.

sections.title: Listening
sections.html:
A man calls Mrs. Lopez and says he is from the electric company. She must pay today with gift cards. She says no and hangs up. Then she tells her adult son, and they check her real account. No money is lost.

A. Listen. Was it a scam? Circle.

a. Yes, it was a scam. b. No, the bill was really late. c. We don't know.

B. Listen again. Which warning signs did you hear? Circle the answer.

  1. The caller said she must pay (today / next month).
  2. He wanted her to pay with (gift cards / a check).
  3. He said, "(Don't tell anyone. / Call your son.)"
  4. He said they would turn off her power in (one hour / one week).
  5. Mrs. Lopez (hung up / paid $200).
  6. Her real account is (fine / late).

C. Listen again. Write who or that.

  1. I'm going to call the number ____________ is on my real bill.
  2. The man ____________ called me knew my name.
  3. A company ____________ asks for gift cards is a scam.
  4. Scammers are people ____________ want your money.
  5. Be careful with texts ____________ ask for your password, too.
  6. never trust a caller ____________ tells you to hurry.

Hear it, say it

gonna = going to: "We're going to turn off your power." You can say going to. The word that is short and weak: a text that asks ("thut"). Stress the key words: NEVER, GIFT cards. Say No, thank you. Goodbye. in a calm, firm voice.

sections.title: Grammar
sections.html:
Read across. A reads from the left side. B answers from the right side. Choose one part from each column.

Grammar Box 1: describing with who / that

QUESTION
What'sa scam?
Whocalled you?
What'sa warning sign?
→
ANSWER
It's a trickthat takes your money.
A manwho said he was from the bank.
It's somethingthat tells you to be careful.

Grammar Box 2: what to do

QUESTION
What abouta text that wants my PIN?
What abouta caller who wants gift cards?
Whocan I trust?
→
ANSWER
Don't answer textsthat ask for your PIN.
Hang up on a callerwho asks for gift cards.
Call the companyat the number that is on your card.

Rule of thumb: who for people; that for things (and also people). The who / that part tells you which person or thing. Don't add he / it after it: a man who called (not a man who he called).

Grammar Box 3: anyone, something, must, should

WORDSEXAMPLE
Never… anyoneNever give your PIN to anyone.
If something…If something sounds too good to be true, it probably is.
mustn't / shouldYou mustn't share your password. You should tell someone you trust.

Grammar Box 4: 4 steps

STEPWHAT TO DO
Stop.Don't answer or click right away.
Don't pay.Never pay with gift cards.
Check.Call the number on your real bill or card.
Tell someone.Talk to a family member or friend you trust.

Questions and answers

Q: who or that?

A: who for people, that for things. that is OK for people too: a man who called / a text that came.

Q: a man who he called or a man who called?

A: a man who called. Don't add he or it after who / that.

Q: Are all calls and texts scams?

A: No. Most calls and texts are real. A few are scams. Stop, check, and ask.

Practice A: Write one word.

  1. A scam is a trick ____________ takes your money.
  2. Don't trust a caller ____________ asks for gift cards.
  3. Be careful with links ____________ look strange.
  4. Never give your PIN to ____________.
  5. If ____________ sounds too good to be true, it probably is.
  6. You ____________ share your password. (must / mustn't)

Practice B: Circle the correct words.

  1. I got a text (that / who) said I won a prize.
  2. The woman (who / what) called was from my bank.
  3. A man (who called / who he called) asked for my PIN.
  4. Don't click on links (that / who) look strange.
  5. You (should / shouldn't) tell someone you trust.
  6. (Hang up / Hang on) if the caller is pushy.

Common mistakes

✗ Don't say✓ Say
the man who he calledthe man who called
a text who saida text that said
Never give your PIN to nobody.Never give your PIN to anyone.
Don't trust a caller asks for money.Don't trust a caller who asks for money.
You must to call the bank.You must call the bank.

Contrast tip (optional): Spanish uses que for people and things: el hombre que llamó, el mensaje que llegó. English uses who (or that) for people and that for things: the man who called, the message that came. Many languages repeat the pronoun (the man who he called); English doesn't. What do you say in your language?

A. Read the notice. Read fast first. Then read again and answer the questions.

RIVERSIDE COMMUNITY OFFICE · A flyer + a sample text (invented)

SMART CONSUMER TIPS. Most calls, texts, and emails are real. But some are scams: tricks that take your money or your information. Here are 5 warning signs. 1. Someone says you must pay today, or something bad will happen. 2. A caller wants you to pay with gift cards. Real companies don't take gift cards for bills. 3. A message says you won a prize, but you must pay to get it. 4. A text has a strange link and asks for your password or PIN. 5. Someone tells you, "Don't tell anyone." What should you do? Stop: don't answer or click right away. Don't pay. Check: call the company at the number that is on your real bill or card. Tell someone you trust. You can also block the number.

SAMPLE TEXT (a scam). "ALERT! Your bank card is locked. Click the link and enter your PIN in 30 minutes, or you will lose your money."

B. Answer the questions.

  1. Are most calls and texts scams? ______________________________________________
  2. Do real companies take gift cards for bills? ______________________________________________
  3. What is the first step? ______________________________________________
  4. Which number should you call to check? ______________________________________________
  5. What are two warning signs in the sample text? ______________________________________________

C. Write a message (5–8 sentences) to a family member about a scam text. Use who or that and Don't….

Example: Hi Mom, I want to tell you about a scam. Some people get texts that say their bank card is locked. The texts ask for your PIN. Don't click on the link, and don't answer. If you aren't sure, call the number that is on your bank card. Also, never trust a caller who asks for gift cards. Love, Ana

My message

lessons.teacher:
How to Use This Plan

You don't need to speak Spanish or any other language. Teach in English. Show, point, and gesture. Some Grammar pages have one short contrast tip, only where a common mix-up exists. Learners read it on their own. You never need to read, translate, or explain it.

Instructions: use the same short task words every week: Listen. Circle. Check. Write. Work with a partner. Work in a group. Ask a follow-up question. Give a reason. An optional Task Words page is at the back of the workbook for learners who want it.

Instruction rule: Model it (do it with one learner while everyone watches), check it (ask: "Is it real or is it a scam? What should you do?"), then go. Say less, show more.

Grouping toolkit: Pairs: turn to a neighbor; with an odd number, make one group of 3. Groups: 3–4 learners. Inside–outside circles: the inner circle faces out, the outer circle faces in; the outer circle moves one person to the right each round. Mingle: everyone stands and talks to many classmates. The teacher joins a pair only if one learner is left over.

When a learner is stuck or speaks another language to you: (1) show it: the picture, a gesture, or the board; (2) give one more short English example; (3) point to the grammar box on their page; (4) a classmate can help for a few seconds, then back to English. You don't need to understand what classmates say to each other.

Three sentences, not one: in Level 4, every Talk Time answer and every exit ticket has about three connected sentences: the answer, a reason, and a detail or example.

Lesson 12 (Week 13): Is It a Scam?

At a glance

Objectives: learners can…

  • describe a person or a message with who / that (a caller who asks for gift cards)
  • name 4 warning signs of a scam
  • say what to do with a suspicious call or text (stop, don't pay, check, tell someone)
  • give a safe answer on the phone (I don't give information on the phone. Goodbye.)
  • write a message (5–8 sentences) to warn a family member about a scam

Materials

  • Student Pages for Lesson 12 (print for the number expected + 3 spares)
  • Board and markers
  • The 10 message cards on the Talk Time page (copy and cut them, optional)
  • A local consumer-help phone number for the "Keep practicing" sheet (check it locally)
  • Listening: no recording yet. Read the listening script aloud (with a volunteer if you can), at a natural speed, two times.
  • Prep time: 15 minutes (read the plan; practice reading the listening script; find and check a local consumer-help number).

Key vocabulary (with pictures on the New Words page)

★ scam • ★ warning sign • ★ suspicious • ★ fake • ★ official • ★ gift card • ★ prize • ★ link • ★ PIN • ★ hang up • ★ block (a number) • trust

Also: a trick, a caller, information, a password, an account, pushy, hurry, a package, a real bill, a consumer.

Clock-time plan

Times are loose. If the listening or Talk Time runs long, take the time from Read & Write.

TimeStepMinGrouping (15 / 7–8)If running behind
6:00–6:08Opening Talk + Homework Check8Pairs (7 pairs + 1 trio / 3–4 pairs)One card only
6:08–6:15New Words (picture page) + pair game (+ My Words)7Whole class, then pairsTeach the ★ words only
6:15–6:30Listening: play 1 (Task A), play 2 (Tasks B and C) + "Hear it, say it"15Individuals, then pairs checkDo Task C together on the board
6:30–6:45Grammar Q&A: who / that + pair check15Whole class, then pairsSkip the pair check; Talk Time practices it
6:45–7:00BREAK15
7:00–7:15Talk Time: Real or Scam? + Safe Answer15Pairs, then groups of 4, then pairsRound 1 only
7:15–7:25Read & Write: A consumer tips flyer + a sample text; a message10Pairs read, then individual writingReading questions only; the writing becomes homework
7:25–7:30Exit Ticket + Homework5IndividualsNever skip

Skip order if you're running behind: (1) the Read & Write writing task (it becomes homework); (2) the pair check at the end of Grammar; (3) the second round of Talk Time. Never skip: the listening tasks, the grammar boxes and the mistakes table, and the exit ticket.

Attendance (15 → 7–8 → 5 or fewer): every step lists the sizes. With 5 or fewer, sort the message cards together as one group, then do Safe Answer in pairs (you are the caller if needed). Late arrivals join the sort and take a caller card in round 2.

Step by step

Step 1 · 6:00–6:08 · Opening Talk · 8 min

  • Grouping: pairs, the same partner for both parts. 15 learners: 7 pairs + 1 group of 3. 7–8 learners: 3–4 pairs. 5 or fewer: pairs, or one group with you.
  • Before class: write on the board: to + verb (why); enjoy + -ing
  • Opening Talk (5 min): learners open the Opening Talk page. A asks a card question; B answers in 3 sentences (the answer, a reason, a detail); A asks one follow-up. Switch after each card.
  • Model with one learner: you say, "Where would you like to go on a trip?" The learner answers with to + verb (I'd like to go to Chicago to see the lake.). Then you ask, "What do you enjoy doing there?" Help them say 3 sentences.
  • Homework Check (3 min): Pairs compare Homework item 1 (to / -ing) and read their trip plan (item 3) to each other. Then they fill in the box on the Opening Talk page. Walk around. Write 2 common errors on the board (often for see (→ to see) and enjoy to travel (→ enjoy traveling)) and correct them together. Also put up 2 corrections from last week's exit tickets.
  • Late arrivals: join any pair as a group of 3.
  • If behind: one card only.

Step 2 · 6:08–6:15 · New Words · 7 min

  • Grouping: whole class, then pairs. Show the New Words page.
  • Do: point to each picture and say the word. Learners repeat once.
  • Show the hard words: scam (a trick that takes your money); warning sign (something that tells you to be careful); suspicious (strange, maybe not true); fake (not real); official (real, from the company); gift card; prize; link (you click it in a text or email); PIN (your secret number); hang up (end the call); block (a number); trust.
  • Check meaning (1 min): ask "Is a fake message real or not real?" (not real) • "Do you give your PIN to a caller or to nobody?" (nobody) • "When a call is suspicious, do you hang up or pay?" (hang up).
  • Pairs (2 min): A says a word; B points to the picture and makes a sentence (Never give your PIN to anyone.). Switch. 15 learners: finish with a quick team round (3 teams; you say a clue, the first team with the word gets a point). 7–8: 2 teams. 5 or fewer: one team against the clock.
  • My Words: "Write any word you want in your language on the My Words page. It's your personal list. It's optional." Learners do it at home.
  • If behind: teach the ★ words only.

Step 3 · 6:15–6:30 · Listening + "Hear it, say it" · 15 min

  • Grouping: individuals, then pairs check. With 5 or fewer, check together as a group.
  • Before you listen (2 min): say: "Mrs. Lopez gets a phone call from a man who says he's from the electric company. Later, she talks to her son, Daniel. Listen: was it a scam?"
  • Play 1 → Task A (the main idea). Pairs compare. Check together.
  • Read Tasks B and C together (1 min) so learners know what to listen for.
  • Play 2 → Tasks B and C. Pairs compare. Then show the answers (answer key).
  • "Hear it, say it" (3 min): Point to the script line. gonna = going to: "We're going to turn off your power." Then practice the weak that (it sounds like "thut"): a text that asks. Stress the key words: NEVER, GIFT cards. Practice a calm, firm voice: No, thank you. Goodbye. The class repeats the two lines twice.
  • No recording yet: read the script aloud with a volunteer (about 1:57), at a natural speed, two times. The script says going to and want to. People often say gonna and wanna; learners only need to recognize those words. When the audio is ready, it plays the conversation once; press play again for play 2. A third play is fine if the class needs it.
  • If behind: do Task C together on the board, reading the lines yourself.

Step 4 · 6:30–6:45 · Grammar Q&A · 15 min

  • Grouping: whole class, then pairs. Show the Grammar page. The left side is the question. The right side is the answer.
  • Show it (2 min): hold up your phone and say, "This morning I got a text. The text said I won a prize. → I got a text that said I won a prize." Then: "A man called. The man wanted my PIN. → A man who called wanted my PIN." Write: who = people, that = things (and people). Cross out a man who he called.
  • The boxes (5 min): Box 1: read across: What's a scam? → It's a trick that takes your money. Box 2: what to do: Hang up on a caller who asks for gift cards. Box 3: never… anyone, must / should. Box 4: the 4 steps.
  • Rule of thumb and Questions and answers (2 min): read the rule of thumb aloud. Read each Q and A; the class reads the right sentence after you.
  • Check questions: "who or that for a text?" (that) • "a man who he called or a man who called?" (a man who called) • "Are most calls scams?" (no, most are real).
  • Practice A and B (3 min): learners write, then pairs check. Go over the answers. Read the Common mistakes table together: "Don't say… Say…".
  • Pair check (last 3 min): A points to a picture and asks, "What's a gift card scam?" B answers with who / that: "It's a call that asks you to pay with gift cards." Switch. 15 learners: swap partners once. 5 or fewer: you join one pair.
  • If behind: skip the pair check. Talk Time practices it.

Break · 6:45–7:00 · 15 min

  • Write on the board: It's a trick that takes your money. • Don't trust a caller who asks for gift cards. • Stop. Don't pay. Check. Tell someone.

Step 5 · 7:00–7:15 · Talk Time: Real or Scam? + Safe Answer · 15 min

  • Model it first (1 min): read card 1: "Your package is late. Click this link and pay $2.99 today." Say, "I think it's probably a scam. It's a text that has a strange link, and it asks for money today." Then model a safe answer: a learner reads caller card 1, and you say calmly, "I don't give information on the phone. I'll call the number on my card. Goodbye."
  • Round 1 (7 min): Real or Scam? (pairs). Pairs sort the 10 invented message cards into probably real and probably a scam and explain with It's a text that… / It's from someone who… Then they compare with another pair.
  • Round 2 (6 min): Safe Answer (pairs). A is a caller with a pushy (but polite) card. B gives a safe answer. Switch.
  • 15 learners: pairs; then groups of 4 to compare; then pairs.
  • 7–8 learners: pairs; then one group to compare.
  • 5 or fewer: the whole group sorts together; then pairs.
  • Every answer needs a reason; every partner asks a follow-up. Walk around and listen. Note 2 good sentences to praise and 1 common error for next week.
  • If behind: round 1 only.

Step 6 · 7:15–7:25 · Read & Write: A consumer tips flyer + a sample scam text · 10 min

  • Grouping: pairs read and answer; individual writing. With 5 or fewer, read the text aloud together.
  • Read (4 min): Learners read the invented flyer and the sample text on the Read & Write page and answer the questions. Say: "Read fast first. Then find the answers." Pairs answer questions 1–5 together.
  • Check (1 min): go over the answers (answer key).
  • Write (5 min): Learners write a message (5–8 sentences) to a family member about a scam text, with that / who and Don't…. Show the example. Learners start in class and finish at home (Homework item 2).
  • If behind: questions 1–5 only; the writing becomes homework.

Step 7 · 7:25–7:30 · Exit Ticket + Homework · 5 min · NEVER SKIP

  • Exit ticket (3 min): learners open the Exit Ticket page and answer in 3 sentences with a reason: What is one warning sign of a scam, and what should you do? Example on the board: A caller who asks for gift cards is a warning sign. You should hang up and call the real company. Don't pay, because real companies don't take gift cards. With 5 or fewer, a learner can say it to you first and then write it.
  • Collect the pages. After class, sort them into ✓ / almost / not yet. Start next week with 2 corrections on the board (no names).
  • Homework (2 min): open the Homework page. Do item 1 together (item 1: don't trust / a caller / ask for gift cards (who) → Don't trust a caller who asks for gift cards.). Say: "About 15–20 minutes. Finish your Read & Write writing at home."

Listening script (not recorded yet; about 1:57 when recorded; the conversation plays once, so press play again for the second listen)

Audio: the recording is coming soon. Until then, read the script aloud two times, with a volunteer if you can, at a natural, friendly speed. The script says going to and want to. People often say gonna and wanna; learners only need to recognize those words.

Narrator: Lesson twelve. Mrs. Lopez gets a phone call. Later, she talks to her son, Daniel.

Caller: Hello, is this Mrs. Lopez? This is Mike from the electric company. Your bill is late. You must pay today, or we're going to turn off your power in one hour.

Mrs. Lopez: What? My bill is late? I paid it last week.

Caller: No, ma'am. You owe two hundred dollars. Go to the store and buy gift cards. Then call me back and read me the numbers.

Mrs. Lopez: Gift cards? That's strange.

Caller: Please hurry. This is your last chance. Don't tell anyone.

Mrs. Lopez: No, thank you. I'm going to call the number that is on my real bill. Goodbye.

Daniel: Hi, Mom. You look worried. What's wrong?

Mrs. Lopez: The man who called me knew my name. He said he was from the electric company. He wanted me to pay with gift cards.

Daniel: Gift cards? That's a warning sign. A company that asks for gift cards is a scam. What did you do?

Mrs. Lopez: I said no, and I hung up.

Daniel: Good! You did the right thing. Scammers are people who want your money. Did you give him any information?

Mrs. Lopez: No. I didn't tell him anything.

Daniel: Great. Let's check your account on the City Power website. OK, here it is. Your account is fine. You don't owe any money.

Mrs. Lopez: Oh, good. I'm glad I didn't pay.

Daniel: Me too. Next time, you can block the number. Be careful with texts that ask for your password, too. And never trust a caller who tells you to hurry.

Mrs. Lopez: You're right. Thanks, Daniel.

Narrator: That's the end of the listening.

Answer key

  • Listening Task A: a (Yes, it was a scam.).
  • Listening Task B: 1 today, 2 gift cards, 3 Don't tell anyone., 4 one hour, 5 hung up, 6 fine.
  • Listening Task C: 1 that, 2 who, 3 that, 4 who, 5 that, 6 who.
  • Grammar Practice A: 1 that, 2 who, 3 that, 4 anyone, 5 something, 6 mustn't.
  • Grammar Practice B: 1 that, 2 who, 3 who called, 4 that, 5 should, 6 Hang up.
  • Talk Time: answers will vary.
  • Homework 1: 1 Don't trust a caller who asks for gift cards. 2 Be careful with texts that ask for your password. 3 Never give your PIN to anyone. 4 A warning sign is something that tells you to be careful. Homework 2 and 3: answers will vary. Homework 4: 1 to, 2 traveling, 3 to, 4 to, 5 covering.
  • Read & Write B: 1 No. Most are real. • 2 No, they don't. • 3 Stop. Don't answer or click right away. • 4 The number on your real bill or card. • 5 It asks for your PIN, and it says you must hurry (30 minutes). • Writing (C): answers will vary.
  • Exit ticket: answers will vary. A good answer: "A caller who asks for gift cards is a warning sign. You should hang up and call the real company. Don't pay, because real companies don't take gift cards."

Teacher notes

  • Keep it calm and practical: "Most calls and texts are real. A few are scams. Stop, check, and ask." No scary stories.
  • Never ask learners whether they lost money or got a scam call. Learners can share if they want to.
  • All messages are invented, with no real numbers or links. List a local consumer-help line on the "Keep practicing" sheet (check it locally first).
  • Teacher-only: if a learner asks about "legal help" or "immigration help" services that ask for money, point only to local legal aid. Don't give advice yourself.
  • Listening: in the scope, a real utility agent confirms the account. To keep 3 speakers, Daniel checks the account on the company website instead. The message is the same: no money is lost.
  • Spanish and other languages: the contrast tip on the Grammar page is optional. Learners read it on their own. You never need to read, translate, or explain it.
  • Reductions: the listening says going to. People often say gonna. Learners only need to recognize it; they can always say the full form.

sections.html:
A former learner, Mariana, gives a short graduation talk about her learning: then, what was hard, now, and next. Her old teacher, Mr. Hill, asks her two questions.

A. Listen. What is Mariana's main message? Circle.

a. Come to class, and don't be afraid to make mistakes. b. Hotel jobs are easy. c. Level 5 is too hard.

B. Listen again. Her story in order: circle the answer.

  1. First, when she started, she couldn't understand the (bus driver / teacher).
  2. Then, in her first year, she worked at a (restaurant / hotel) at night.
  3. After Level 2, she got a job at a (hotel / clinic).
  4. Last year, she called the (clinic / school) by herself.
  5. Next, after Level 5, she's going to take a (training class / vacation).
  6. Her biggest challenge was (the phone / the bus).

C. Listen again. Write before, after, or when.

  1. ____________ I started English classes here, I couldn't understand the bus driver
  2. ____________ I finished Level 2, I got a new job at a hotel.
  3. ____________ I started that job, I practiced my interview with my teacher.
  4. ____________ I called someone, I couldn't understand them very well.
  5. ____________ I was tired, they supported me.
  6. ____________ class ended, we often studied together.

Hear it, say it

gonna = going to: "I'm going to take a training class." You can say going to. Listen for the short pause at the comma: When I started, (pause) I couldn't… Do the same in your talk. Stress the key words: NOW I can…, NEXT…

sections.title: Grammar
sections.html:
Read across. A reads from the left side. B answers from the right side. Choose one part from each column.

Grammar Box 1: before / after / when

QUESTION
What did you doafter you finished school?
How did you feelwhen you started this job?
What couldn't you dobefore this class?
What will you doafter you finish this class?
→
ANSWER
After I finished school,I worked in a store.
When I started this job,I didn't know anyone.
Before I started this class,I couldn't fill out a form.
After I finish this class,I'll take Level 5.

Grammar Box 2: couldn't / was able to; was …ing

QUESTION
Could youunderstand the bus driver?
Were you able tocall the clinic?
What were you doingwhen you met your friend?
→
ANSWER
No, I couldn't.Now I can.
Yes, I was able tocall by myself last month.
I was working at a restaurantwhen I met her.

Rule of thumb: before / after / when + a full sentence (I started, I finished). The time part can come first (with a comma) or second (no comma). For the future, use the present after when / after / before: After I finish this class, I'll take Level 5.

Grammar Box 3: the comma

TIME PART FIRST: commaTIME PART SECOND: no comma
When I started, I didn't know anyone.I didn't know anyone when I started.
After I finish this class, I'll take Level 5.I'll take Level 5 after I finish this class.

Grammar Box 4: the talk frame

PARTSAY
ThenWhen I started…, I couldn't…
What was hardIt was hard because… But I've…
NowNow I can… I'm more confident.
NextAfter I finish…, I'll… because…

Questions and answers

Q: When I will finish or When I finish?

A: When I finish this class, I'll take Level 5. Use the present after when / after / before, like after if.

Q: Do I need a comma?

A: Time part first: comma. After I finished school, I worked. Time part second: no comma. I worked after I finished school.

Q: couldn't or wasn't able to?

A: Both are OK: I couldn't drive. / I wasn't able to drive. For one success in the past, use was able to: I was able to call the clinic.

Practice A: Write one word.

  1. ____________ I started this job, I didn't know anyone.
  2. Before I came here, I ____________ speak English. (can't)
  3. After I finish this class, I ____________ take Level 5.
  4. Last month, I was ____________ to call the clinic by myself.
  5. I was ____________ at a store when I met my friend. (work)
  6. When I ____________ this class, I'll celebrate. (finish / will finish)

Practice B: Circle the correct words.

  1. When I (finish / will finish) the class, I'll look for a new job.
  2. (After I finished school, / After I finished school) I worked in a store.
  3. Before I started class, I (couldn't / can't) read the bus schedule.
  4. I (was able to / could to) fill out the form by myself.
  5. I used to (work / working) at night, but now I work days.
  6. I've (made / make) many friends in this class.

Common mistakes

✗ Don't say✓ Say
When I will finish, I'll call you.When I finish, I'll call you.
Before I came here I couldn't drive.Before I came here, I couldn't drive.
I could to fill out the form.I was able to fill out the form.
After finish class, I go home.After I finish class, I go home.
I was work when I met her.I was working when I met her.

Contrast tip (optional): Spanish uses a special verb form after cuando for the future: Cuando termine la clase, voy a celebrar. English uses the simple present: When I finish the class, I'm going to celebrate (not When I will finish). What do you say in your language?

3. Finish your graduation talk (12–15 sentences, about 2 minutes). Start with your email from Read & Write. Bring it next week.

PARTMy notes
Then (When I started…)
What was hard (It was hard because…)
Now (Now I can…)
Next (After I finish…, I'll…)

4. Review (Lesson 12). Write one word.

  1. A scam is a trick ____________ takes your money.
  2. Don't trust a caller ____________ asks for gift cards.
  3. Never give your PIN to ____________.
  4. You ____________ share your password. (must / mustn't)
  5. Be careful with texts ____________ ask for your PIN.

sections.title: Read & Write
sections.html:
A. Read the notice. Read fast first. Then read again. Underline the time words (when, before, after, now, last month). Answer the questions.

RIVERSIDE ADULT LEARNING · Class Newsletter (invented)

MY STORY SO FAR, by Tomás R. When I came to this city four years ago, I didn't know anyone. I couldn't read the bus schedule, and I was afraid to go to the doctor alone. I used to stay at home on weekends because everything was difficult.

Two years ago, my neighbor told me about the free English classes at the library. Before I started, I was very nervous. But on the first night, I met my teacher and three classmates who also worked at night. They became my friends.

The first year was a challenge. I was working at a warehouse, and I was always tired. After I finished my shift, I came to class. Sometimes I fell asleep! But I didn't stop.

Now I can do many things by myself. Last month, I was able to fill out a job application online, and I got an interview. I've made friends at work, and I'm more confident on the phone.

When I finish Level 4, I'm going to take a forklift training class. My advice? Come to class, even when you are tired. Small steps make a big change.

B. Answer the questions.

  1. When he came to the city, what couldn't he do? ______________________________________________
  2. How did he hear about the classes? ______________________________________________
  3. What did he do after his shift? ______________________________________________
  4. What was he able to do last month? ______________________________________________
  5. What will he do when he finishes Level 4? ______________________________________________

C. Write an email (5–8 sentences) to your teacher about your story so far: when you started, what was hard, what you can do now, and your next step, with a reason. Use when / before / after.

Example: Dear Mr. Hill, When I started this class in September, I couldn't understand the news on TV. The hardest part was the phone. After I practiced with my classmates, I felt more confident. Last week, I was able to call my child's school by myself. Now I can help my neighbors with forms. After I finish this class, I'll take Level 5, because I want a better job. Thank you for your help! Rosa

My email
